### 🛑 The pattern, which is what makes this worth an item

**Four of the five were closed by the item immediately following them.** 617 even says "Next item."
That is the mechanism: an item ends by naming what it leaves open, the next item closes exactly
that, and nothing goes back to amend the first. The record was accurate when written and wrong as a
whole — and the audit is APPEND-ONLY by design, so the only place that can carry a current status is
the index.

CLAUDE.md already says _"when a change refutes a lever or settles a question, add its line to
`CLOSED.md` in the same commit. A list that lags is the failure it exists to prevent."_ The habit
that was missing is narrower and worth stating: **when an item closes something a PREVIOUS item left
open, amend that previous entry too, not only append the new one.**

Cost of not doing it, measured: item 685 lost part of a tick re-deriving finished work off item 600's
header, and this tick nearly repeated it on 617's.

### Item 588's note is a different case, and the best thing in this sweep

588 kept a mutation SURVIVOR deliberately, writing that trail depth "is a RECORDED OPEN TARGET, so
the detector's bound will be relaxed, and this is then the only line between a trail and the walk's
arithmetic (32 against 28)". It also coined a category for it: _reachable-after-a-planned-change_,
beside provably-dead and reachability-unknown.

**That came true at 692, word for word.** The depth-4 form relaxed the detector's bound, left that
one at 3, and a depth-4 trail answered the walk count — 3 where the trail answers 0 on a triangle.
Item 690's oracle caught it on the first run.

A guard kept for a planned relaxation, a note addressed to whoever would land it, and a test able to
see the failure: all three were needed and all three fired. Annotated as fulfilled rather than left
as a forecast, with the note now addressed to whoever lands depth 5 — and with item 693's finding
that the Rust twin of that guard is a PERF gate rather than a correctness one, because declining
there returns `None` and the caller enumerates.

## 697 — the sorted-hop target re-prices to 2.26x (was 3.9x), its blocker is NOT what 605 said, and I retracted a reading mid-tick

**RE-MEASUREMENT. No engine change.** Item 696's mechanical pass left a short list of genuinely-open
targets; this prices the largest.

### The target survives at about half its recorded size

200,000 vertices / 600,000 edges, min of 5, all in ONE process:

|                                    | ms        | rows    |
| ---------------------------------- | --------- | ------- |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) RETURN b.k` | 60.2      | 600,000 |
| `… ORDER BY k`                     | **136.2** | 600,000 |
| `… ORDER BY k LIMIT 5`             | 135.2     | 5       |
| `… ORDER BY uniq LIMIT 5`          | 124.2     | 5       |

**2.26x**, against the 173.0/44.5 = 3.9x items 603-605 recorded. The target is real and smaller.
A `LIMIT 5` saves nothing (135.2 against 136.2): all 600,000 rows are sorted to emit five.

### 🛑 The blocker is not the one item 605 named — that check was built at 610

Item 605 recorded this as waiting on _"item 426's conservative cannot-fault check"_. **That check
exists.** `ordered-rows.ts` says so in its own header: _"WHY THIS EXISTS (item 610). It is the
'conservative cannot-fault check on the projection' item 426 deferred."_

And the NODE path behaves accordingly — windows ride the sorted rung, flat across every size:

| node path                     | ms                        |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `RETURN a.k`                  | 14.3                      |
| `ORDER BY k`                  | 17.2                      |
| `LIMIT 1 / 5 / 1000 / 200000` | 17.0 / 17.3 / 17.1 / 18.1 |
| `OFFSET 0`                    | 17.1                      |

So only the HOP half is open, and its blocker is the one constraint 605 listed SECOND:
`farDrivenHopWalk` must keep the sort off itself or establish that its arrival order is
unobservable. With a STABLE sort, tie order is arrival order, so a different walk order changes
which tied rows a `LIMIT` keeps — and both engines have to agree, which makes it a cross-engine
question rather than a local one.

**This is a stale marker found by reading CODE, not the index.** Item 696 tooled the index check and
this one was still invisible to it: the marker named a dependency, item 610 satisfied it, and
nothing connected the two. `open-markers.ts` pairs a marker with the next ITEM; it cannot know that
a check named in prose got built nine items later.

### 🛑 And a reading of my own, retracted inside the tick

An intermediate run had the node path at `ORDER BY k` 18.3 ms and `ORDER BY k LIMIT 5` **26.0 ms**,
and I was about to write up "adding a LIMIT costs 1.42x while returning 5 rows instead of 200,000",
which would have been a clean-looking anomaly.

It was a **POSITION PENALTY**. Those queries ran last in that run's list and `LIMIT 5` ran first
among them. Re-running with the window sweep in one process put every variant at 17.0-18.1 ms.

This is the exact effect `spelling-probe.ts` documents — _"SWAPPING the two made the penalty follow
the POSITION, not the spelling"_, which cost audit items 180 and 181 a 1.5-2.1x phantom. The probe
answers it by timing every member in both positions and keeping the better reading; a one-off probe
has no such protection, so **the first number out of a fresh list is the one to distrust.**

### What a fix would have to establish

Not "is the sort safe" — 610 settled that. It is: does `farDrivenHopWalk`'s arrival order differ
observably from the general path's, and if so can both engines be made to agree on it? Until that is
answered the route must keep declining, because the alternative is a byte-identity divergence in tie
order under a `LIMIT`.

**REFUTED (degree 1) / RE-PRICED to 1.58x (degree 3). No engine change.**

| source     | figure                                   | what it compared                                                   |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 604/605    | **3.9x**                                 | 173.0 against a 44.5 ms unordered reference, degree 1              |
| 697 (mine) | 2.26x                                    | 136.2 against 60.2 — **degree 3**, against 604's degree-1 baseline |
| **698**    | **0.86x at degree 1, 1.58x at degree 3** | against the engine's own FLOOR                                     |

### On item 604's own fixture there is nothing left

200,000 vertices at **degree 1**, both-position timing, rows realised and counted:

|                                              | ms       |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| engine, unordered (200,000 rows)             | 38.3     |
| a bare sort of the engine's OWN rows         | 10.0     |
| **the honest floor = unordered + that sort** | **48.3** |
| engine, `ORDER BY k`                         | **41.8** |

**0.86x of the floor** — the engine sorts _more cheaply than materialising and sorting separately_.
Item 604's own framing asked for exactly this reference: _"the honest bound is 173.0 → ~(44.5 + a
sort or a top-k)"_. Measured against it, the target is gone, and item 605's marker is corrected.

### At degree 3 a real gap remains, at 1.58x

|                                  | ms        |
| -------------------------------- | --------- |
| engine, unordered (600,000 rows) | 58.9      |
| a bare sort of its own rows      | 26.5      |
| **floor**                        | **85.4**  |
| engine, `ORDER BY k`             | **135.0** |

**1.58x** — against 2.94x if the unordered query is used as the reference. The unordered reference
OVERSTATES the gap because sorting genuinely costs something, which is items 659/660's whole lesson
("a floor built from the obvious algorithm can sit above the engine and then proves nothing"; the
right floor is the engine's own algorithm). Here the right floor shrank the target by ~1.9x and
refuted it entirely at degree 1.

### 🛑 Item 697's error: I matched the fixture to the SUBJECT and not to the BASELINE

Item 697 measured at degree 3 and compared against 604's degree-1 numbers, concluding "the 3.9x does
not survive". Both halves were wrong: the comparison was unmatched, and the target is weaker still
than the 2.26x it reported.

CLAUDE.md's rule is _"match the fixture to the claim"_, and I applied it to the thing I was measuring
while inheriting the denominator from a six-year-old table without checking its shape. **A recorded
baseline carries a fixture, and quoting the number without the fixture is the same error as quoting
a ratio without its control.** The degree matters enormously here: the unordered reference is
~38-59 ms at both degrees (it is dominated by the 200,000-source scan) while the SORT scales with
rows, so the ratio moves from 1.11x to 2.54x on degree alone.

Also corrected: 697 reported `LIMIT 5` saving nothing (135.2 against 136.2). With both-position
timing they separate — 132.5 against 153.2 at degree 3, so the window does save ~14%.

A 1.58x gap above the floor on a 600,000-row sorted hop projection. That is a real number on a real
shape, and it is small enough that the arrival-order work item 605 contemplated — a cross-engine
tie-order question — is not obviously worth its risk. **Recorded at its true size rather than
carried forward at 3.9x.**

## 699 — depth 2 was slower than depth 3: route it to the level recurrence, 1.53-1.85x

**SHIPPED (TypeScript).** Found by a full bench sweep rather than the index — three ticks of
index archaeology had yielded corrections, not targets.

### The anomaly the sweep showed

`count var-length 1-2 hops` read **213.3 ms** against native's 4.5 (47.9x) — and **slower than the
deeper `{3}` trail at 170.5 ms**. Reproduced on an own fixture (50,000 vertices, degree 3):

| query | ms      | paths         |
| ----- | ------- | ------------- |
| `{2}` | 15.4    | 449,998       |
| `{3}` | **9.2** | **1,349,976** |

Depth 3 is faster while counting 3x the paths. The cause is the dispatch: `takesTheLevelRecurrence`
is `max >= 3`, so depth 3 runs the level recurrence over a flat CSR of typed arrays — _"after this
no level consults a Map at all, which is the whole point"_ — while depth 2 runs the older
`max <= 2` arithmetic over the Map-based adjacency. Same algebra, worse representation.

### The alternated A/B, with a control the change cannot reach

For `max === 3` the dispatch predicate's value is unchanged, so `{3}`/`{1,3}` are controls. Three
rounds each, rebuilding the dist between every round:

| row             | BEFORE | AFTER | ratio     | answers |
| --------------- | ------ | ----- | --------- | ------- |
| `{2}`           | 13.9   | 9.1   | **1.53x** | SAME    |
| `{1,2}`         | 15.9   | 8.6   | **1.85x** | SAME    |
| `{3}` CONTROL   | 9.4    | 9.3   | 1.01x     | SAME    |
| `{1,3}` CONTROL | 9.8    | 9.8   | 1.00x     | SAME    |

**A single cross-process pair had said the control moved 9.2 → 11.1**, which would have
disqualified the change. Under alternation it is 1.01x. That is the third time in four ticks a
cross-process reading has been wrong in a way alternation fixed.

### 🛑 Lowering the bound alone answers the WALK count

The first attempt changed only `max >= 3` to `max >= 2`. It gave the speedup **and the wrong
answers**: `{2}` read 450,000 where the trail is 449,998 — the walk count — because `trailCorr` was
`trail3 || trail4` and the level-2 correction never ran.

That is item 692's mistake exactly, one engine over and one depth down. **It was caught by the
ANSWERS, not by any timing**, because the probe prints them beside the times — item 600's rule
(_"Pointing a WALK recurrence at a TRAIL answers 2,500,000 for 2,499,936 — a wrong answer no timing
would reveal. Print the answers beside the times."_). A probe that printed only milliseconds would
have shown a clean 1.5x win on a wrong result.

`trail2` is now wired, and the correction it needs was already present in `trailCorrectionAt`'s
`len === 2` branch — the one the old route applied.

### Mutation 3/4

Caught: the depth-2 correction dropped (answers the walk count), `trailCorr` forgetting `trail2`,
and the level-2 term ignoring the endpoint mask. The survivor — reverting the dispatch bound to 3 —
is **answer-equivalent and labelled so in advance**: it is the pre-699 route, correct and 1.5-1.9x
slower. [[perf-gate-needs-its-own-test]]: a route choice cannot be caught by a differential test,
and the guard here is the alternated A/B.

Item 690's brute-force oracle covers `{2}`, `{1,2}` and `{2,3}` directly, which is why this change
had a correctness check waiting for it rather than needing one written.

### The other engine does NOT have this problem

From the same sweep: native's `count var-length 1-2 hops` is **4.5 ms** against its
`count 3-hop quantified` at 16.1 — the opposite ordering. Its `max <= 2` closed form is already
the cheaper route, so there is nothing to move. ("Grep the pattern elsewhere", answered from data
already in hand.)

2,945 TS tests pass, all seven byte-identity fuzzers pass, lint and check 0.

## 700 — the canonical `ORDER BY … LIMIT k` reaches NO top-k, and the one that does is the shape you would not guess

**DIAGNOSED (TypeScript), not fixed. No engine change.** Item 699's rule — read a sweep for
orderings that are impossible on their face — applied to the next row.

### The impossible ordering

| row                                | ts       | ffi     | ts/ffi    |
| ---------------------------------- | -------- | ------- | --------- |
| ordered projection **[no window]** | 20.7     | 28.1    | **0.74x** |
| ordered projection **+ limit**     | **21.4** | **1.0** | 21.70x    |

TS is FASTER than native without the window and 21.7x slower with it. Adding a `LIMIT` cannot cost
more than not adding one.

### The floor, from the engine's own scan-and-keep

`min(n.age)` is top-1 over the same column by the same route family, so it is the floor items
659/660 ask for. 200,000 vertices, both positions:

| query                                  | ms                        | rows    |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ------- |
| `min(n.age)` — **the floor**           | **4.6**                   | 1       |
| project all, unordered                 | 8.1                       | 200,000 |
| `ORDER BY a` (full sort)               | 17.9                      | 200,000 |
| `ORDER BY a LIMIT 1 / 5 / 100 / 50000` | 18.7 / 17.0 / 16.8 / 17.7 | —       |

**Flat at every k.** A bounded selection would make `LIMIT 5` land near the 4.6 ms floor.

### 🛑 Two top-k implementations exist. Instrumentation says which runs, and it is not what reading suggested.

`boundedTopK` is a careful O(n log cap) heap with its own doc, two call sites in `applyProjection`,
and a REJECTED-optimization note carrying numbers (item 424's parallel-arrays experiment, 2.4%,
under the floor). **It fired zero times for any query above** — verified by a counter, and verified
that the counter reached `dist`, because a null result from instrumentation is otherwise
indistinguishable from a build that did not take.

That is not the finding it looks like. An EARLIER branch holds a specialised single-key heap
(parallel `bs`/`ks`/`ix` arrays with their own siftUp/siftDown, sorting a permutation of only the
survivors), which supersedes the generic one. Reading the code without instrumenting would have
produced "the top-k is unreachable"; reading it after instrumenting gives the real shape.

**And that specialised heap fires for exactly ONE of eight shapes:**

| query                                            | reaches a top-k?           |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------- |
| `RETURN n.age AS a ORDER BY a LIMIT 5`           | **no**                     |
| `… LIMIT 1` / `LIMIT 100` / `LIMIT 50000`        | **no**                     |
| `… ORDER BY a DESC LIMIT 5`                      | **no**                     |
| `RETURN n.age AS a ORDER BY n.age LIMIT 5`       | **no**                     |
| `… ORDER BY a SKIP 2 LIMIT 5`                    | **no**                     |
| **`RETURN n.name AS nm ORDER BY n.age LIMIT 5`** | **YES** (cap=5, n=200,000) |

The one that reaches it is the one whose sort key is an input property **not among the projected
columns**. Every spelling where the sort key is also projected — the common case, and the cheaper
one, since the value is already computed — sorts all 200,000 rows.

### A hypothesis refuted on the way

I predicted the discriminator was the ALIAS: `ORDER BY a` (output column) versus `ORDER BY n.age`
(input property), since `executor.ts:3045` says an alias spelling "forces `orderNeedsOutput` and
gives up the top-k". Measured: 17.3 against 17.0 — **both spellings miss the top-k equally**, so
the alias is not the gate. The gate is whether the sort key is projected at all.

### What a fix has to respect

Not a new algorithm — both heaps exist. The work is widening the gate, and the constraint is the
one `ordered-rows.ts` and item 604 exist for: the general path keeps top-k INPUT bindings and
projects only survivors, so a route that projects every row then selects can RAISE where the query
does not. `cannotFault` (item 610) is the licence, and it is already written.

Item 424 measured this family at "50.1 ms against the `max(a.u)` fold's 20.7 over the same rows,
and it is NOT allocation" — consistent with the 17.0-against-4.6 here, and now explained: the gap
is not allocation because **the bounded selection is not running at all.**

## 701 — item 700's missing top-k was in a DIFFERENT module: the shortcut full-sorts, 2.9-6.4x

**FIXED (TypeScript).** Item 700 instrumented `applyProjection` and found its bounded heap firing
zero times for `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN n.age AS a ORDER BY a LIMIT 5`. The reason is not a gate
inside that function at all: **the query never reaches it.** `detectNodeProjection` takes the shape
first, and that route sorted every row and sliced.

That is why item 700's alias hypothesis measured flat. Both spellings miss the heap because
neither one gets near it — `aliasDefinition` would have rewritten `ORDER BY a` to `ORDER BY n.age`
and cleared `orderNeedsOutput` anyway. **Instrumenting one function tells you it did not run; it
does not tell you what ran instead.** Finding that cost a second tick and the fix took one edit.

### The change

`sortRowsByColumns` (`ordered-rows.ts`) selects instead of sorting when the window is small:

```ts
if (limit !== undefined && (skip + limit) * 16 <= rows.length) {
  return boundedTopRows(rows, sorts, skip + limit).slice(skip);
}
```

`boundedTopRows` is a max-heap of ROW INDICES, capped at `skip + limit`. Indices rather than rows
because the index is also the tiebreak: `rows` arrives in arrival order here, so `x < y` IS the
arrival comparison, where the `applyProjection` heap has to carry an index alongside because it
evicts from a permuted array. `compareSort` stays the one comparator.

**Why a tiebreak at all.** `Array.prototype.sort` is stable, so the full sort this replaces broke
ties by arrival order, and tie order is observable between the engines (item 605). Appending
`x < y` makes the heap's order a TOTAL order that agrees with the sliced full sort row for row —
which is what the hashes below check.

### The alternated A/B, with four controls the change cannot reach

200,000 vertices, 50 distinct ages over them (deliberately tie-heavy) and 2% null ages. Min of 7
per arm, three alternated rounds, rebuilding the dist between every arm. The hash is over EVERY
row, not a head — the fixture ties so densely that a wrong tie order would be invisible in the
first four rows (item 600's rule, strengthened).

| row                       | BEFORE | AFTER | ratio     | rows+hash |
| ------------------------- | ------ | ----- | --------- | --------- |
| `LIMIT 1`                 | 41.6   | 14.2  | **2.93x** | SAME      |
| `LIMIT 5`                 | 41.5   | 14.1  | **2.94x** | SAME      |
| `LIMIT 100`               | 38.8   | 12.3  | **3.15x** | SAME      |
| `LIMIT 1000`              | 37.0   | 11.6  | **3.19x** | SAME      |
| `LIMIT 2500`              | 37.4   | 13.8  | **2.71x** | SAME      |
| `LIMIT 5000`              | 37.3   | 18.6  | **2.01x** | SAME      |
| `LIMIT 10000`             | 37.5   | 25.5  | **1.47x** | SAME      |
| `ORDER BY a DESC LIMIT 5` | 38.5   | 11.6  | **3.32x** | SAME      |
| `SKIP 2 LIMIT 5`          | 38.3   | 10.5  | **3.65x** | SAME      |
| two sort keys, `LIMIT 5`  | 77.7   | 12.2  | **6.37x** | SAME      |
| the bench row, `LIMIT 5`  | 37.1   | 9.4   | **3.95x** | SAME      |
| `LIMIT 20000` CONTROL     | 37.4   | 36.6  | 1.02x     | SAME      |
| `LIMIT 50000` CONTROL     | 37.1   | 37.5  | 0.99x     | SAME      |
| no window CONTROL         | 38.6   | 37.0  | 1.04x     | SAME      |
| unordered CONTROL         | 7.1    | 7.2   | 0.99x     | SAME      |
| `min(n.age)` CONTROL      | 4.6    | 4.9   | 0.94x     | SAME      |

### The `* 16` is a measured crossover, and a looser bound was BUILT and rejected

The heap is O(n log cap) against the sort's O(n log n), so it stops paying as `cap` approaches
`n`. The first version used `* 8` and the same sweep caught it: `LIMIT 20000` read **0.95x** — a
real regression, inside the bound, that only a cap sweep would have found. The sweep puts the
crossover at about `n/10` (20,000 of 200,000 reads 0.99x either way), so the bound admits to
`n/16`, which is inside the win at 1.47x. `LIMIT 20000` and `LIMIT 50000` are now controls, and
they are flat.

### Mutation: 7 caught, 1 survivor labelled SURVIVE in advance

Against `ordered-rows-topk.test.ts`, the one file whose claim this change makes, each mutant
applied to a pristine copy and the tree restored BEFORE the next one, all under
`timeout 300 systemd-run -p MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`.

Caught: the tiebreak dropped from `less`; the candidate test inverted; the heap keeping `cap + 1`;
`siftDown` ignoring the right child; `siftUp` stopping at the first parent; the one-key path
forgetting `descending`; the survivors not re-sorted. The survivor is the gate widened to `* 1`,
which is a ROUTE CHOICE and answer-equivalent by construction — no differential test can catch
one (item 611), and its guard is the cap sweep above.

**The test's fixture is the test.** The bounded branch needs `(skip + limit) * 16 <= rows.length`,
so a case over a handful of rows exercises the full sort no matter what it asserts — the fixture
mistake this repo has now made six times, where the subject is unreachable from the fixture. Every
case keeps 320 rows against a window of at most 10, and each asserts that bound explicitly so the
guard cannot rot into vacuity.

### The sweep, and the impossible ordering closed

| row                                | before | after   | ffi |
| ---------------------------------- | ------ | ------- | --- |
| ordered projection **+ limit**     | 21.4   | **8.9** | 1.0 |
| top-k by property                  | 15.6   | **8.9** | 1.0 |
| ordered projection **[no window]** | 20.7   | 16.1    |     |

Adding a `LIMIT` is now cheaper than omitting it, which is the ordering item 700 flagged as
impossible. The ts/ffi ratio on the windowed row goes 21.70x to 8.85x. The no-window row moving
20.7 to 16.1 is cross-process variance, not this change — it is a control in the table above and
reads 1.04x under alternation, which is the measurement that counts.

**The native engine does not have this gap** and nothing moved there: it was already 1.0 ms on
both windowed rows, which is what made the TS row readable as impossible in the first place.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run check` 0
(typecheck+lint+fmt:check); `bun run test` — all 21 projects pass; all seven byte-identity fuzzers
pass, which this change needs rather than merely survives, because row order under `ORDER BY` is
cross-engine observable.

## 702 — RETRACTED: the "14x chain-count gap" was my own fixture, and the answer could not reveal it

**RETRACTED (TypeScript). No engine change.** I read the sweep for another impossible ordering and
found one: `count 3-hop` — the explicit chain `(a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b)-[:KNOWS]->(c)-[:KNOWS]->(d)`
— at **318 ms**, worse than `count var-length 1-3 hops [WALK]` at 145, which counts strictly MORE
paths, and worse than the `{3}` TRAIL at 154, which has to subtract repeats. A chain is a walk, so
the cheapest spelling of the three was the most expensive.

Then I built a fixture and measured the chain at **23.0 ms** for the same 25,000,000 paths. A 14x
discrepancy against the bench. That looked like the find of the week. It was my fixture.

### The chain of checks, and where each one failed to catch it

| check                                   | result                          |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| answers agree across spellings          | yes — 25,000,000 everywhere     |
| answers agree across fixtures           | yes — 25,000,000 everywhere     |
| graph built by `addEdge` vs NDJSON load | no difference (338 vs 321)      |
| which route fires (INSTRUMENTED)        | the SAME one, all four fixtures |
| **distinct edge targets in my fixture** | **14,378 of 200,000**           |

Only the last one is the fixture. My LCG is `(s * 1103515245 + 12345) & 0x7fffffff` in **f64**:
`s * 1103515245` for `s` near 2^31 is about 2^61, past the 2^53 where a double stops being exact,
so the low bits are fabricated and the period collapses from 2^31 to **11,154 / 14,469 / 16,403
draws** (seeds 1 / 7 / 12345). Over 1,000,000 edges that is ~70 trips round a short cycle: 93% of
vertices end with IN-DEGREE ZERO, and `buildThreeHopCount`'s `if (waysToA === 0) continue` skips
93% of its outer loop. Not a faster route — 93% less graph.

### Why the answer could not reveal it, which is the part worth keeping

The count is **invariant to the in-degree distribution**. With out-degree regular at 5,

    walk3 = Σ over middle edges (b→c) of indeg(b) · outdeg(c) = 5 · Σ_b indeg(b) · 5 = 25 · |E|

so concentrating every edge on 7% of the vertices gives **exactly 25,000,000**, the same as a
uniform fixture. Printing answers beside times — item 600's rule, which caught the real bug at 699
and again at 692 — is blind here by construction.

**The rule this adds: an answer that is INVARIANT to the property you varied cannot validate the
fixture.** Check the fixture's own statistics instead. Here, one line (count the distinct targets)
would have refuted the target before any of the four experiments above.

Twice in this session a fixture has had to be checked rather than its output: item 698 (a degree-3
claim judged against a degree-1 baseline) and now this.

### Confirming the degenerate generator is NOT in the repo

Two repo files use the same expression, so the obvious worry is that the trail brute-force oracle
(items 690-693, 699 all lean on it) has been generating far fewer distinct graphs than believed.
**It has not.** The oracle draws a few hundred values per graph over 60 graphs — far inside even
the 11,154-draw period — and `floor(r * 6)` / `floor(r * 8)` were measured to cover every residue.
`PropertyIndex.test.ts` is the same shape. The Rust harness (`examples/support/harness.rs`) is
`u64::wrapping_mul(6_364_136_223_846_793_005)`, which is exact. And `bench.ts` uses arithmetic
strides (`(k * 7919) % N`), not an RNG — which is why the bench fixture is the honest one.

So: fine at test scale, measured, and fatal at fixture scale, measured. Nothing in the repo needs
fixing, which is worth recording so a later pass does not re-raise it.

### What the row actually is

Already priced. **Item 310** measured this same row at 401.6 ms against native's 4.8 and diagnosed
it: not one hash per edge, but the `edgesOfTypes` generator frame, the `Edge` property reads and
two hash lookups spread across it — "the CSR item 300 recorded as needing a dense adjacency the TS
graph does not expose". Its memoization lever was rejected there with numbers (1.063x target
against a 1.052x control that could not reach the change). **Item 489** records the row as a CSR
ceiling. The ordering against the quantified spellings is real but it is not a missing fast path:
the chain pays O(E) with a heavy per-edge constant while the quantifier's closed form pays O(E)
with a light one.

`count 3-hop` is therefore CLOSED as a quick win and open only behind the dense-adjacency work.
I should have reached item 310 before building a fixture rather than after — the sweep row named
the target and `CLOSED.md` had already answered it.

## 703 — the CSV encoder's per-element allocations: 1.10x, and the remaining 1.9x is now priced against pg-text

**FIXED (native), with the rest of the gap diagnosed.** This tick's target came from the Rust side
on purpose — 699-702 were all TypeScript. Two candidates were REFUTED by reading before measuring,
which is the lesson 702 just paid for:

- `query: project 3 columns` (native 44.3 ms against TS's 8.4, the worst native ratio on the
  sweep) is **CLOSED at item 289** — it is the JSON carrier, not execution, and ~80% of it is
  `JSON.parse` on a 4.5 MB result.
- `encode csv`'s own deferred fix — "CSV is the only format left on `to_graph_data`" (item 100) —
  **has already landed.** `serialize_csv` streams, with
  `streaming_csv_encode_is_byte_identical_to_the_graphdata_path` pinning it.

What is left is the row still being the worst native codec per byte.

### The floor is the sibling encoder, not a guess

`serialize_pg_text` is the same FLAT two-pass shape over the same store, and on this fixture it
emits 28.95 MB against CSV's 32.66 — so it is the floor items 659/660 ask for, built from the
engine's own algorithm rather than the first comparison to hand:

| native encoder | ms, min of 5 |    MB | MB/ms     |
| -------------- | -----------: | ----: | --------- |
| **csv**        |    **514.0** | 32.66 | **0.064** |
| pg-text        |        237.6 | 28.95 | 0.122     |
| pg-json        |        260.9 | 113.3 | 0.434     |
| graphson       |        472.7 | 223.7 | 0.473     |

### What landed: three allocations per element that the streaming rewrite left behind

`serialize_csv` no longer builds a `Vec<CNode>`, but it still allocated per element:

- `node_vals` / `edge_vals` held `(String, CValue)` — a **cloned property key per (element,
  property)**, 1,200,000 of them on this fixture, when `node_keys` outlives the whole function and
  a `&str` borrow does.
- the row loops **collected a fresh `Vec<(&str, &CValue)>` per row**, now one reused buffer.
- the edge external id was `edge_ext_id(..).map(|x| x.to_string())` — **a String per edge, 1,000,000
  of them**, allocated only to be lent back as a `&str`. `edge_ext_id_ref` already existed and
  returns `Option<&str>`; `serialize_pg_text` next door already used it.

### The alternated A/B, with four controls the change cannot reach

Four separate encoders, none of which goes through `serialize_csv`. Min of 5 per arm, three
alternated rounds, rebuilding the `.so` with `--features capi` between every arm. The change is
1.10x, which is UNDER the 10% CLAUDE.md wants an isolated harness for, so alternation is the gate
rather than a courtesy.

| format           | BEFORE | AFTER | ratio     | bytes |
| ---------------- | -----: | ----: | --------- | ----- |
| **csv**          |  500.3 | 455.4 | **1.10x** | SAME  |
| pg-json CONTROL  |  262.5 | 271.7 | 0.97x     | SAME  |
| graphson CONTROL |  394.1 | 388.2 | 1.02x     | SAME  |
| ndjson CONTROL   |  278.1 | 282.1 | 0.99x     | SAME  |
| pg-text CONTROL  |  223.4 | 227.5 | 0.98x     | SAME  |

Byte length identical on every format, which is the invariant that matters here.

### Mutation 4/4, against the one test whose claim this is

`streaming_csv_encode_is_byte_identical_to_the_graphdata_path`. Caught: the node row buffer never
cleared; the edge row buffer never cleared; the edge external id borrowed from the wrong edge; the
node keys borrowed in the wrong order. Reusing a buffer is exactly the change that fails by
LEAKING the previous row, so "never cleared" is the mutant that had to be run, and it is caught.

### The remaining 1.9x, priced and left with its blocker written down

`node_vals` / `edge_vals` are still **a `Vec` per element** — 1,200,000 small allocations held at
once — and that is the whole of the gap to pg-text, which holds `Vec<(&str, &Column)>` ONCE and
reads `col.present_at` / `col.read` per element, allocating nothing per row.

CSV cannot simply copy it: it needs the COLUMN pass before it can write a header, so values are
read twice or cached once. **Caching in two reused buffers does not borrow-check** — a
`Vec<(&str, &CValue)>` keeps the value buffer borrowed for as long as the row vector lives, so it
cannot be cleared for the next row. The two ways out are to re-read the store on the row pass (two
column reads per property, no allocation) or to give `CsvColumns::writer` an interface taking keys
and values as two slices. Neither is measured; the 455-against-227 above is what it is worth. Noted
in the code at the `node_vals` it would change, per the repo's rule for deferred levers.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` 1215 + 13 +
725 pass, 0 fail; all seven byte-identity fuzzers pass — required rather than merely survived,
since a codec change is exactly what the TS/Rust byte-identity invariant is for.

## 704 — REJECTED: removing 1,200,000 allocations from the CSV encoder is worth 1.02x, and the control says so

**BUILT, MEASURED, REVERTED (native). No net change beyond a corrected comment.** Item 703 ended
by naming its own next lever and pricing it: the `Vec` PER ELEMENT in `serialize_csv`, 1,200,000
small allocations held at once on the bench fixture, asserted to be "the whole of the gap" to
`serialize_pg_text` (225 ms against CSV's 452 for a nearly identical 29 MB of flat text). This tick
built exactly that and the prediction is refuted.

### What was built

The row pass RE-READS the store instead of caching, so nothing per element is retained — and
neither is the 1,000,000-triple edge-id vector, since the edge walk runs twice rather than
collecting. Two reused buffers (`Vec<&str>` plus `Vec<CValue>`) replaced the per-element `Vec`.

That needed a new codec entry point, because the obvious version does not compile: a
`Vec<(&str, &CValue)>` keeps the value buffer borrowed for as long as the row vector lives, so it
can never be cleared for the next row. `CsvWriter` therefore grew `node_row_split` /
`edge_row_split` taking parallel key/value slices, behind a `RowProps` trait with two impls — one
row writer, two property shapes, so the cell layout stays single-sourced.

It worked and it was byte-identical: `streaming_csv_encode_is_byte_identical_to_the_graphdata_path`
and `streaming_csv_decode_matches_the_graphdata_path` both pass.

### The alternated A/B, and why the control is the whole answer

Min of 5 per arm, three alternated rounds, both files swapped together and the `.so` rebuilt with
`--features capi` between every arm.

| format           | BEFORE | AFTER | ratio     | bytes |
| ---------------- | -----: | ----: | --------- | ----- |
| **csv**          |  460.4 | 452.0 | **1.02x** | SAME  |
| pg-json CONTROL  |  267.1 | 261.9 | 1.02x     | SAME  |
| graphson CONTROL |  394.5 | 390.5 | 1.01x     | SAME  |
| ndjson CONTROL   |  302.2 | 311.3 | 0.97x     | SAME  |
| pg-text CONTROL  |  230.1 | 224.8 | 1.02x     | SAME  |

**The target moved exactly as far as four encoders the change cannot reach.** That is item 310's
rule applied to my own work — "the control moved as far as the target, so the memo is worth 1.01x
at most" — and it is the reason a 1.02x reading is not a small win but a null one.

### A measurement I am not claiming

I tried to justify keeping the change on MEMORY instead, since the reverted arm retains nothing
per element. Both arms read a peak RSS of 34,424.8 MB, identical to a tenth of a megabyte and far
larger than this process can plausibly use — my harness resolved the wrong cgroup and read the
user slice rather than the scope. **That is a broken instrument, not a result**, so there is no
memory claim here either way, and the change reverts on the timing alone.

### What this rules out, which is worth more than the lever was

Two allocation-removal passes over the same encoder now bracket the question:

| 703  | ~2,200,000          | **1.10x** |
| 704  | 1,200,000 more      | **1.00x** |

So **the remaining 2x against pg-text is not allocation.** The unexamined candidates are per-CELL,
and reading `csv.rs` for this item turned up two: `write_row` resolves each column with

The second one is allocation again and this tick's result predicts it will not matter; the first is

Recorded in the code at the `node_vals` it would have changed, per the repo's rule for rejected

### Mutation found a test gap in the formula-injection guard — 3 survived, then 3 caught

Both arms of a `Cow` are a risk, so both got a mutant. All three **SURVIVED** the whole lenke-codec
suite: the guard never applied, the guard applied to every field, and half its condition dropped.

The diagnosis, not the tally: **a round trip cannot test this guard, because `unguard_field` is the
exact inverse of `guard_field`.** Encode-then-decode is symmetric under all three mutations, so it
passes. `quoting_labels_and_formulas` covers the same rule for property VALUES and LABELS, and
nothing covered `id` / `:START_ID` / `:END_ID`. The engine's
`streaming_csv_encode_is_byte_identical_to_the_graphdata_path` cannot help either — it compares two
implementations that SHARE the cell layer, so a change in the shared layer moves both sides
identically. This repo's own rule, one layer down: _two gates covering one shape means neither is
testable through it._

That is not a cosmetic gap. `guard_field` exists so that an id beginning with `=` does not become a
live formula when the CSV is opened in a spreadsheet, and nothing was checking it.

`an_id_that_reads_as_a_formula_is_guarded_in_the_text` asserts the EMITTED BYTES for `=cmd`,
`\back` and `+e`, asserts the other arm (a plain id stays bare), and keeps the round trip as a
third claim. With it, **the same three mutants are all caught (exit 101)** — survived before,
caught after, which is the only demonstration of teeth worth having.

- **the field quote scan is 4% at identical bytes** (36.47 both) — pure per-field overhead;
- **`bag.get` is 3%**, the difference between "no property cells" and "no cell value write", both
  of which emit 31.53 MiB. That is the linear scan over a row's properties for every column, and it
  is 3% only because this fixture has ONE property per element. It is `O(columns × properties)`, so
  a wide-property graph pays proportionally more — a scaling risk recorded rather than a lever.

The remaining ~174 ms writes 25.6 MiB of ID CELLS, four fixed fields per edge row. That is the
format, not a defect.

## 707 — the label join was allocating four times a row: 1.21x, and the ablation predicted it

**FIXED (native).** Item 706 priced the label stage at 18% of the encode, which is where this went.

`join_labels` allocated four times per row for the commonest shape there is — a single label:
`escape_element` calls `str::replace` TWICE, and `replace` allocates unconditionally whether or not
there is anything to replace; then `collect::<Vec<_>>()`; then `join`. ~4,800,000 allocations per
encode on the bench fixture. One label holding no `\`, no `;` and no leading formula char is
returned borrowed, which is byte-identical by construction: `escape_element` returns such input
unchanged, `guard_element` returns it unchanged, and joining one element is that element.

### The alternated A/B

Three alternated rounds, min-of-7, in-process; the four other formats are controls that cannot
reach `csv.rs`.

| format           | BEFORE |  AFTER | ratio     | MiB  |
| ---------------- | -----: | -----: | --------- | ---- |
| **csv**          | 298.82 | 246.90 | **1.21x** | SAME |
| ndjson CONTROL   | 134.48 | 134.20 | 1.00x     | SAME |
| pg-json CONTROL  | 123.06 | 123.62 | 1.00x     | SAME |
| pg-text CONTROL  | 125.46 | 123.78 | 1.01x     | SAME |
| graphson CONTROL | 158.00 | 156.16 | 1.01x     | SAME |

17% of the total, against the ablation's 18% for the stage — the prediction and the result agree,
which is the first time in this cluster that has happened.

**This corrects item 704's generalization, which was too broad.** I wrote "the remaining 2x is not
allocation" after removing 1,200,000 ENGINE-side allocations for nothing. The accurate statement is
narrower: a `Vec` per element in the engine's bridge was not the cost, while the CODEC's per-row
allocations were — 705's 3.2M for 4% and now 707's 4.8M for 21%. The difference is that these sit
inside the per-row loop that runs 1,200,000 times with nothing else to hide behind.

Cumulative over the four items: **csv 514 ms to 247 on the in-process harness, 2.08x.** CSV is now
0.148 MiB/ms against pg-text's 0.268, so the per-byte gap is 1.8x rather than 2.2x.

### Mutation: 2 of 4 survived, then all 4 caught

A fast path is only correct where its condition is, so every clause got a mutant. **The backslash
clause and the formula clause both SURVIVED the whole crate.** The reason is the fixture rule, one
turn of the screw from item 705: every existing fixture with a label needing escape work carries
TWO labels, which takes the other branch — `quoting_labels_and_formulas` has
`["has;semi", "Plain"]`, so it pins the semicolon clause and nothing else. **A case where the fast
path is not taken cannot test the fast path's condition.**

`a_lone_label_is_still_escaped_and_guarded` asserts the emitted text for a lone `a\b` (doubled) and
a lone `=form` (prefixed), with the round trip as a third claim — a round trip alone passes under
both mutants, which is exactly what item 705 found for the id guard. With it, **all four mutants
are caught (exit 101)**.

That is the second untested escaping path this encoder has yielded in two items, both found by
mutation and neither by any failure. The pattern in both: the escaping rules are covered for the
MULTI-element spelling and were never covered for the single-element one.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0;
`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0 both crates; `cargo test --release` 1215 + 13 + 725
(engine) and 34 (codec) pass, 0 fail; all seven byte-identity fuzzers pass.

## 708 — the same label-join allocation in the TypeScript codec: 1.11x, and its tests already had teeth

**FIXED (TypeScript).** "Grep the pattern elsewhere" is a step in the method and this is what it is
for: the TS CSV encoder has the identical shape item 707 just fixed in Rust.

```ts
const joinLabels = (labels: Iterable<string>): string =>
  [...labels].map((l) => guardElement(escapeElement(l))).join(LIST_SEP);
```

Five allocations per row for the commonest shape there is — the spread, the `map` array, two
`replaceAll` (which allocate whether or not there is anything to replace), and the `join` — over
1,200,000 rows. The single-label case is now returned directly, and an ARRAY skips the spread as
well.

**The condition is the Rust twin's character for character.** These two encoders are byte-identical
by invariant, so a fast path admitted on one side and not the other is precisely how that invariant
would break; the comment says so at both sites, and the codec fuzzer is the check.

### The alternated A/B, and the reading I am actually claiming

Three alternated rounds, min-of-7 per arm, rebuilding the dist between every arm (`@lenke/*`
resolve to dist, so a source edit is invisible to the probe until it does). Controls are four
separate TS encoders, none of which goes through `csv/index.ts`.

| format           | BEFORE |  AFTER | ratio     | MiB  |
| ---------------- | -----: | -----: | --------- | ---- |
| **csv**          | 550.23 | 494.62 | **1.11x** | SAME |
| ndjson CONTROL   | 386.78 | 366.75 | 1.05x     | SAME |
| pg-json CONTROL  | 289.81 | 291.91 | 0.99x     | SAME |
| pg-text CONTROL  | 371.03 | 380.63 | 0.97x     | SAME |
| graphson CONTROL | 545.75 | 547.75 | 1.00x     | SAME |

The control spread is ±5% (`ndjson` moved 1.05x off one low reading), so 1.11x alone would be a
weak claim. **The stronger one is the rank separation:** csv's three AFTER values (494.62, 503.39,
497.74) are all below its three BEFORE values (550.23, 591.20, 552.54), while every control's arms
INTERLEAVE — ndjson 396/390/366 against 393/386/406, and the others likewise. Only the subject
separates, which is the shape a real effect has and a noisy control does not. Item 310's warning is
the reason to say it this way: disjoint ranges are not proof when the change's own unreachable
control moves with it, so the argument has to rest on something the controls fail.

### Mutation 4/4 — and the TS suite needed no new test, where Rust did

Every clause of the condition got a mutant, plus one taking the path for a multi-label set. **All
four caught, with nothing added.** That is the opposite of the Rust twin, where the backslash and
formula clauses both survived and needed
`a_lone_label_is_still_escaped_and_guarded` written for them.

The reason is one test: `formula-leading labels and edge types are neutralized and round-trip (any
position)` builds an EDGE with a single formula-leading label, and `assertNoFormulaCells` asserts
the emitted text rather than only a round trip. The Rust fixtures only ever gave a
needs-escaping label to a node carrying TWO labels, which takes the other branch.

**So the same rule had different coverage in the two engines, and only mutation could tell them
apart.** A green suite on each side says nothing about this; running the same four mutants against
both is what showed one of them was testing the claim and the other was not.

### Where the two engines now stand on this row

TS csv 494.62 ms against native's 246.90 on comparable fixtures — the TS engine is 2.0x the Rust
one here, which is inside the 1.5-4x band CLAUDE.md describes and no longer the outlier it was
before items 703-707 moved native 2.08x.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0 (one
`prefer-destructuring` fix, which touches the binding and not the condition the mutants target);

## 709 — the quote-doubling allocation Rust removed at item 100 and TypeScript kept: ~3%, measured per call rather than end to end

**FIXED (TypeScript), and the size claim comes from a micro-measurement, not from the sweep.**
Continuing item 708's grep across the two codecs turned up an asymmetry: Rust's `write_cell` doubles
quotes straight into the output buffer and skips `str::replace` when the text holds none — that is
item 100's own fix, with its numbers. The TS twin still ran

```ts
encoded.forceQuote ? `"${encoded.raw.replaceAll('"', '""')}"` : quoteField(encoded.raw);
```

and **every `Str` column sets `forceQuote`**, so a graph of quote-free strings paid one throwaway
string per cell.

### The fixture had to change before the subject was reachable

Every earlier probe in this cluster used NUMERIC properties, where `forceQuote` is false and this
line never executes. A string-heavy fixture (two string properties per node, one per edge,
1,200,000 string cells) is the first one in the cluster that can see it at all — items 705 and 707's
lesson one layer out.

### The end-to-end A/B cannot resolve it, and says so plainly

Three alternated rounds, min-of-7, dist rebuilt between arms:

| format           | BEFORE |  AFTER | ratio     |
| ---------------- | -----: | -----: | --------- |
| csv              | 545.52 | 530.95 | 1.03x     |
| ndjson CONTROL   | 439.92 | 441.06 | 1.00x     |
| pg-json CONTROL  | 440.22 | 433.66 | 1.02x     |
| pg-text CONTROL  | 517.66 | 497.70 | **1.04x** |
| graphson CONTROL | 622.02 | 582.63 | **1.07x** |

**The target moved LESS than two of its own controls**, and the csv arms interleave (BEFORE
556/598/545 against AFTER 589/552/530) where item 708's separated cleanly. On this evidence alone
the change is null.

### So price the operation instead of the encode

`replaceAll` on text with no match is NOT free in V8 — which is the question, since the whole
premise came from Rust, where `str::replace` always builds a new `String`. Three million calls,
min of 5:

| operation                        |      ms |
| -------------------------------- | ------: |
| baseline (identity)              |     1.2 |
| `replaceAll`, NO match           |    45.6 |
| `includes` then skip (the guard) | **1.2** |
| `replaceAll`, one match          |   180.2 |

**~15 ns per call, and the guard removes all of it.** 1,200,000 cells × 15 ns = **18 ms of the
545 ms encode, 3.3%** — which is exactly the 1.03x the A/B read. The arithmetic and the
unresolvable end-to-end reading agree, so the claim here is 3%, derived, not 1.03x, observed. I am
not claiming the A/B confirmed anything.

That is the difference between this and item 704: there the lever was BUILT and measured at 1.02x
against controls also at 1.02x, with no independent account of what it should have been worth. Here
the operation removed is priced on its own, and the predicted total matches the noisy reading.

Both instances of the pattern in the file are guarded, not just the hot one: `quoteField` reaches
its `replaceAll` for a cell needing quotes for any of FIVE reasons, only one of which is a quote, so
a comma-containing cell was paying it too.

### Mutation 4/4

The risk in a guard like this is silent corruption — a cell holding a quote sent down the
don't-double branch emits broken CSV rather than failing — so both guards had both arms mutated:
never doubling, and the condition inverted. All four caught (exit 1).

### What this closes

The CSV encoder has now been gone over on both engines (703, 705, 706, 707 native; 708, 709 TS) and
the remaining cost in each is the byte writing itself, which item 706's ablation measured directly.
**The per-byte gap to pg-text is 1.8x on native and the shape of it is known**; no allocation lever
above ~3% is left on either side. A further attempt should start from item 706's table, where the
untouched line is `bag.get`'s linear scan — 3% at one property per element, and `O(columns ×
properties)`, so it is a wide-property risk rather than a win on these fixtures.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0;
`bun run check` 0; `bun run test` — all 21 projects pass; 47 CSV + conformance tests pass; all seven
byte-identity fuzzers pass, which is the gate that matters: a quote-doubling change is exactly what
would put the two codecs' bytes apart.

## 710 — the widest gap in the sweep, profiled: 70% is the closed insert path, and a 15.85% profile line ablates to ZERO

**REFUTED (TypeScript). No code change.** `decode pg-text (5 edges/node)` is the widest gap in
`bun run bench` — ts 3470.9 against ffi 332.4, **10.4x** — and item 104, which optimized the TS
pg-text decoder, only ever looked at the NODE-ONLY variant. Five sixths of this document's elements
are edges, so the row looked unexamined.

Reproduced first: an own probe over a re-encoded 5-edges/node document read **3473.2 ms** against
the bench's 3470.9, so the row is the row.

### The profile says it is not the parser

`bun --cpu-prof`, self-time, 4,682 samples at 100,000 nodes / 500,000 edges:

| frame                 | self-time  |
| --------------------- | ---------- |
| `indexEdgeLabel`      | **21.19%** |
| `getVertexById`       | **15.85%** |
| `commitElementLabels` | 7.50%      |
| `#commitNormalized`   | 6.81%      |
| `insertEdge`          | 5.85%      |
| `Set`                 | 5.47%      |
| `getEdgeById`         | 4.59%      |
| `validateLabel`       | 3.78%      |
| `parseLabelsAndProps` | 3.01%      |

Every parser frame together — `parseLabelsAndProps`, `labels`, `tokenizeLine`, `parseId`,
`idToken`, `elementTokens`, `parseScalar` — is **~11%**. About 70% is the core graph's write path,
which is `CLOSED.md`'s "the TS insert path, CLOSED as a constant factor". `indexEdgeLabel`
specifically has been priced, split across its three indexes, and ablated (items 312, 357, 358);
its only surviving lever is item 300's dense integer-keyed adjacency, parked at 348, **and the
audit already notes four items arriving there. This is the fifth.**

### The one line that looked newly actionable, and why it is not

`getVertexById` at 15.85% is not the same claim as the audit's. `addEdge` re-resolves both endpoints
by id although the caller hands it `Vertex` objects, and the audit prices that pair at **43ns**, 1.5%
— measured through `addEdge` as an API call. The audit's own warning in that very entry is that **a
decomposition measured through a different entry point than the row is a decomposition of the entry
point**, and the decode path is a different entry point: the decoder resolves both endpoints itself
from text ids, so an edge costs FOUR lookups, not two.

So it was ablated here, in this row. The ablated arm is incorrect code — it drops the membership and
liveness check entirely, passing `params.from`/`params.to` straight through — which makes it an
**upper bound on what any correct version could buy**. Three alternated rounds, min of five per run:

| arm                   | round 1 | round 2 | round 3 |    min |
| --------------------- | ------: | ------: | ------: | -----: |
| CONTROL               |  1575.7 |  1658.9 |  1556.1 | 1556.1 |
| ABLATED (upper bound) |  1663.1 |  1642.8 |  1639.1 | 1639.1 |

**0.949x — the ablation is SLOWER than the control**, and the arms interleave. Removing two
string-keyed `Map.get`s per edge from a 500,000-edge decode is worth nothing measurable, so the
upper bound on the correct version is zero and the audit's 43ns holds in this entry point too. Both
arms answered 600,000 elements.

### The method lesson, which is the tick's product

Item 700's lesson was _reading the code is not instrumenting it_. This is one level further: **a
profiler's self-time is an attribution, not a counterfactual.** 15.85% of the row sat under a
function whose call count I could halve for free, and halving it moved nothing — because the samples
land there whether or not those particular calls exist, and because what the row is actually bounded
by (string-keyed hashing at a million entries) does not get cheaper when you do less of it in one
place. Only ablation answers "what would it cost without this", and the ablation has to run in the
row rather than in a probe of the function.

`addVertex` holds a genuine duplicate — `if (params.id && this.getVertexById(params.id)) { return
this.getVertexById(params.id)!; }` looks up the same id twice — but it is **not a cost in this row
and I nearly recorded it as one**: the second lookup runs only when the first returned something,
and a decode creates only new vertices, so it never fires here. It is an upsert-path cleanup worth
zero on ingest.

Gates: no code change to gate. The ablation arms were restored from the pristine copy and the tree
verified clean (`git status` and `git diff --stat` both empty) before this was written.

## 711 — REFUTED: the `repeat().times(n)` spelling gap is the TRAIL GUARD, not a missed rewrite — and the engines disagree about it

**BUILT, REFUTED BY A TEST, REVERTED (native). No code change, and a verified cross-engine
divergence found on the way.**

### The target, which looked like this repo's named bug class

`bun run bench:gremlin` on 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges:

| traversal                          |   ts | native |
| ---------------------------------- | ---: | -----: |
| `V().out().out().count()`          | 53.0 |   2.77 |
| `V().repeat(out).times(2).count()` | 52.7 |   3.76 |

The same traversal — item 574 settled that against a real TinkerPop console — costing **1.36x more
in one spelling**, in the engine whose whole claim is that speed is a property of the optimized
plan. TS has converged; native had not. And `spelling_probe` covers GQL predicate forms only, so
no instrument was watching this pair.

Re-measured in isolation, min of 9, **both list positions** (item 697's position penalty): chain
2.69/2.69, repeat 3.76/3.76. Stable and not a harness artifact.

### The equivalence check that passed, and the one I did not think to run

Before changing a walk into a chain, the question is whether `VarLength` is a TRAIL where the
chain is a WALK. The 5,000,000-row fixture cannot tell: a 2-walk can only reuse an edge if a
reciprocal pair or self-loop exists. So: six tiny fixtures built to contain exactly those —
reciprocal pair, self-loop, self-loop + reciprocal, triangle both ways, parallel duplicate edges,
two self-loops on one node — crossed with `out`/`both` at `times(1..3)`, every count compared
across both spellings AND both engines. **24 cases, all equivalent.**

So the unroll was built: `flush_repeat` already unrolls a fixed `times(n)` when the body carries an
inner `.as('tag')` (the tag must bind per iteration), and the change extended that to a plain body
under an `UNROLL_MAX`. It worked — **repeat 3.76 → 2.59 against the chain's 2.62, converged, same
answers.**

Then the test suite refuted it. `trail_limit_caps_runaway_traversal_and_is_configurable` expects
`g.V().repeat(both()).times(3)` to raise `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` under `limits.trail = 2000`, and
got rows. **The `VarLength` walk is governed by the trail/row cap; a chain of explicit `Expand`s is
not.** So the 1.36x is the price of a resource guard, the two spellings are not equivalent in the
dimension that matters, and the unroll silently deleted a runaway-traversal defence. Reverted;
1,953 tests green again.

**My equivalence probe compared ANSWERS and could not have caught this.** It is the fixture rule in
a new dimension: a probe that only compares results cannot see a difference in which inputs are
REFUSED.

### The divergence this exposed, verified

If the guard is the difference, does the other engine apply it? The Rust test's own fixture and
limit (200 nodes, 800 edges, `trail = 2000`), rows materialized — **no `count()`, because a count
folds the rows away before the cap governs them, and that mistake made my first run report "ok" on
all four cells**:

| engine | spelling                  | outcome                     |
| ------ | ------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| native | `repeat(both()).times(3)` | **raises** (trail exceeded) |
| native | `both().both().both()`    | ok, 102,400 rows            |
| ts     | `repeat(both()).times(3)` | **ok, 102,400 rows**        |
| ts     | `both().both().both()`    | ok, 102,400 rows            |

And the TS limit was **verified set** rather than assumed — the probe prints
`{"range":1000000,"trail":2000,"intermediate":50000000,"operatorChain":1024}` beside the outcomes,
because "the limit silently did not apply" is the same failure as item 700's "the counter did not
reach dist", and I had already made it once in this item.

So: **native guards one of two spellings of the same traversal; TypeScript guards neither.** A
raise against 102,400 rows is observable, so this is a divergence and not a tuning difference.

**NOT fixed here, deliberately.** Three outcomes are defensible — guard both spellings in both
engines, guard neither (the cap arguably exists for an UNBOUNDED `repeat`, and `times(n)` is
finite by construction), or keep native's asymmetry and document it — and which one is right is a
semantics decision about resource limits, not an optimization. Recorded for the open-divergence
list with the repro above.

### What is settled

`repeat(out()).times(n)` is the n-fold walk in both engines, now checked as a multiset on fixtures
designed to separate a walk from a trail (24 cases). The 1.36x native gap between it and the chain
is **CLOSED as expected behaviour**: it buys the trail cap. Anyone re-finding that row in
`bench:gremlin` should read this item rather than re-deriving the unroll, which takes about twenty
minutes and ends at a failing test.

Gates: no code change to gate. Reverted from the pristine copy under `target/`, full Rust suite
re-run green (1215 + 13 + 725), tree verified clean (`git status` and `git diff --stat` both empty).

## 712 — a LIVE spelling flag the probe has been printing: inline props in a product cost 2.8x, and it is per-SCANNED-VERTEX

**DIAGNOSED (TypeScript), not fixed. Plus one stale marker corrected.**

Two surfaces were checked before this and both were already triaged, which is the 702 lesson
working: the Gremlin bench's biggest ratio (`V().out().has().count()`, 27.9x) is a **shared floor**
closed at 235/661, and item 661 states that _no row in either bulk screen is an unexplained
target_. Item 662 names the serving regime as the uncovered one, so `bench:usage` was next.

### The serving regime points at the spelling probe, not at a new row

`bench:usage` at 20,000 users shows `read: keyed dedup lookup` at **76.9k ops/s against its
`[inline]` twin's 58.2k** in TS (1.32x), where native converges (59.4k / 60.3k). That is item 579's
known flag, which item 669 then re-priced as a bounded constant factor rather than a divergence.

Running the repo's own instrument at the settings memory records (`SPELL_N=200000 SPELL_REPS=9`,
because single runs are bimodal) shows those seek groups have since CONVERGED — 8.56 / 7.58 / 8.55
on the clause/inline/inline-WHERE triple, 1.13x — and the numeric group is now under the 1 ms
floor. But the probe flags three groups, and one of them is live:

```
a product's one-sided predicate: comma vs MATCH MATCH (item 285)        2.28x
      11.84ms  MATCH (a:S), (b:P) WHERE b.k = 7 RETURN b.k AS x
      10.85ms  MATCH (a:S) MATCH (b:P) WHERE b.k = 7 RETURN b.k AS x
      11.79ms  MATCH (a:S), (b:P WHERE b.k = 7) RETURN b.k AS x
      24.71ms  MATCH (a:S), (b:P {k: 7}) RETURN b.k AS x        <-- 2.1x, three siblings converged
```

**The group's own commentary does not mention this member.** It explains the comma-vs-`MATCH MATCH`
cause that item 285 fixed (`pushWhereIntoNode` declining on `patterns.length !== 1`, 15.6x) and
predates the inline-props member being added. So the probe has been printing a flag whose
explanation is for a different pair — which is how a flagged group goes unread.

The other two flags are both documented as correct: `label on start: redundant vs absent` (5503x) is
an O(1) bucket size against an O(|label|) degree sum and is kept as a regression guard — and its
recorded "~2100x" is at the default `SPELL_N=20000`, so 5503x at ten times the nodes is sub-linear,
not drift. `one end labelled, the other free` at 2.02x is item 286/287's pair.

### The mechanism, and the fixture mistake that hid it first

In a SINGLE-pattern MATCH the inline form is the FASTER one (6.44 against the clause's 7.63), so
this is specific to the product. The test is to hold the SCANNED side fixed and vary the product
MULTIPLIER: a predicate applied once per scanned vertex is flat in the multiplier, one applied per
product ROW scales with it.

**The first version of that probe could not answer it.** With `k: i % 11`, `b.k = 7` matched ~18,000
vertices, so the OUTPUT grew with S too (36,364 rows to 290,912) and all three spellings scaled
together — 4.56x / 6.59x / 6.70x, saying nothing. With `k` unique, the output is S rows:

| spelling        |  S=2 |  S=4 |  S=8 | S=16 | rows     |
| --------------- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | -------- |
| clause `WHERE`  |  5.2 |  7.0 |  5.4 | 10.1 | 2/4/8/16 |
| inline `WHERE`  |  5.1 |  7.1 |  5.2 |  9.4 | 2/4/8/16 |
| inline `{k: 7}` | 14.5 | 17.8 | 27.9 | 33.4 | 2/4/8/16 |

**2.8x at S=2 and 3.3x at S=16** — so it is NOT per-product-row (that would be 8x across this
sweep); it is a per-SCANNED-VERTEX penalty of about 2.8x, with a smaller multiplier-dependent term
on top.

### Where it goes

A CPU profile of the inline spelling names `withBinding` (19.85% of samples) and `generatorResume`
(13.04%). **The profile is fixture-build dominated** — 12 queries against a 200,000-vertex build, so
`addVertex`/`indexVertexLabel`/`commitElementLabels` crowd it and no percentage here is a share of
the QUERY; those two are simply the only query frames that surface. Taken with item 285's own note
that a product materializes _"a binding `Map` per product row before anything filters it"_, the
hypothesis is that the inline-props predicate is applied AFTER the binding is built while
`start.where` is applied before it — so the inline spelling pays a binding allocation per scanned
vertex.

**Stated as a hypothesis, not a finding.** Item 710 is three ticks old: a profiler's self-time is an
attribution, not a counterfactual, and the next step is the ablation — move inline props into
`start.where` at plan time and re-measure the sweep above — not more reading.

### The stale marker

`CLOSED.md` still carries **"PRICED, NOT BUILT: `DETACH DELETE` is O(deleted x TOTAL NODES)
natively (442)"** with the fix named in it ("removing `id` from just those buckets makes it O(its
labels)"). **Item 663 built exactly that** — the same sweep over every label bucket in
`Store::delete_nodes` — and measured 501x at 200,000 nodes. The entry is corrected in place rather
than left to be re-derived, which is the failure `open-markers.ts` exists to catch and which three
passes in one session have already paid for.

Gates: no engine change. `bun run lint` 0; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0; tree verified clean
of probes before the record was written.

**RETRACTED (TypeScript). The only change is a comment where the flag is printed.**

Item 712 diagnosed the spelling probe's live flag — inline `{k: 7}` in a product at 2.8x against
three converged siblings — and named the next step: _"move inline props into `start.where` at plan
time and re-measure"_. This tick did that. The ablation worked:

| spelling                 |  S=2 |  S=4 |  S=8 | S=16 |
| ------------------------ | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| inline `{k: 7}` before   | 14.5 | 17.8 | 27.9 | 33.4 |
| inline `{k: 7}` AFTER    |  5.0 |  5.9 |  8.5 |  5.0 |
| clause `WHERE` (control) |  5.4 |  6.0 |  8.4 |  5.2 |

Converged exactly onto its siblings. A second ablation localized the mechanism further: KEEPING
`properties` and merely ADDING the equivalent `where` is **also** fast (5.3 / 6.5 / 5.3 / 9.2), so
the win comes from the `where` being PRESENT rather than from the properties being absent — i.e.
something gates on `where` instead of on "is this node constrained".

### And then the code said it had all been done

`rejectedByElementDirect` carries a 🛑 marker at the top:

> **EXTENDING THIS TO INLINE `props` WAS TRIED AND REVERTED (item 644). It is NOT a tuning
> question: it changes WHICH QUERIES RAISE.**

Item 644 has the same diagnosis, the same mechanism (only `eqProps`/`cmpProps` reach the
pre-filter, so inline props evaluate per VERTEX and the other spellings per SURVIVOR — **20,004
evaluations against 404** at 20,000 vertices), and the same magnitude (**1.89x at 1,000,000**, with
the clause spelling and a null control both flat). It also records why it was reverted: the
pre-filter runs BEFORE the binding, so rejecting a candidate skips a binding that would RAISE.

**My ablation reproduces that failure exactly.** Re-applied and run against the test 644 names:

```
(fail) product-of-counts shortcut > a PATH variable colliding with a node variable
       declines, preserving the raise
       Expected: "raised"    Received: "answered 0"
```

Same query as 644's comment (`MATCH p = (a:P {k: 1}), (p:P {k: 2})`), same wrong answer. So the
candidate I built is the candidate that was already rejected, and the guard that rejects it has
teeth — demonstrated rather than assumed, which is the one useful thing this tick produced beyond
the retraction.

### Why I missed it, and the one change that follows

CLAUDE.md's rule is to match the store to the kind of fact, and "has this lever been tried?" →
`CLOSED.md`. I searched `CLOSED.md` — for `inline`, for `clause`, for the row names — and found
items 579, 669, 285, 286, 287. **Item 644 is not in `CLOSED.md` under any of those terms; its
reason lives in a code comment in `executor.ts`, three files from the probe that prints the flag.**

So the fix is not in the planner, it is at the point of printing. The spelling probe's group now
carries the 🛑 note: that the inline member is closed at 644, what the mechanism is, what was
reverted and which test killed it, and the general point — **a flag is only readable where it is
printed.** The group's existing commentary explains the comma-vs-`MATCH MATCH` pair item 285 fixed
and predates this member entirely, so a reader following the probe's own words was being pointed at
the wrong pair.

### What item 712's record should now say

Its diagnosis stands as measurement — the 2.8x, the per-scanned-vertex finding, the multiplier
sweep and the fixture correction are all correct and reproduce — but its framing as an open target

## 714 — the second store has an index now: `closed-levers.ts`, and it failed its own motivating case first

**TOOLING (both engines). One annotation added to the Gremlin lowering; no behaviour change.**

Items 710, 712 and 713 were each spent on a target that turned out to be closed, and 713 found the
mechanism: CLAUDE.md names TWO stores for refutations —

- "has this lever been tried?" → `CLOSED.md`, then the audit item it cites;
- "Record rejected optimizations with their numbers, **next to the code they would have changed**."

— and only the first had an index. `CLOSED.md` has two (`open-markers.ts` plus its own tables); the
source had none, while holding **47 refutation markers across 830 files**. Item 713's miss was not
carelessness and not the wrong pattern: it was the wrong STORE, and the store that held the answer
could not be searched as a whole.

### `docs/reviews/closed-levers.ts`

```text
bun docs/reviews/closed-levers.ts                  # the whole index
bun docs/reviews/closed-levers.ts inline props     # "has this been tried?" in one command
bun docs/reviews/closed-levers.ts --orphans        # markers carrying no item number
```

It scans `packages/` and `crates/` for the vocabulary this repo actually uses — `REJECTED`,
`REVERTED`, `REFUTED`, `WITHDRAWN`, `NOT BUILT`, `WAS TRIED`, `DECLINED ON`, `🛑` — gathered by
grepping for each form rather than guessed, and prints `item · file:line · the marker`.

**COMMENTS ONLY**, because `REJECTED` in code is an identifier or a string and including those made
the first run 40% noise. And it does NOT decide whether a hit is a rejected OPTIMIZATION:
`store.rs` says "REJECTED if `key` backs a unique constraint", which is API behaviour, and a script
that tried to tell them apart would become one more thing to distrust — the same choice
`open-markers.ts` makes, for the same reason.

### It failed the one case it was built for, which is why this item has numbers

The first version returned **ZERO hits for `inline props`** — the marker it exists to surface. That
marker reads inline `` `props` ``, and the backticks broke a literal match. Items 694/695 made the
same mistake one store over, and 695's own note says it: _a sweep is only as good as its pattern._

Two fixes, both found by testing the instrument against its motivating case rather than by reading
it:

- **fold to bare words** before matching, on both the text and the needle, so punctuation and
  backticks cannot hide a term;
- **search the whole COMMENT BLOCK**, not the matched line. A lever's subject is usually named a
  line or two below the word `REJECTED`. This also raised the count of markers whose item number
  could be extracted from **15 to 27**, because the number sits below the marker as often as on it.

With both, `inline props` returns item 644's marker, which is what cost three ticks.

### And it immediately found a gap in my own previous item

`closed-levers.ts unroll` reported **nothing** — because item 711's refutation went into `CLOSED.md`
and the audit and NOT to the call site, which is the half of CLAUDE.md's rule I skipped one tick
earlier. `flush_repeat` now carries it: what was tried, the 3.76-against-2.69 it was chasing, that
it converged to 2.59, that a `VarLength` walk is governed by `limits.trail` while a chain of
`Expand`s is not, and which test caught it.

**20 of the 47 markers still cite no item**, which `--orphans` lists. Those are the ones a reader
cannot follow up, and annotating them is a standing piece of work rather than something to do in
one pass.

### What this does not do

It does not replace `CLOSED.md`. A lever refuted in an audit item and never annotated at the call
site is invisible here — item 711 was exactly that until this item, and the empty-result message
says so in those words rather than letting silence read as "never tried".
