## 751 — a filtered query slower than its unfiltered parent is NOT automatically a bug: the filter removed the closed form

**NEGATIVE RESULT. No change. The finding is a limit on the heuristic that produced items 748 and 749.** Those two came from reading a sweep for an ordering impossible on its face. Applied to the TS
side of the same family, it produces a candidate that looks at least as strong and is not a defect
at all.

### The apparent anomaly

TS, isolated, 200,000 vertices:

| row                          |       ts |
| ---------------------------- | -------: |
| `count 2-hop` (ungated)      | **72.8** |
| `count 2-hop + start filter` | **89.9** |
| `count 2-hop + mid filter`   |     42.3 |
| `count 2-hop + end filter`   |     99.8 |

A start filter narrows the sources to ~39% — strictly fewer — and costs **1.23x MORE than no filter
at all**, and 2.1x more than a mid filter. On its face that is 748's shape: less work, more time.

### Reachability first, and it ruled out the obvious answer

A throw in `walkSegments` (the general matcher): **all four rows answer** — none falls off the
shortcut family, so this is not shortcut-versus-general. A throw in `longChainCount`: the **3-hop**
row reaches it and none of the 2-hop rows do, so two hops has its own route.

### The cause: the filter does not shrink the problem, it changes the algorithm

Two documented routes, and the file states the reason plainly:

- `buildTwoHopCount` iterates the **MIDDLE** and multiplies the two sides — `Σ_b indeg(b) ×
outdeg(b)`. It never traverses an edge; two degree lookups per middle vertex answer the whole
  count.
- `buildFilteredTwoHopCount` drives from the **START**, because _"once a predicate selects which
  `a`s count, the start side's factor is no longer a plain degree"_. Gate a vertex, then expand it.

So the operation counts run the other way from the input sizes. Ungated: ~400k degree lookups, zero
edge visits. Start-gated: ~200k predicate calls, ~390k edge visits, ~390k lookups — **more total
work on 61% fewer sources**, because the degree product is unavailable once the start side is
conditional.

The gated route is also already the better of its options: item 206 built it precisely because the
filtered shape fell to the general pipeline at 97.7 ns a scanned vertex against the one-hop walk's
25.7.

### 🛑 What this costs the heuristic, which is the part worth keeping

"An ordering impossible on its face" is a good detector — it found a 4.12x and a 1.53x in the two
items before this one. This is its failure mode, and it is specific: **a filter can remove a closed
form.** When it does, the filtered query is legitimately dearer than its unfiltered parent, and the
comparison that looked impossible was never valid, because the two rows are not the same algorithm
with different inputs.

So the refined rule: before treating `filtered > unfiltered` as a defect, ask whether the unfiltered
case has a route the filtered one cannot take. Where the answer is no — items 748 and 749, where
`count 2-hop + start filter` and the 3-hop ran the SAME sweep with the same gates — the ordering
really is impossible and the defect is real. Where the answer is yes, as here, there is nothing to
fix.

Noted too: the mid filter at 42.3 is the fastest of the four and cheaper than ungated, which is the
reverse again. That one IS consistent with work done — a mid gate prunes the frontier between the
hops, which is the one position where a predicate removes work from the remaining pass rather than
adding a pass of its own. It needed no separate investigation once the start case was understood.

### What was checked and left alone

No code changed. Both probed files were restored and `git status` is clean of source edits; the
throws were temporary. `count 2-hop` and the three filtered rows all already exist as bench rows
(the ungated one added at item 749), so the family stays measurable without anything new.

Gates: no change to gate. `bun run build` 0 on the restored tree.

## 752 — `bench:usage`'s two index columns are not independent: the second is warmer, and on a parse-dominated row that beats the effect being measured

**DIAGNOSED AND PROVED; the cheap fix was tried and did NOT survive, so nothing ships but the
warning.** The serving benchmark holds the largest cross-engine ratios in the repo, so items
739/740's rule — re-run the harness that priced it — pointed here.

### The impossible reading

| row                           |     ts(-) |      ts(+) | engine(-) | engine(+) |
| ----------------------------- | --------: | ---------: | --------: | --------: |
| `write: append node`          | **88.7k** | **135.0k** |    463.7k |    427.5k |
| `write: append node [params]` |    548.0k |     410.0k |    462.6k |    417.4k |

**Indexing makes TS's plain append 1.52x FASTER.** It cannot: an index adds maintenance to a write,
which is what native shows (8% cost) and what the parameterized twin shows (1.34x cost). Isolated
and repeated, the ordering held 3/3: ts(-) 77.2/90.5/106.5k against ts(+) 97.1/137.6/134.7k.

### The cause, proved by reversing it

`rate` warms with ONE operation — the pilot that sizes the batch, which is a different job and is
labelled "Warm" in the source — and `[false, true].map(…)` runs both columns in ONE process,
unindexed first. The interpolated append is parse-dominated (6x its parameterized twin), so by the
time `(+)` runs, the `(-)` cell has executed that path thousands of times.

**Reversing the column order moved the advantage with the ORDER, not with the index:**

| order    | measured FIRST    | measured SECOND        |
| -------- | ----------------- | ---------------------- |
| original | unindexed 77-106k | indexed **97-137k**    |
| reversed | indexed 94-105k   | unindexed **128-145k** |

That is decisive. The difference is tier-up, and `best of BATCHES` cannot see it because every
batch of the first column is colder than every batch of the second.

### 🛑 Three fixes tried; the cheap one does not hold

| fix                               | result                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 600-op warmup before both columns | converged ISOLATED (131.8 vs 131.6) but **not** in the full matrix (112.7 vs 138.7)                                                                                                         |
| 3000-op warmup                    | **corrected the SIGN** — ts(-) 111.2k against ts(+) 88.7k, indexed slower, which is what index maintenance should look like — but minutes of extra wall clock, and only one round completed |
| discard each cell's FIRST BATCH   | **INCONSISTENT**: 1.54x, 0.98x, 1.11x over three rounds                                                                                                                                     |

The third was the one I expected to ship: it costs one 250ms box a cell instead of thousands of
operations, and at ~100k ops/s a discarded batch is ~25,000 warm operations, far above the 3,000
that worked. It still does not reliably remove the bias, and **a fix whose benefit cannot be
demonstrated is the thing items 726 and 737 were reverted for.** So the harness is back at HEAD.

What the three together do show: the unindexed arm is the unstable one (77-133k across every run
this item made) while the indexed arm is steady (127-138k). That is consistent with warming as the
mechanism — sometimes the first column warms enough inside its own batches and sometimes it does
not — and it is why one round of any arm proves nothing here.

### What this costs the record

**Every `(-)` vs `(+)` figure in `bench:usage` was taken under this bias**, including the recorded
claim that TS's indexed column WINS. Where the columns differ by orders of magnitude the index
effect obviously dominates — `read: point lookup` is 2.2k against 927.3k, and no amount of tier-up
explains 400x. Where they sit within ~1.5x the comparison is confounded, and `write: append node` is
the case that was.

A second casualty: that row's own comment says it "carries an INDEXED key deliberately" so the
columns differ and indexes do not "look free on writes". With the bias removed at a 3000-op warmup
the honest reading is ts(-) 111.2k against ts(+) 88.7k — so the row CAN show the cost, but only
under a warmup the harness does not perform.

**So the rule until someone fixes it: read `(-)` against `(+)` only from an isolated run of that
row, and only on a row whose columns differ by more than ~1.5x.** The corrected full matrix is in
this item for the rows where that holds.

Gates: `bun run check` 0 on the reverted tree; `git status` clean. No change shipped.

## 753 — `bench.ts` has the SAME one-call warmup and is not affected, and the reason is the unit size

**AUDIT. One comment added; no behaviour change.** Item 752 found `bench:usage`'s index columns
confounded by tier-up. `bench.ts`'s `best()` warms with a single call too — `f(); // warm` — and it
is the instrument every A/B this session has been measured on, so whether it shares the defect is
not an idle question.

### It does not, and the discriminator is measurable

`BENCH_REPS=1` (the warm call plus ONE timed run) against the default min-of-5:

| row                                    | REPS=1 | min of 5 | residual |
| -------------------------------------- | -----: | -------: | -------: |
| `count 3-hop`                          |  353.3 |    312.5 |    1.13x |
| `query: project the element [ts lazy]` |    7.9 |      6.6 |    1.20x |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter`              |   44.6 |     40.9 |    1.09x |

So one warm call leaves **9-20%** in the first timed run — not nothing. Two things make it harmless
where the same pattern was fatal in `bench-usage`:

1. **The unit is a whole query over the fixture**, not one small operation. One call of `count
3-hop` runs the entire pipeline over 200,000 vertices; one call of `INSERT (:Event …)` does
   almost nothing. The same line of code is a real warmup in one harness and a no-op in the other.
2. **The min discards it, and every column pays it identically.** Each engine gets its own warm call
   and its own min, so an engine-vs-engine ratio is not a warmth comparison. `bench-usage`'s bias
   was _between_ the two cells being compared and its best-of-batches could not reach across them.

That second point is the one that matters, and it is why **every alternated A/B in this session
stands**: each arm ran in its own process with its own warm call and its own min-of-5, so the two
arms were at the same warmth by construction. The defect at 752 required comparing two columns
measured at _different_ warmth inside one process, which an alternated per-build A/B never does.

### The generalisable rule

A one-call warmup is adequate or not depending on **how much work one call does**, and a warming
bias only distorts a comparison when the two things compared sit at **different warmth**. Both
halves have to hold before a residual matters: `bench.ts` has a 9-20% residual and sound
comparisons; `bench-usage` has a 26-52% residual and unsound ones.

The note is in `bench.ts` rather than only here, because the live risk is someone reading item 752
and "fixing" this file — or, worse, discounting the session's measurements on the strength of 752.

### What stays open from 752

Why a discarded first batch (5,000 operations for a `grows` row, since those are fixed-count rather
than time-boxed) warms _less reliably_ than 3,000 explicit operations is still unexplained. The
difference in setup is that the explicit warmup ran once on its own graph before both columns, while
a discarded batch runs inside each column on a freshly loaded graph — so a graph-shaped inline cache
is the obvious suspect and is not evidence. Left open rather than guessed, which is item 734's
standing lesson.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `bun run fmt` 0; `bun run check` 0.
Comment only.

## 754 — `bench:usage` rates do not COMPOSE across rows: the interleaved pair is 1.34-1.56x faster than its own two halves

**NEGATIVE RESULT, short. No change.** A third limit on this harness, found while looking for an
engine target in it, and recorded because the inference it invites — "interleaving is free" — is one
a reader would otherwise draw from the matrix.

### The contradiction

Three rows run byte-identical queries on identical keys:

| row                               | query                                                  |  ts(+) |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | -----: |
| `read: point lookup`              | `MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.name = $n RETURN u.score AS s` | 927.3k |
| `write: property update`          | `MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.name = $n SET u.score = $v`    | 293.6k |
| `interleaved: write + point read` | **both of the above, in sequence**                     | 347.3k |

Neither declares `units`, so the interleaved row reports PAIRS per second. One pair therefore costs
**2.88 µs**, while its two halves cost **1.08 + 3.41 = 4.48 µs** measured alone — the pair is
**1.56x faster than the sum of its own parts.** Using the warmest write figure this item produced
(360.0k at a 1000 ms box) the gap narrows to 1.34x and does not close.

### What it is not

- **Not different work.** The query texts are identical and the keys are the same distribution
  (`user${i % GRAPH}`, the read offset by one).
- **Not laziness.** `@lenke/gql`'s `query` returns `R[]`, so `void e.query(..)` materializes; the
  unindexed read row's 455 µs an operation is real work.
- **Not index degradation under repeated writes.** That was the hypothesis — the standalone write
  row performs ~2x more writes per box than the interleaved one, and `score` IS indexed, so
  degradation would depress exactly the row that looks depressed. The box sweep refutes it: longer
  boxes are FASTER, not slower (276.2k at 50 ms, 328.8k at 250 ms, 360.0k at 1000 ms), which is
  warming again and the opposite of degradation.

### What it is, and the rule

The rows are independently warmed cells, each with its own pilot and its own batches, and the matrix
is built to span five orders of magnitude rather than to support arithmetic between cells. **So a
rate from one row may not be composed with a rate from another**, and the interleaved rows cannot be
read as "the pair costs its parts plus a penalty".

Why the pair comes out FASTER rather than merely incomparable is unexplained, and is left that way:
the box sweep shows the per-cell rate is a function of how many operations the cell got through, and
the interleaved cell gets through half as many of each query — which predicts it should be SLOWER,
not faster. So the mechanism is not simply warming either. Item 734's lesson applies: a measured gap
with no cause beats a guessed cause.

**Together with items 752 and 753 this closes what `bench:usage` supports**: not `(-)` against `(+)`
on a row whose columns are within ~1.5x (752), and not one row's rate against another's (754). What
it does support is one engine against another within a single cell, which is what its biggest
recorded figures are, and which nothing here disturbs.

Gates: no change to gate. `git status` clean.

## 755 — I re-priced frontier `sum`, which `CLOSED.md` forbids by name; the figure is 34x and the search terms are the fix

**RE-PRICED REFUTED GROUND. No change but the index.** Item 419 ends with: _"the native frontier
`sum` is refuted and `CLOSED.md` says in as many words: **do not re-price frontier `sum` as a
target**."_ I priced it anyway. The useful parts are the number, which is larger than the one on
record, and the reason my search did not find the refutation.

### What the measurement said

`AggFn` looked like an enum with an uncovered variant — 38 `AggFn::Count` mentions in `fastpath.rs`
against 54 for Sum/Min/Max/Avg, so the coverage question was which _shapes_ each reaches. In-process,
200,000 vertices of degree 5, identical 3-chain, varying only the aggregate:

| query                             |        ms |
| --------------------------------- | --------: |
| `count(*)`                        |       4.7 |
| `count(d.age)`                    |       4.7 |
| `min(d.age)`                      |       5.2 |
| **`sum(d.age)`**                  | **177.3** |
| **`avg(d.age)`**                  | **178.3** |
| 1-hop `sum(x.age)` (for contrast) |       5.5 |

**34x between `min` and `sum` on the same shape**, and the 1-hop sum is fast, so it is specifically
the multi-hop case. It also looked implementable: the sweep already builds `ways[]`, so
`Σ ways[d] × age(d)` is one weighted pass.

### Why it is refused, which the code says twice

- `try_frontier_multi_agg`: _"`count` folds the per-node multiplicities because it does not care
  about order, and `min`/`max` ignore multiplicity entirely. `sum`/`avg` would have to add a value
  `c` times in an order the general path does not promise."_
- `try_frontier_prop_agg`: _"SUM/AVG would change the summation order."_

Floating-point addition is not associative and byte-identity is a hard invariant, so
`Σ ways[d] × age(d)` is not the same f64 as the general path's path-order addition. The weighted
pass I had in mind is precisely the thing that breaks it. Items 376 and 419 settled this on both
engines.

The hazard note I _did_ find first pointed the other way and nearly misled me: _"DO NOT add `Sum` to
`try_frontier_prop_agg` while it sits earlier in the chain"_ reads as a PRECEDENCE problem, and item
375 has since moved `try_scan_num_agg` above it (verified: `exec.rs` 1663 before 1671), so that
precondition is now inverted and the note looks satisfied. It is not the blocker. The blocker is one
level up and unaffected by ordering.

### 🛑 The figure that is new, and worth having anyway

`CLOSED.md` prices this decision at **2.5x on hops** — a one-hop figure. On a 3-chain it is **34x**
(177.3 against 5.2). That is not a reason to reopen it: the contract is the contract, and
`order-is-unspecified` plus the summation-order rule are load-bearing. But a reasoned decline is
worth more with its true price attached, the same point item 743 made about `Dir::Both`, and 2.5x
understates what byte-identity costs here by an order of magnitude.

### What actually failed: my search terms, not the record

I checked `CLOSED.md` before implementing — correctly — and grepped `weighted sweep`, `chain sum`,
`sum over a chain`, `multi-hop sum`. All empty. The record's vocabulary is **"frontier"**, and a
measurement does not suggest that word: the thing I measured was a 3-hop CHAIN, and only the code
calls its endpoint set a frontier.

What found it was the CODE's doc chain — `try_frontier_prop_agg`'s note → item 376 → item 419 —
reached by grepping `AggFn::Sum` in `fastpath.rs`. **For "has this lever been tried", the fast path's
own doc comment is the better index than `CLOSED.md` keywords**, because the comment sits on the gate
you are about to change and cannot be missed by vocabulary.

So this item adds the missing terms deliberately — **chain sum, multi-hop sum, 3-chain sum,
sum(d.age) over a chain, weighted sweep** — so the next grep in any of them lands here and then on
376/419.

Gates: no code change. `git status` clean; the probe example was deleted.

## 756 — `count(DISTINCT y)` over `->{1,2}` ERRORS where its `MATCH WALK` twin answers in 0.5 ms, and the gate is stricter than its own argument

**MEASURED. No change — the widening it suggests needs a correctness proof this item does not
have.** Item 374 left a note that `try_varlen_distinct_count` and `try_varlen_distinctby_count`
"decline their own shapes even unlabelled". Following the method that worked at item 755 — read the
fast path's own doc before measuring — explains it, and measuring it turns up something sharper than
slowness.

### What the gate says, and what it does

The path answers `count(DISTINCT endpoint)` by multi-source BFS in O(V+E) instead of enumerating
every path. Its TRAIL region is `max <= 1`, and item 68 (`fastpath_fuzz`, seed 3249) is why: on two
nodes and one edge, `(x)-[:R]-{2,3}(y)` returns NO rows as a trail — length 2 needs two distinct
edges — while the BFS walks `a -> b -> a` and reports 2.

**TRAIL is the DEFAULT mode.** So the shape a user writes declines, and only an explicit
`MATCH WALK` reaches the fast path. That is the whole of item 374's note.

### The cliff, at 50,000 vertices of degree 5

| query                                                     | result                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->{1,2}(y) … count(DISTINCT y)` | **E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED** (27.8 ms to fail) |
| `MATCH WALK (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->{1,2}(y) … same`         | **0.5 ms** → 49,657                        |
| `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->{1,1}(y) … same`              | 0.5 ms → 49,657                            |
| `MATCH WALK … ->{1,3}(y) … same`                          | 0.7 ms → 49,657                            |
| `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->{1,3}(y) … same`              | **E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED**                   |

This is not a perf gap, it is a **failure**: the default spelling blows the 1,000,000-row trail
limit on a graph of 50,000 nodes, while one keyword makes it sub-millisecond. `{1,1}` answers because
`max <= 1` is inside the safe region, which confirms the mechanism from the outside.

Every spelling that answers agrees on **49,657**, so on this fixture the trail and walk
distinct-endpoint sets coincide — which is what makes the next section tempting and is not proof of
anything.

### 🛑 The gate is stricter than the argument in its own doc, and I could not close the gap

The doc argues: _"a node with ANY walk of length `L ≤ max` has shortest distance ≤ L, so a `min ≤ 1`
reachability is the same set whether paths are walks or trails (the shortest path is simple, reusing
no edge)"_ — a **`min <= 1`** condition. The gate then implements **`max <= 1`**, which is far
narrower, and item 68's counterexample had `min = 2`, so `min <= 1` would already have excluded it.

That looks like a free widening worth the cliff above. **I am not making it**, because trying to
construct the correctness argument produced a case I cannot dismiss: undirected `x—y`, one edge,
`{1,3}` from `x`. A WALK of length 2 reaches `x` itself, so the walk endpoint set is `{x, y}`; the
set of nodes at shortest distance in `1..=3` is `{y}`, since `x` is at distance 0. If the BFS
computes the latter — which is what the doc says it computes — then it and the true WALK answer
differ at `min = 1`, and the equivalence the doc asserts does not hold in the direction that matters.

Either my reading of the BFS is wrong or the doc's argument is loose. Settling it needs the actual
BFS read line by line plus a `fastpath_fuzz` run over that fixture shape, which is more than this
item did. So: **a candidate widening with a measured 0.5 ms-against-failure payoff, blocked on a
semantics question, with the exact fixture to test first written down.**

### Why the note said "even unlabelled"

Item 373/374's family note says a fix here "needs a MIXED fixture to be measured honestly and a
mixed fixture to be TESTED at all". That is true of the LABEL-filtered variants and is a separate
blocker: `social_store` gives every node `["Person"]` and every edge `"KNOWS"`, so a label or type
test excludes nothing (item 721's trap). None of the figures above depend on a label, which is why
they could be taken at all.

Gates: no code change. `git status` clean; the probe example was deleted.

## 757 — the widening item 756 floated is REFUTED on two nodes and one edge, and the doc that suggested it is now a test

**REFUTED AND PINNED. Doc corrected, one test added; no behaviour change.** Item 756 measured a real
cliff — `count(DISTINCT y)` over `->{1,2}` fails with `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` at 50,000 vertices while
its `MATCH WALK` twin answers in 0.5 ms — and floated widening the fast path's trail region from
`max <= 1` to `min <= 1` on the strength of the fast path's own doc. It left the semantics question
open with the fixture to test first. This tests it.

### My reading of the BFS was wrong; the doc's argument was wrong too, differently

756 suspected the BFS computed shortest distance, which would make it wrong for WALK as well.
Reading it line by line: the `min <= 1` arm sets `reached[nbr] = true` on **every encounter** and
uses `visited` only to gate RE-EXPANSION, and the `min >= 2` arm walks level sets. Both admit a node
arrived at by a walk longer than its shortest path, which is exactly WALK semantics. **The code is
right and the doc's "nodes at shortest distance" phrasing was the loose part.**

That relocated the question rather than answering it, and the answer is a counterexample. Two nodes,
one edge, `(x:S)-[:R]-{1,3}(y)`:

| spelling        | distinct endpoints | rows |
| --------------- | -----------------: | ---: |
| `MATCH WALK`    |              **2** |    3 |
| default (TRAIL) |              **1** |    1 |
| both at `{1,1}` |                  1 |    — |

A WALK returns to the source by re-crossing the single edge; a TRAIL cannot. So the source is a walk
endpoint and not a trail one, and the sets differ at `min = 1`.

**The doc's argument fails on exactly one word.** It said walk and trail reachability coincide for
`min <= 1` because "the shortest path is simple, reusing no edge" — true, but the shortest path is an
admissible answer only when its length is **`>= min`**, and for a SOURCE on a cycle that length is
**0**. Item 68's counterexample had `min = 2` and so looked like the only hazard; this one has
`min = 1` and `max = 3`.

So `max <= 1` is the trail region and the gate was right all along: at one hop no edge can be
reused, which the same fixture confirms (both spellings answer 1 at `{1,1}`).

### The guard is a test, not the corrected comment

The widening produces a **wrong answer** (2 against 1), not a slow one, so a comment cannot refuse
it. `a_trail_distinct_endpoint_count_is_not_the_walks_at_min_one` pins both halves — that the two
spellings DIFFER at `{1,3}` and AGREE at `{1,1}` — and **the mutation is the widening itself**:
`PathMode::Trail => max <= 1` relaxed to `true` fails that test and nothing else in 1,223. Verified,
not assumed.

That is the mirror of `perf-gate-needs-its-own-test`: a route choice is answer-equivalent and needs a
perf A/B, while a SEMANTICS choice needs a pinned answer. This one is the second kind, and item 756
had correctly declined to make it without one.

### What remains true from 756

The cliff is real and unaddressed: the DEFAULT spelling of a distinct-endpoint count over a
var-length hop enumerates and can exhaust the trail limit, where the `WALK` spelling is
sub-millisecond. What is now settled is that the cheap fix is not available — a trail-correct
distinct-endpoint count past one hop needs per-path edge sets, which is not a BFS, as the fast
path's own doc says. Anyone revisiting it should price the general path instead of widening the
gate.

Gates, each its own command with its exit code read UNPIPED: `cargo fmt` 0; `cargo clippy
--all-targets --features capi -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo test --release` **1223** + 13 + 725 pass, 0
fail; `fastpath_fuzz` 1 pass; the seven byte-identity fuzzers 13 pass 0 fail; `bun run fmt` 0; `bun
run check` 0.

## 758 — the engine's doc comments carry exactly THREE priced-open perf levers, and item 457's is the one worth doing: 43.45 ns/row still stands

**RE-PRICED AND SIZED. No change — the refactor is 52 match arms and is not being half-done at a
tick boundary.** Five consecutive candidates this stretch turned out already closed (751, 755, 756,
757, and the `element_id` ordering below), so this tick enumerated the open set instead of sampling
it, using the index that has actually worked: **the code's own doc comments**, not `CLOSED.md`
keywords (item 755's finding).

### The whole priced-open set, which is smaller than I expected

Grepping the engine and the TS planner for an open marker carrying a measured figure, excluding
tests and fuzzers, returns **three**:

| lever                                            | price                                                          | state                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| the generic scalar-call resolver (**457**)       | ~15 ns of ~27 ns fixed overhead, every non-vectorized function | **open, no contract risk**                                                                                                                                                               |
| hop `max(b.s)` on a string/dict column (**422**) | 14.172 against 9.372, **1.5x**                                 | deliberately left: it folds path MULTIPLICITIES, and item 376's `count` yes / `sum` never rule must be re-read for a dictionary first                                                    |
| `element_id(x) <ordering> '<lit>'` (**opt.rs**)  | 25.20 against 7.08 ns/row, **3.6x**                            | needs reproducing the value contract's string total order — the thing item 375 declined for min/max over `-0.0`; also a rare shape, and its own doc says to price it against this number |

Three, across both engines. That is the strongest evidence yet for what item 731 claimed and 739/740
corrected: the reachable space really is worked out, and the remainder is contract-blocked,
multi-tick, or rare.

### Item 457's target re-priced, because a price can die (739)

| shape                                | ns/row now | item 457 |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------: | -------: |
| `count(a.age)` — the floor           |       0.46 |     0.47 |
| `count(abs(a.age))` VECTORIZED       |       4.11 |      4.8 |
| `count(round(a.age))` VECTORIZED     |       4.75 |      4.3 |
| **`count(power(a.age, 2))` GENERIC** |  **43.45** | **45.2** |
| `count(coalesce(a.age, 0))`          |   **3.22** |     37.5 |

**The generic overhead stands at 43.45 ns/row**, and `coalesce` has since dropped **11.6x** — which
is the item at `CLOSED.md`:4218 shipping two coalesce-specific wins (the identity, 8.9x, and the
dispatch resolved once, 1.67x). So the function-specific work landed and the GENERAL resolver did
not, exactly as that entry predicted: _"the dispatch resolved once … IS what a general resolver
would give every non-vectorized function. So item 457's target stands with its size now known: the
per-row `call_scalar_checked(name, …)` string match is ~15 ns of the ~27 ns fixed overhead."_

`power` is now the shape that exposes it, since `coalesce` no longer does. Subtracting `pow`'s own
~12 ns leaves ~31 ns of fixed overhead on `power`, of which ~15 is the name match — so hoisting it
should read about **43.45 → ~28 ns/row, ~1.5x**, on every non-vectorized scalar.

### The work, sized rather than guessed

The string match is not in `call_scalar_checked` (134 lines, 5 grouped arms over 55 names — mostly
null/arity pre-checks). It delegates at its last line to **`call_scalar(name, args)`: 388 lines, 52
string match arms.** So the change is:

1. an enum of 52 variants,
2. `resolve(name) -> Option<ScalarId>` called ONCE per `Expr::Call`, not per row,
3. 52 arm patterns changed from a string to a variant, with `name` still threaded through for the
   error messages that interpolate it,
4. the evaluator's `Expr::Call` arm resolving before the row loop.

Mechanical, no semantics, no contract exposure — but 52 arms is not a thing to leave half-converted
at a tick boundary, and a typo in one arm is a silently wrong function. It gets its own tick with
the 1,223 unit tests and the seven byte-identity fuzzers as the guard, plus an alternated A/B on
`count(power(a.age, 2))` with `count(abs(a.age))` as the control the change cannot reach (a
vectorized function never enters this dispatch).

Gates: no code change. `git status` clean; the probe example was deleted.

## 759 — the two-argument numerics vectorized: `power` 3.33x, `mod` 3.55x. And item 457's PREMISE is REFUTED: the per-row name dispatch costs ZERO

**TWO things close here, and the second is the one to read before pricing anything in the scalar
path.**

**DONE.** `binary_num_fn` + `eval_binary_num` are the binary twins of item 459's pair, with a
typed-slice arm for two `Col::Num` operands. Min of three ALTERNATED rounds from two saved
binaries, 200,000 rows: `count(power(a.age, 2))` 42.88 -> 12.88 (**3.33x**),
`count(power(a.age, a.age))` 43.77 -> 13.78 (3.18x), `count(mod(a.age, 7))` 34.91 -> 9.83
(**3.55x**). Five controls: `abs` 1.00x and `round` 1.00x (vectorized, cannot enter the dispatch),
`coalesce` 0.98x, `nullif` 1.00x (generic AND two-argument but not numeric — it isolates
"two-argument" from "numeric"), the no-`Expr::Call` floor 0.93x on 0.04 ns. `query_bench` (95
comparable rows) and `value_bench` (6) swept from both arms: the one flag, `element p` at 1.12x,
goes to **1.00x** over three alternated rounds with interleaving ranges, and everything else was
sub-nanosecond rounding.

**REFUTED — do not re-price this.** Item 457 priced the per-row `call_scalar_checked(name, …)`
string match at ~15 of ~27 ns; item 459 re-sized it at **~20 ns a row**; items 458/459 and two code
comments credit their (real) wins to "matching the function NAME as a STRING against dozens of
arms". Item 759 BUILT the hoist — 50-variant `ScalarId`, `resolve_scalar` called once per
`Expr::Call`, all 50 arms and all five pre-check passes re-keyed on the id, 1,223 tests green — and
measured **43.45 -> 44.04 ns/row on `count(power(a.age, 2))`. Zero.** The hoisted code was the
measured path, confirmed POSITIVELY: deleting `"power"` from `resolve_scalar` makes the probe assert.
The refactor was reverted.

So what items 458/459 actually removed was the generic path's per-row `Vec<Value>` argument buffer,
the read-back of each operand out of it, and the boxed output — not the name match, which rustc
compiles to a length switch and which is free. **The cost of a generic scalar call is the per-row
buffer and boxing; the dispatch is not in it.** The next instance is `nullif` at 28 ns a row, and
the general fix is a vectorized two-argument form keyed on the ARGUMENT kinds, not another
per-function arm.

A third thing, for whoever next reads a surviving mutant: `eval_binary_num`'s `-0.0` fold is
UNREACHABLE and deliberately kept. `atan2` is the one function here that can see the sign of a
zero, and `broadcast` does put a `-0.0` literal into a `Col::Num`, but the parser has already
folded the literal and ingest has already folded a stored property — so the mutant survives as
EQUIVALENT, not as a gap. A panic probe confirms the tests reach the arm; the end-to-end contract
is pinned by `a_negative_zero_literal_beside_a_column_still_folds_in_atan2`.

## 760 — TS: a scalar CALL cost 35-43 ns a row OVER the floor, flat across every family. Unary and binary numerics now 1.93-2.24x

**DONE (TypeScript).** `unaryNumCall`/`binaryNumCall`, resolved in `compileFunc` while the query
compiles instead of once per row. Alternated A/B, both dists in ONE process: `abs` **2.07x**,
`sqrt` 1.96x, `power` 1.93x, `mod` **2.24x**, `atan2` 1.66x. Four controls, each unreachable for a
different reason — `nullif` (generic AND two-argument), `upper` (string family, gated out),
`round(x, d)` (two-argument numeric but in the switch, not `BINARY_NUM`), and the no-`Expr::Call`
floor — read 1.16x / 0.97x / 1.08x / 0.99x.

**The diagnosis, which is the part to not re-derive.** At 200,000 rows a scalar call cost 35-43 ns
a row over a `count(a.age)` floor of 20.9, and it was FLAT across unary, binary, generic and
string — with `nullif`, which `callScalar` reaches last, CHEAPER than `abs`, which it reaches
first. So it is not dispatch depth. The per-row work that does not vary by function is the fresh
argument ARRAY from `args.map((f) => f(env))`, three dictionary misses in
`assertScalarArgTypes`, the walk down the chain, and a read of `env.graph.limits`.

**This INVERTS one half of item 759 and the two must not be carried across.** In Rust, hoisting the
name match alone measured ZERO (rustc compiles a 50-arm string match to a length switch). In
JavaScript the same hoist is most of a 2x, because a `Record` lookup on a megamorphic string key
and a per-row array allocation are not that. "The cost is the machinery, not the function" holds in
both engines; WHICH machinery is free does not.

`SCALAR_NEEDS_ARG_ASSERT` gates the specialized path away from any name whose arguments
`assertScalarArgTypes` validates by POSITION, and is BUILT from the same three tables that function
reads, so a new position cannot leave it stale. Emptying it is an EQUIVALENT mutant today (no
numeric function is in those tables) and was predicted to survive as one.

**Teeth, and a gap in the unit tests worth knowing.** Dropping the null guard on a binary
numeric's SECOND argument — so `power(a.age, null)` throws instead of propagating null — **passes
all 2,586 gql unit tests and is caught only by the byte-identity fuzzers.** That also settles
positively that the fuzzers reach this path.

**Still open here:** `upper` at 64 ns over the floor is now the most expensive row, and the string
family is gated out because its argument positions are asserted; folding that assert into a
specialized closure has to reproduce the `dataException` messages exactly, since they are
byte-identical cross-engine. The generic path still allocates the per-row argument array, which
needs `callScalar` to stop taking an array.

## 761 — TS: the one-argument STRING family specialized. `char_length` 2.03x, `lower` 1.64x, `upper` 1.49x — and the rest of `upper` is the `toUpperCase`

**DONE (TypeScript).** `unaryStrCall`, resolved in `compileFunc`. It needs its own factory rather
than a reuse of 760's `unaryNumCall` because this family IS argument-checked by position, so the
check moves INTO the closure instead of being skipped. Three alternated A/B runs: `char_length`
2.03/2.19/2.21x, `lower` 1.64/1.82/1.81x, `upper` 1.49/1.65/1.58x. Five controls, every one
straddling 1.0 across the three runs (0.90-1.15x), which is this instrument's noise band.

**The decomposition is the part worth keeping.** `upper` was 46 ns over the string floor, but it
allocates a string per row, so that is machinery plus work. `char_length` is gated out for the same
reason and returns a NUMBER: it cost **35.19 ns over the floor — the same machinery figure item 760
measured for the numerics — so only ~11 ns of `upper`'s 46 is the `toUpperCase` itself** and is not
available to any change here. That is why `upper` improves least of the three.

**A flag retracted:** the single-process probe showed `starts_with` — a control this change cannot
reach — at 1.26x SLOWER. Three alternated rounds put it at 1.08/1.10/1.03x. A single-process,
single-order probe is not enough to flag a 1.26x on this harness.

**A duplicated cross-engine contract, caught by reading rather than by a test.** The first version
spelled the `requires a string (a number is not coerced)` message a second time in the new closure,
with a doc comment claiming a test pinned the two copies together. Nothing pinned it anywhere: the
text existed in exactly two places (this engine and `exec::scalar.rs`) and the only `upper` test
asserted a bare `toThrow()`. There is now ONE `requiresStringMessage` helper behind both TS paths
and a test pinning the exact text through the specialized path (`upper`) and the general one
(`replace`).

**Gate mutation, same finding as 760's:** widening `SCALAR_ASSERTS_STR0_ONLY` (dropping its numeric
and polymorphic conditions) is EQUIVALENT today, because the names it would admit —
`left`/`right`/`substring`, `reverse`/`size`/`cardinality` — are not in `UNARY_STR`. Defensive only,
verified rather than assumed. Also recorded: a mutant that RENAMES an export only breaks the build,
which says nothing about test teeth; it was replaced with the widening one.

**Still open here:** `starts_with` at 62 ns over the floor is now the most expensive row. The
two-argument string predicates (`starts_with`, `ends_with`, `contains`, `regex_match`, `split`)
live in `callScalar`'s switch rather than in a table, as do `byte_length`/`octet_length`, so
specializing them means pulling bodies into a table first — wider than either of these ticks.

## 762 — REFUTED: skipping the positional argument assert is worth nothing. And the TS A/B harness flatters any change that redistributes call sites

**REFUTED AND REVERTED.** `callScalarUnasserted` — the assert-free half of `callScalar`, picked by
the compiler once per `Expr::Call` for names with no positional check — was built and measured
three ways. Three rows that take the IDENTICAL path do not agree in sign: in-process 1.09 / 1.03 /
1.07x, isolated run 1 1.25 / 0.97 / 1.07x, isolated run 2 1.06 / **0.90** / **0.89**x. The
positional assert is not a measurable cost, the same shape of result as item 457's dispatch.

The decomposition that pointed here was not wrong about the numbers (`starts_with`, two asserted
positions, 62 ns a row over the string floor; `nullif`, no asserted position, 35) — it was wrong
that the difference was the assert. Do not re-derive it.

**TWO INSTRUMENT DEFECTS, which matter beyond this item.**

1. **A multi-shape in-process two-dist A/B flatters any change that REDISTRIBUTES call sites.**
   For 762 it reported the targets at 1.03-1.09x and the CONTROLS — `starts_with` 1.56x,
   `byte_length` 1.47x, `substring` 1.23x — four times higher, in the change's favour, on rows the
   change cannot reach. Cause: in the PRE arm every shape funnels through one `callScalar` site; in
   the POST arm some are routed elsewhere, so the remaining site is less polymorphic. This applies
   to items 760, 761 and 762, all of which redistribute call sites. It also corrects 760's own note,
   which read `nullif` at 1.16x on an unreachable row and called the residual "probably real" — the
   mechanism was right, the conclusion was not.

2. **`min`-of-N is the wrong estimator for the TS general path, and it was hiding the win.** The
   per-rep series for pre-760 `count(abs(a.age))` is `128.8 87.0 98.4 98.9 90.7 83.9 80.3 85.9 83.4
83.8 87.0 89.4 83.5 51.9`: a ~84 plateau with ONE outlier at 51.9, which is what `min` reports.
   The post arm is flat (16.5-17.1), so `min` summarizes it fairly — the two arms were estimated
   differently. `nullif` oscillates between a ~45 and a ~82 mode WITHIN one process. The
   no-`Expr::Call` floor and the specialized closures are not bimodal; the general path is, and the
   per-row argument array (200,000 arrays a rep) is what it points at.

**THE INSTRUMENT THAT WORKS, for any future TS per-row A/B:** one shape per PROCESS, 14 reps, drop
the first three as warm-up (visibly the JIT tiering), take the MEDIAN of the rest, and the min of
that across three order-alternated rounds. Both controls land inside 5% — which nothing earlier in
this session managed — and items 760/761 re-confirm on it: `abs` **2.73x**, `char_length`
**2.50x**, `upper` **1.34x**, `nullif` 0.99x, floor 0.95x. The two biases above pushed in opposite
directions and roughly cancelled, so 760/761's published figures were the right size by luck rather
than by method.

**A qualitative benefit nothing had stated:** specializing removed the general path's BIMODALITY,
not just its mean. A specialized closure measures 16.5-17.1 across every rep; the general one
swings 45-83 in the same process.

**Still open:** the general path's ~35 ns, now known not to be the assert. What is left is the
per-row argument ARRAY, the dispatch-chain walk and an `env.graph.limits` read. The native engine's
fix for the same thing reuses ONE buffer across rows, which is safe there because Rust makes
retention explicit; here `args` reaches `callExtendedScalar` and then `callTemporalFn`,
`callStringListFn` and `callListSetFn`, so it needs a retention audit of all three first — an
aliasing bug of that kind would pass every test.

## 763 — TS: ONE argument buffer per compiled call instead of one array per row. `nullif` 1.39-1.55x, `starts_with` 1.32-1.34x

**DONE (TypeScript).** `bufferedScalarCall` replaces `args.map((f) => f(env))` in the general
`Expr::Call` closure: one buffer per compiled call, filled in place. The native engine's
`Expr::Call` arm has done the same for the same reason; this is its TS twin, and it is the lever
item 762's bimodality finding pointed at.

Measured on 762's instrument (one shape per PROCESS, 14 reps, first three dropped, median of the
rest, min across three order-alternated rounds), TWO independent reads: `nullif` 1.55x / 1.39x,
`starts_with` 1.32x / 1.34x, `byte_length` 1.15x / 1.32x, `substring` 1.07x / 1.11x, `replace`
1.10x / 1.07x. Three specialized controls that never enter the factory: 0.95-1.01x.

**Quote the ns, not the ratio.** The saving is a near-constant **10-27 ns a row**, so the ratio
falls as the function's own work rises — `nullif` does almost nothing and moves 1.5x, `replace`
and `substring` have expensive bodies and move 1.1x. Any single headline figure from this change
is an artifact of which function it was measured on.

**THE RETENTION AUDIT IS THE PRECONDITION, and it is recorded in the factory's doc comment.** A
reused buffer is only safe because nothing below `callScalar` keeps the array: `callScalar`
destructures it, reads `args.length` and calls `args.find` (returning an ELEMENT);
`callExtendedScalar`, `callTemporalFn`, `callStringListFn` and `callListSetFn` only index it.
Nothing returns, stores or closes over it. A future arm that does turns this into a
use-after-free in slow motion — the returned value would be rewritten on the next row, and a
single-row result still looks right. Re-entrancy cannot alias it: the buffer belongs to one
compiled `Expr::Call`, and a nested call is a different node with its own buffer.

**Mutation, all three as predicted:** a STALE last slot (`i < n - 1`) FAILS tests and fuzzers — it
is the exact failure mode a retention bug would have; the buffer hoisted to MODULE scope, which is
the aliasing bug the doc warns about, also FAILS, so nested general calls already have coverage
and there is no gap; and allocating per row again SURVIVES as EQUIVALENT, so the route choice's
guard is the A/B rather than a test.

`bun run spelling`: 0 groups disagree on the ANSWER. It flagged a THIRD group over 2x,
`one end labelled, the other free` at 2.03x — which item 504 already measured at **1.09x in
isolation** (the flag was shared-process contamination) and which a later entry records as
straddling the 2.0x threshold, flagging 2 of 3 runs on one tree and 0 of 3 on HEAD. Not chased,
on those two records.

**Still open:** the general closure's remaining cost is the walk down `callScalar`'s dispatch chain
(four `Record` lookups and a `Set.has` before the switch) and a read of `env.graph.limits`. Note
that the two relevant precedents point OPPOSITE ways — item 457 refuted the name dispatch as a
cost in the NATIVE engine, while item 760's table specialization in TS was most of a 2x — so this
one has to be measured in isolation, not reasoned from either.

## 764 — REFUTED: `callScalar`'s dispatch DEPTH is free (the deepest call is the cheapest). The cost was `coalesce`'s per-row CLOSURE

**REFUTED, AND A SMALL WIN SHIPPED.** Item 763 left the dispatch chain as the general path's last
suspect, with the two precedents pointing opposite ways (457 refuted the name dispatch NATIVELY;
760's TS table specialization was most of a 2x). Depth settles it:

| shape                | depth                                 | over a 21.2 ns floor |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------- | -------------------: |
| `coalesce(a.age, 0)` | switch case **1**                     |             **38.3** |
| `nullif(a.age, 7)`   | switch case 2                         |                 26.9 |
| `to_integer(a.age)`  | later in the switch                   |                 32.6 |
| `_is_nan(a.age)`     | past every table AND the whole switch |             **17.8** |
| `abs(a.age)`         | specialized at compile time (760)     |                  3.5 |

**The DEEPEST path in the library is the CHEAPEST general call and the shallowest is the dearest.**
Depth is anti-correlated with cost, so the chain is not the cost — do not re-derive it, and do not
convert the switch to a handler table on the strength of it.

**What the ordering pointed at instead:** `coalesce`'s body was
`args.find((x) => !isNullish(x)) ?? null`, a FRESH CLOSURE on every row. Replaced with a loop
(`firstNonNullish`, named because inlining it put `callScalar` at complexity 36 against a limit of
35). `coalesce` is now the cheapest general call, at 17.7 over the floor.

**Two instruments, two answers, both reported.** Seven shapes in one process: **1.53x** (59.49 ->
38.97 ns/row). One shape per process, two reads: 1.06x / 1.18x on `coalesce(a.age, 0)` and 1.24x /
1.02x on the null-first form, with five controls at 0.95-1.04x. So: ~5-20% isolated, 1.53x mixed.
A monomorphic call site lets V8 escape-analyze that closure away; a megamorphic `callScalar` in a
mixed workload does not. Item 762's redistribution bias does NOT apply (this change moves no call
sites), so the mixed figure is not an artifact — and a real workload has many shapes.

**A TEST GAP, found by mutation and now closed.** `coalesce` had NO value test anywhere — only two
arity tests asserting `not.toThrow()`. Two wrong-answer mutants (returning `args[0]` regardless of
null; falling out as `undefined` instead of `null`) **both passed all 2,586 unit tests** and were
caught only by the byte-identity fuzzers. There is now a value test, and its teeth are verified:
both mutants FAIL the unit suite where they previously passed.

**A method corollary for TS mutation runs.** An interrupted run left `src` pristine but the DIST
carrying the mutant, because the assert fires before the write while the build is a separate step.
Restoring the source is not enough in this repo — the artifact the tests read is a build away.

`bun run spelling`: 0 groups disagree on the ANSWER; the two groups over 2x are the pre-existing
pair (items 325 and 285), and 763's third flag is absent again. NOTE: the first reading of this
gate was piped through `tail -8`, which cut the answer line — the only non-heuristic thing it
prints — and had to be re-run.

**Still open:** the structural gap, now better posed. `abs` (specialized) is 3.5 ns over the floor;
`_is_nan` (the cheapest GENERAL call) is 17.8. That ~14 ns is not the assert (762), not the chain
(this item) and not the argument array (763). What is left is that a specialized closure is tiny
and monomorphic while `callScalar` is a ~100-line megamorphic function that cannot inline into the
aggregate loop. Also unpriced: the list set-ops allocate a closure per ELEMENT at four
`a.some((w) => structuralEq(w, b))` sites plus the dedup helper — they CAPTURE, so they need loops
rather than hoists, and no fixture here has lists.

## 765 — NATIVE: the one-argument STRING family vectorized. `char_length` 2.47x, `upper` 1.89x — and an ASCII fast path in `utf16_len` is REFUTED

**DONE (Rust).** `unary_str_fn` + `eval_unary_str`, the string twins of item 459's numeric pair,
reading `&str` straight out of a `Col::Str` instead of cloning each cell into a `Value`. Three
ALTERNATED rounds from two saved binaries: `char_length` **2.47x** (12-byte column) and **2.40x**
(13-byte), `upper` **1.89x** / **1.63x**. Four controls — the numeric floor, vectorized `abs`, and
both bare string projections — at **1.00x** to two decimals.

**The diagnosis, so nobody re-derives it.** `count(abs(a.n))` is vectorized and produces the
IDENTICAL `Col::Gen` output column, and it cost 4.14 ns a row against `char_length`'s 30.33. Output
identical, dispatch refuted at 759 — so the ~26 ns was the INPUT boxing: `value_at` clones the
`GStr` into a `Value` that the arm derefs and drops.

**REFUTED on the way there: an ASCII fast path in `utf16_len`** (`if s.is_ascii() { return s.len();
}`, exactly equal since one ASCII byte is one UTF-16 unit). **30.33 -> 30.09 ns a row, noise.** A
panic probe confirms `utf16_len` is ON this path, so it is a refutation and not an unreachability
null: `encode_utf16().count()` over a short ASCII string is already cheap, and the counting was
never the cost.

**Also measured, also small:** the `GStr` heap clone itself. `GStr` inlines up to 12 bytes, so a
fixture one byte either side of the cap (`{:012}` against `{:013}`) isolates the atomic refcount
from length-proportional work — `char_length` cost 30.33 against 35.90, so **~5.6 ns is the heap
clone's two atomics**. Real, but a fifth of what the boxing cost. (`upper`'s +15.3 across the same
pair is TWO effects, since its result is also heap over 12 bytes.)

**A CONTROL THAT MUST NOT BE READ AS A BASELINE.** The bare string projections measure 0.46 ns a
row. That is the count-over-projection SHORTCUT, which never materializes a value — it is useless
as "what a per-row string read costs" and valid only as a row the change must not move.

**A COVERAGE FACT: the byte-identity fuzzers do NOT catch a UTF-16-versus-bytes error.** Mutating
`char_length` to count bytes FAILS the Rust corpus test (which has non-ASCII data) and PASSES all
seven fuzzers, because they generate no non-ASCII strings and the two lengths agree for every ASCII
input. The UTF-16 string model is a standing rule in `CLAUDE.md`; the fuzzer is not its guard.

**Still open:** `upper` still allocates a `String` via `to_uppercase` and converts it to a `GStr`
per row (a heap block for results over 12 bytes). An in-place ASCII uppercase would avoid both but
is correct only for ASCII, so it is a second fast path rather than a simplification. The
TWO-argument string family (`starts_with`, `ends_with`, `contains`, `split`, `substring`, `left`,
`right`, `replace`) still boxes both arguments per row — the same pair of functions extends to it,
keyed on two `Col::Str` columns, and that is the native twin of what item 761 left open in TS.

## 766 — NATIVE: the two-argument string PREDICATES vectorized with a `Col::Bool` output. `starts_with` 4.49x, `ends_with` 4.19x, `contains` 3.61x

**DONE (Rust).** `binary_str_pred_fn` + `eval_binary_str_pred`, reading `&str` out of each
`Col::Str`. Three ALTERNATED rounds from two saved binaries: `starts_with` **4.49x** (37.58 ->
8.37), `ends_with` **4.19x**, two-slot `starts_with` **4.15x**, `contains` **3.61x**. Controls:
`abs` 1.00x, item 765's `char_length` 1.00x, `left` 1.00x, `replace` 1.00x, `substring` 0.98x, the
numeric floor 0.84x on 0.09 ns of a 0.46 ns row.

**Why these reach 4.5x where item 765's family reached 2.5x — the OUTPUT column.** Every other
vectorized arm in `scalar.rs` must return `Col::Gen` because its function can make a null, a NaN or
an infinity (item 459 says so in as many words). A predicate over two `Col::Str` columns cannot: a
`Col::Str` holds no null and no non-string, so every row yields a real bool and the result is a
`Col::Bool` — one byte a row instead of a `Value`. `regex_match` is excluded on purpose; it
compiles or caches a regex rather than scanning.

**TWO THINGS MEASURED AND REJECTED AS TARGETS, so they are not re-derived:**

1. **The literal's broadcast.** `Expr::Lit` becomes `Col::Str(vec![s; n])` — 200,000 `GStr` clones
   per call, which looks like an obvious cost. The two-slot form prices it at **~2 ns a row**
   (40.22 against the literal form's 38.00). Not worth a special case.
2. **`substring` (119 ns) and `left` (102), the two biggest numbers in the family.** Their cost is
   an allocation per row plus the UTF-16 index walk, NOT argument boxing — removing the boxing
   would be a 1.2x there. Item 765 separately refuted the UTF-16 DECODE as a cost (an exactly-equal
   ASCII fast path in `utf16_len`: 30.33 -> 30.09), so what remains in those two is the allocation.
   `replace` (68) has the same shape. Price the allocation before touching them.

**A flag retracted:** the single-run probe read `substring` at +15%, on a row this change cannot
reach. Three alternated rounds: 0.98x.

**The guard that caught the sharpest mutant already existed.** Negating only the TYPED arm — leaving
the general loop correct — is caught by `gql::tests::typed_and_gen_columns_agree`, which is the
invariant every fast arm in this file depends on. Deleting the typed arm SURVIVES, which is also
direct evidence that `Col::Bool` and `Col::Gen` are observationally identical here.

**METHOD, now observed twice: an unexpected fuzz failure inside a MUTATION LOOP is unconfirmed
until re-run on its own.** Item 765's mutant 3 and item 766's mutant 3 both reported `fuzz=FAIL`
where SURVIVE was predicted, and both pass in isolation — the documented run-many flake. Believing
either would have meant reporting a non-equivalence that does not exist. After re-running isolated,
the fuzzers were run THREE times on the real tree: 13 pass, 0 fail, every time.

## 767 — NATIVE: `utf16_slice` allocated TWICE a row. `substring` 2.53x, `left`/`right` 2.10x — and item 765's refutation DIED because its denominator shrank

**DONE (Rust).** `utf16_slice` did `encode_utf16().collect()` into a `Vec<u16>` and then
`String::from_utf16_lossy`, and the caller converted that into a `GStr` — up to three heap
allocations for one `substring` row. For ASCII a unit index IS a byte index, so the slice is
already valid UTF-8 and the `GStr` is built straight from it (inline, zero allocations, when the
result is ≤ 12 bytes). Three ALTERNATED rounds: `substring` **2.53x** (114.21 -> 45.09), bounded
`substring` **2.15x**, `left` **2.11x**, `right` **2.10x**. Controls: `replace` 1.02x,
`char_length` 0.98x, `starts_with` 1.04x, numeric floor 1.00x.

**THE CONTROL WAS INSIDE THE FUNCTION, and it caught a regression a neighbouring control would
have missed.** A non-ASCII column (`é…`) cannot take the fast path, so it exercises the same
function and call site and must not move. The first version returned `Cow<'_, str>` and borrowed on
the ASCII arm — that cost the NON-ASCII rows **0.92x / 0.95x**: an enum discriminant and a failed
`is_ascii` on the one path that cannot use the fast arm. Returning the `GStr` the callers want
anyway removed the wrapper, took non-ASCII `substring` to 1.01x AND improved the ASCII win from
2.31x to 2.53x. The residual 0.96x on non-ASCII `left`/`right` is two failed `is_ascii` scans (~4 ns
on a 100 ns row) — an accepted, measured trade.

**A REFUTATION DIED ONE TICK AFTER IT WAS RECORDED, and the mechanism generalizes.** Item 765
refuted an ASCII fast path in `utf16_len` at **30.33 -> 30.09 ns**, correctly, with a panic probe
confirming reachability. The same three lines are now worth **1.16x** on `char_length` (12.16 ->
10.47, four alternated rounds, non-overlapping series). Nothing about the lever changed — the
DENOMINATOR did: the saving was ~1.7 ns throughout, which was 6% of a 30 ns boxed path and is 16%
of the 12 ns vectorized one. **A refutation is relative to the path it was measured on, and
vectorizing a path resurrects every small lever inside it.** The mirror of item 739's "a price can
die".

**Teeth, and a question item 765 left open.** Taking the ASCII slice arm UNCONDITIONALLY (byte
indices where unit indices are required) FAILS `corpus_tests_b` and the fuzzers; ignoring `start`
FAILS `substring_edges`. So UTF-16 SLICING _is_ pinned — whereas 765 found UTF-16 LENGTH is pinned
only by the corpus test, because the fuzzers generate no non-ASCII strings. Removing both fast
paths SURVIVES, so their guard is the A/B.

**A CORRECTION to items 765 and 766 about my own harness.** Both records blamed an unexpected
in-loop fuzz failure on "the documented run-many flake". With stdout captured the evidence is
specific: the output stops after `bun test v1.4.0` with NO test-result line, so the process never
ran a test and its exit code says nothing about the mutant. The real defect is that **a mutation
harness reading only an exit code cannot distinguish "ran and disagreed" from "never ran"** — it
will report a mutant as CAUGHT when nothing executed, invisibly, because FAIL is the prediction.
All verdicts in 765-767 stand (every FAIL came with NAMED failing tests), but that was reporting
luck, not a check. Now a rule in `CLAUDE.md`: require a result line before believing either
verdict.

**Still open:** `replace` (67 ns) allocates a result per row through `str::replace`, so the fix is
not this shape; `split` (a list per row) has never been priced.

## 768 — TS: `sanitizeSurrogates` built an ARRAY per row (`substring` 1.85-1.91x) and `replace` split into one (1.48-1.60x). `replaceAll` and a `str()` fast path are REFUTED

**DONE (TypeScript).** `replace` was the engine's most expensive row at **249.80 ns** (natively
67). The cost was two per-row allocations, not the dispatch:

- `sanitizeSurrogates` — called per row by `substring`, `left` and `right` — did
  `fromUtf16UnitsLossy(Array.from({length: s.length}, (_, i) => s.charCodeAt(i)))`: **an array with
  one element per character**, built and re-joined. A module-scope surrogate regex returns any
  string with NO surrogate code unit unchanged: **83.17 -> 8.15 ns a call, 10.2x**. The
  equivalence does not depend on what the slow path does with a surrogate — the guard only SKIPS
  it when there is none.
- `replace` used `split(search).join(repl)`, which allocates an array of pieces. An `indexOf` loop
  is **60.56 against 118.64, 1.96x** on the body.

Alternated A/B, two reads: `substring` **1.85x / 1.91x**, `replace` **1.60x / 1.48x**. Controls
0.93-1.09x (`char_length` drifts 1.18 -> 1.09 across reads, which is noise, not an effect).

**TWO REFUTATIONS, both worth not re-deriving:**

1. **`String.prototype.replaceAll` is NOT the fix** — and the first measurement said the opposite.
   Over a CONSTANT string `split`/`join` reads 54.44 and `replaceAll` 102.62, so `replaceAll` looks
   1.9x slower; over 200,000 VARYING strings the order flips (118.64 against 103.28) because the
   constant-string loop lets the JIT cache the split. **A per-row helper must be benchmarked over
   per-row DATA.** It is still not used, for a SEMANTIC reason: `replaceAll` expands `$&`/`$1` in
   the replacement where `split`/`join` and native's `str::replace` do not, so it would diverge
   cross-engine on any replacement containing a `$`.
2. **A `typeof v === 'string'` fast path in `str()` is worth nothing.** It tries `isRecord`,
   `isElement`, `Array.isArray` and `instanceof Path` before `String(v)`, and `replaceScalar` calls
   it three times a row — measured **0.202 ns a call either way**. The JIT folds the chain when the
   site is monomorphic.

**TWO UNTESTED BEHAVIOURS, found by mutation and now pinned.** Both mutants passed the 2,587 unit
tests AND all seven fuzzers:

- **`sanitizeSurrogates` had NO test.** Making it never sanitize was invisible — the fuzzers
  generate no non-ASCII strings (item 765 found this for `char_length`; it covers this whole
  function). Now pinned: a surrogate PAIR sliced in half yields U+FFFD through `substring`, `left`
  and `right`; an INTACT pair survives; a no-surrogate string is unchanged.
- **No test used a MULTI-CHARACTER search in `replace`.** Advancing by one unit instead of
  `search.length` is wrong for every longer search and nothing noticed. Now pinned, including an
  OVERLAPPING search (`replace('aaa', 'aa', 'b')` is `'ba'` — one match) and a kept tail.

Teeth verified: both surviving mutants now FAIL the unit suite. This was also the first unexpected
mutation result this session to arrive WITH evidence of execution, which is the check item 767 put
in `CLAUDE.md` after three runner-startup failures were nearly read as findings.

**Still open:** the two-argument string PREDICATES remain on the TS general path (59-71 ns against
`char_length`'s 24). Natively they went 4.5x at item 766, but partly through a `Col::Bool` output
with no TS equivalent, so expect less. `substring` at 87 ns is still the dearest string row.

## 769 — TS: the two-argument string predicates 1.57-2.43x, `byte_length` 1.49-1.76x. The check ORDER had no test, and `regex_match` is unreachable from GQL

**DONE (TypeScript).** `BINARY_STR_PRED` + `binaryStrPredCall` for `contains`/`starts_with`/
`ends_with`, the counterpart of item 766's native `eval_binary_str_pred`. Two alternated A/B reads:
`starts_with` **2.43x / 2.00x**, `contains` **2.05x / 1.68x**, `ends_with` **1.93x / 1.87x**,
two-slot `starts_with` **1.79x / 1.57x**. The sharpest control is `split` — two arguments, the SAME
two asserted positions, unspecialized — at 0.95x / 1.02x.

**Quote the range, not a figure.** The controls span 0.87-1.17x across the two reads, so this
instrument's band for these rows is about ±15%.

**Smaller than native's 4.5x, as item 766 predicted:** part of that was writing a `Col::Bool`
output column instead of a boxed one, and TypeScript has no typed columns.

**`byte_length`/`octet_length` were in the wrong dispatcher.** They are ONE-argument string

the tables are organized by family rather than by arity.

positions before the nullish short-circuit, so `starts_with(null, 5)` THROWS while
`starts_with(null, 'a')` is null. Writing the specialized closure the other way round — nullish
first, one branch cheaper, the way it reads most naturally — **passes all 2,589 unit tests and all
seven byte-identity fuzzers** while silently turning that data exception into a null. Pinned now,

had no test** (768: `sanitizeSurrogates`, multi-character `replace`; 764: `coalesce`'s values).

**A CONFORMANCE QUESTION, not a perf one:** `regex_match` is in `STR_ARG_POSITIONS` and in the
scalar library, but the GQL surface REJECTS it — a probe using it died with
`E_UNKNOWN_FUNCTION: regex_match()`. So the presence of a name in the scalar tables does not mean
the surface accepts it. Worth deciding deliberately rather than leaving as an accident.

**Still open:** `split` at 164-180 ns a row is now the dearest TS string shape, and part of that is
inherent — it returns a LIST per row. Whether the rest is the general path or the split itself has

## 770 — a zero-allocation dense-id render is REFUTED at 1.00x; item 342's per-key term re-confirmed at ~2.1 ns/key; `regex_match` is Gremlin's by design

**NO ENGINE CHANGE.** Ten ticks (759-769) worked inside the scalar path, so this one re-priced the
whole `query_bench` surface first. Element projection dwarfs everything: `hop node, NO distinct`
**599 ns/row** and `distinct node` **603**, against `cmp str prop/prop` at 48 and `project 3` at 27.

**REFUTED — a zero-allocation dense-id render.** `node_result_value` does
`GStr::from(id.to_string())` for any node with no EXTERNAL id: a malloc, the digits, a copy into
the `GStr`, a free, per rendered element. A `u32` is ≤10 digits and `GStr` inlines 12 bytes, so a
stack buffer makes the allocation impossible. **Three alternated rounds, two saved binaries: 1.00x,
1.00x, 0.98x, 1.01x, 0.98x.** Nothing. Do not re-derive it.

**AND THE 65 ns GAP THAT MOTIVATED IT IS UNATTRIBUTED, not explained.** `RETURN p` over 200,000
three-property nodes cost **383 ns/row without external ids against 312 with**, stable across three
runs. That looked like the id formatting; the refutation above proves it is not. The two sides are
two different STORES (one carries a 200,000-entry ext-id index), not two paths through one store —
item 339's rule applies (_"if the sentences differ in more than one clause the ratio needs a third
measurement, not an explanation"_), and the zero-allocation A/B was that third measurement. Also
WITHDRAWN from this item's first draft: the claim that corpus element rows are inflated by the
id-less fixture. The per-row id cost is zero, so they are not.

**ITEM 342'S LADDER IS NOT REFUTED — its term is re-confirmed.** Holding PRESENT properties at
three and varying the store's column count: `RETURN n` 376 / 393 / 440 ns/row at 3 / 10 / 30
columns, so **~2.1 ns per extra store key per row**, matching the 1.79 ns/key recorded at items
340/740 about thirty items later. `RETURN n.a` is flat (2.45-2.48) and `count(*)` takes the
shortcut. I nearly wrote that the ladder "buys 1.5%" from the 3-key case; the record already says
the lever is for a HETEROGENEOUS store (50-200 keys, a handful per node), where the term is ~180
ns/row, and a 3-30 key fixture cannot speak to it. Confirmed from the code too: `render_nodes` and
`render_edges` already hoist the per-key column resolution, so the ~2.1 ns/key IS the hoisted
figure and there is nothing left to hoist.

**`regex_match` — item 769's open conformance question, CLOSED.** The NATIVE parser rejects
`regex_match` and `_regex_match` too, so both engines agree, and native's own comment names the
owner: it is the Gremlin `regex()` predicate sharing the scalar library. By design, not a gap.

**Still open and NOT tick-sized:** element rendering's floor is the allocation per element — the id,
the labels `Value::List`, the properties `Value::Map` behind an `Arc`. Item 341 found the structural
answer (the TS engine does not materialize an element at all, and does the same work in 213 ns/row
against native's 492), so the lever is LAZINESS, a representation change.

## 771 — element rendering: 1.03-1.04x from the LOOP FORM, the pair-`Vec` growth ladder is refuted, and a multi-case probe faked a 3.2x regression

**DONE (Rust), small and attributed to the right cause.** `render_nodes`/`render_edges` build the
property pairs with an explicit `for` loop instead of
`.iter().enumerate().filter().map().collect()`, reserving on the FIRST push. One case per process,
three alternated rounds: **dense (3 of 3 present) 1.04x, sparse (0 of 3) 1.03x**, controls `p.a`
1.00x and `labels(p)` 0.99x, series non-overlapping.

**THE DECOMPOSITION, which is the part to keep.** `RETURN p` over 200,000 three-property nodes, by
part: `p.a` 2.70, three scalars 24.81, `element_id(p)` 9.54, `labels(p)` **85.91**, id + labels +
three scalars 141.48, **the element 383.46**. So ~242 ns is the map ASSEMBLY rather than reading
values. On ONE store with three property columns: a node with **3 of 3 present costs 393.21 ns
against 104.23 with 0 of 3**.

**REFUTED — the pair `Vec`'s growth ladder as the cost.** `collect()` from a `filter` reserves
nothing (`size_hint` lower bound 0), so the pairs grow 1, 2, 4 and ~96 ns per property looked like
three allocations and two copies. Pre-sizing is worth **~15 ns of 384, not ~190**: the 289 ns for
three properties is the property WORK (reads, `Value` clones, key clones). The arithmetic was fine
and the causal story was wrong.

**AND THE GAIN IS NOT THE RESERVATION.** `dense` and `sparse` both move 3-4%, and a sparse node
reserves nothing and pushes nothing — so the loop form is what moved them. The reservation is kept
because it is correct and cannot fire on an empty node, but it is NOT separately measurable and
should not be cited as a win.

**A MULTI-CASE PROBE FAKED A 3.2x REGRESSION, and the tell was a control.** The first version used
`Vec::with_capacity` UP FRONT, which allocates even when nothing is present — a real design flaw,
since a heterogeneous store is mostly sparse. The multi-case probe showed the sparse row at
96.76 -> 308.19 (3.2x worse) — and in the same table a store with NO property columns, where the
reserve is `min(0, 16) = 0` and the code is unchanged, went 216 -> 91 (2.37x FASTER). A row the
change cannot reach cannot move 2.37x. The probe builds seven stores and runs sixteen queries in
ONE process, so a change to the early rows' allocation pattern moves the late ones — exactly why
`strag_421` carries `PROBE_ONLY`. One case per process showed no regression anywhere (sparse
1.03x). The design flaw was still real, so the shipped version reserves on the first push.

**Still open:** `labels(p)` at 86 ns for a ONE-label list — `labels_of_refs` allocates a `Vec<&str>`
to sort and then the renderer allocates a `Vec<Value>`, two where one would do. `GStr::cmp` is
`as_bytes().cmp()`, the same order as `&str`, so sorting the `Value`s directly is byte-identical;
it needs an iterator accessor on the store. Expect ~15 ns of 384 by the same reasoning as above, so
measure it with the one-case-per-process harness before believing it. The structural answer for
this row remains item 341's: the TS engine does not materialize an element at all (213 ns/row
against native's 492).

## 772 — the labels path: ONE allocation instead of two. 1.07x at one label, 0.99x at three — and item 767's execution check confirmed the in-loop fuzz failure mechanism

**DONE (Rust), with the trade stated both ways.** Item 771 priced `labels(p)` at 85.91 ns a row for
a ONE-element list: `labels_of_refs` allocates a `Vec<&str>` to sort, then every caller that wants
`Value`s allocates a second `Vec`. `Store::label_names_of(id)` now yields the names borrowed and
UNSORTED with no allocation, and the three render sites collect the `Value`s once and sort them in
place. Byte-identical by construction — `GStr` orders by `as_bytes().cmp()`, which IS `&str`'s byte
order.

One case per PROCESS, three alternated rounds (item 771's instrument): `labels(x)` with ONE label
**1.07x** (87.93 -> 82.14, series separate), with THREE labels **0.99x**, with ZERO labels 1.01x,
`x.a` scalar control 0.99x, full `RETURN x` element **1.02x**.

**THE TRADE GOES BOTH WAYS, so do not quote only the 1.07x.** At one label the saved allocation
wins 7%; at three it loses ~1%, because sorting `Value` enums costs a `match` per comparison where
sorting `&str` did not, and that grows with the label count while the saved allocation does not.
One label is overwhelmingly the common case and 0.99x is inside the band the untouched controls
show, so it ships — but a multi-label-heavy store does not benefit.

**The accessor's contract is a hazard worth reading before reusing it:** `label_names_of` returns
INTERN order, not sorted. The canonical order every consumer relies on is by NAME (item 724), so a
caller that forgets to sort is wrong in a way no type catches. Mutation confirms the order is
pinned: removing the sort FAILS, reversing it FAILS, and the unreachable non-`Str` arm is
EQUIVALENT (it is `Equal` rather than a panic so a future caller cannot turn a render into an
abort).

**ITEM 767'S EXECUTION CHECK EARNED ITSELF ONE TICK LATER — the mechanism is now confirmed by
instrument.** The equivalent mutant's first in-loop reading was `fuzz=FAIL(1)` where SURVIVE was
predicted, the FOURTH time this session (765, 766, 767, 772). Item 767 had diagnosed it as a
runner-startup failure and added the rule that a mutation verdict needs evidence of EXECUTION, not
an exit code. The harness now checks for a result line and prints **`fuzz=DID-NOT-RUN`**, and the
verdict reads SURVIVE as predicted. Items 765/766 called this "the documented run-many flake";
that attribution is superseded — the fuzz process exits non-zero WITHOUT running a test.

**One self-inflicted error, caught by the gate:** the new accessor was spliced between
`labels_of_refs`' own `#[must_use]` and its signature, so the attribute landed on a function
returning an `Iterator` (already `#[must_use]`) and clippy failed with `double_must_use`. Same
shape as item 733's orphaned doc block — inserting above a function means inserting above its
ATTRIBUTES, not just its doc comment.

**Still open:** `labels(p)` at 82 ns for one label is still 30x a scalar read; what remains is the
`Value::List` allocation and a `GStr` per label. For the full element, item 771 stands: ~242 ns is
map assembly, and the structural answer is item 341's laziness.

## 773 — TS: `split` joins item 769's two-argument string table, 1.24-1.54x. The empty-delimiter contract had NO test, and the in-loop fuzzers run NOTHING

**DONE (TypeScript).** `BINARY_STR_PRED` widened to `BINARY_STR_FN` (`(s, sub) => unknown`) with
`split` added, so it uses the closure item 769 built — whose check-ORDER test now guards all four
names. Two alternated reads, one shape per process: `count(split(a.s, '0'))` **1.36x / 1.24x**,

and `s.split('0')` in a tight loop over the same 200,000 strings is 56.06 — so ~50 ns was
machinery, above `to_list`'s ~29, which fits one more argument step and one more asserted position.

**`split`'s body MUST stay in `splitScalar`** — the entry is `(s, sub) => splitScalar(s, sub)`, not
`s.split(sub)`. They differ on exactly one input class: an EMPTY delimiter over a surrogate pair.
JS keeps the lone surrogates; this engine replaces each with U+FFFD (native's UTF-8 cannot carry
one — item 768's deviation). **The simplification passed all 2,590 tests**, so it is now pinned:
`split('a😀b','')` is `['a','�','�','b']`. FOURTH consecutive tick where a contract one of
my own fast paths depends on had no test (768, 769, 764 being the others).

**A SWEEP RESULT WORTH MORE THAN THE CHANGE: TS edge projection is ~22x node projection per row.**
`project the edge [ts lazy]` 496.6 ms over 1,000,000 rows (496 ns/row) against
`project the element [ts lazy]` 4.5 ms over 200,000 (22.5 ns/row); materialized, 933 against 130.
No record covers this. The sweep's largest rows are the decode fixtures (3425.9 ms for pg-text at 5
edges/node) and those were NOT chased — `ts-ingest-is-constant-factor` closes them.

**THE IN-LOOP FUZZERS CONTRIBUTE NO SIGNAL, and the check from 767/772 now says so out loud.** All
three mutants this tick reported `fuzz=DID-NOT-RUN` — no result line at all, not a failure. Without

**Also recorded:** the mutation script crashed mid-run on a variable name AFTER building mutant 1
