## 1113 — 🔶 LOCATED (Rust): the multi-column render writes the output buffer TWICE — a second NUMERIC column is **+12.5 ns a row**, 2.7x the first column's whole cost

Item 1111's decomposition had `hop prop` 4.7 ns/row against `hop two props` 23.9 — but those rows
differ in TYPE as well as COUNT (`q.age` versus `q.age, q.city`). Two rows separate the axes:

```text
  hop prop (1 numeric)        4.7 ns/row      hop two num props (2 numeric)  17.2 ns/row
  hop str prop (1 string)    14.9             hop two props (num+string)     23.9
```

- **TYPE: +10.2 ns** for a string over a number — a `GStr` clone against an f64 move. The cost of
  the data, not a defect.
- **COUNT: +12.5 ns** for a second NUMERIC column — 2.7x everything the first column costs.

**Cause:** `exec::try_run` has two shapes. `ncols == 1` moves the column's cells straight into the
row buffer ("their cells ARE the rows, no transpose"); `ncols >= 2` allocates
`vec![Value::Null; n * ncols]` and then `render_col_into` strides `out[i * ncols + c]` per column —
so the whole buffer is **written twice**, once as NULL and once with values. Every cell is covered
by the column loop, so the pre-fill is pure waste. One extra pass over a multi-word-enum buffer at
memory bandwidth is ~10 ns a row, consistent with the 12.5.

**NOT BUILT.** The obvious restructurings trade one pass for another (columns to `Vec<Value>` then
interleave = columns written once + output once = still two). The win needs the buffer filled
without the `Value::Null` init, and the safe routes must be measured against item 828's finding in
`render_nodes` — rows-outside/columns-inside costs K cache lines a row, which bit hard at K=200 and
should not at K=2, but "should not" is what this corpus exists to check. Controls for that
measurement are already in the bench: `hop prop` (one column, unreachable) and `hop str prop` (the
type axis, must not move).

## 1114 — ❌ REFUTED, and it CORRECTS 1113: the multi-column pre-fill is worth **~2 ns a row, not ~10**, and removing it costs any STRING column more than it saves

1113 attributed its +12.5 ns-a-row multi-column penalty to the output buffer being written twice
(pre-filled with `Value::Null`, then overwritten), estimating ~10 ns of it. Built
`render_rows_major` — one row-major pass, `Vec::with_capacity` + push, element/`Gen` columns
resolved once per column — and measured both ways of getting a cell out:

```text
                       PRE        clone per cell     move per cell
  hop two num props   1719.0         1519.6             1536.1
  hop two props       2393.9         2619.3             2784.3
  project 3            493.7          508.6              679.1
  hop prop   CONTROL   469.6          468.2              474.7
  hop str prop CTRL   1485.0         1504.1             1480.1
```

- **Two NUMERIC columns 1719.0 → 1519.6 (11.6%)** — no string, so no clone, so this isolates the
  pre-fill: **~2 ns a row.** 1113's estimate was out by 5x and its ~10.5 ns remainder is NOT the
  extra pass.
- **Any STRING column regresses.** Indexing instead of consuming forces a CLONE (+9.4%) or a
  `mem::take`, which writes a placeholder back — exactly the write the pre-fill was — and is worse
  still (+16%; `project 3` 1.38x the wrong way).

⚠️ **The general reason, so this is not re-attempted:** you cannot move a cell out of an indexed
`Vec` without writing something in its place. Column-major gets its moves free from `into_iter()`;
any row-major build clones or writes back, and both cost about what the pre-fill cost. Controls held
throughout (`hop prop` 468-475 vs 469.6; `hop str prop` 1480-1504 vs 1485.0).

**NOT SHIPPED**, reverted, baseline reproduces. A numeric-only variant is genuinely available at
11.6% (every output column `Num`/`Bool`), unshipped because it buys ~2 ns a row on a narrow shape
for a second render path — recorded so that is a decision, not a rediscovery.

**Still open:** the +12.5 ns. The render is now measured at ~2 ns of it, so the remaining ~10.5 ns
is upstream — the PROJECTION evaluating two expressions instead of one. `hop two num props` vs
`hop prop` isolates it with the type axis held constant.

## 1115 — 🔶 PRICED, and it corrects 1114's remaining framing: the extra output column's cost is **being a column**, not reading anything — a CONSTANT column costs 11.4 ns a row against a gathered one's 12.3

1114 left +12.5 ns a row per extra output column with ~2 ns attributed and pointed at "the
projection evaluating two expressions", still assuming the cost involved READING a second value.

```text
  hop prop (1 col)               5.0 ns/row
  hop prop + const col          16.4          +11.4   <- no source, no gather, no presence check
  hop two num props             17.3          +12.3
  hop prop + three const cols   30.2          +8.4 per extra column, linear
```

**The read is worth under 1 ns of the 12.** Every output column is MATERIALIZED as a full `Col` and
then COPIED into the row-major buffer — for a constant that is `exec::broadcast`'s
`Col::Num(vec![x; n])`, 100,000 copies of one f64 allocated and written so the render can copy each
once more. Decomposition: fill the `Col` ~6-9 ns, pre-fill the output ~2 ns (refuted as a target at
1114), copy in ~2 ns.

**Actionable but not built:** a constant column need not be materialized — `broadcast` could be a
scalar plus a length. Bounded, but it needs a new `Col` variant and every `match` on `Col` in the
engine must handle it, for a shape rare in real queries. Recorded so it is a trade, not a
rediscovery.

**Not a defect:** a columnar projection that materializes each column and then transposes pays for
the transpose. The alternative is row-wise evaluation into the output buffer, and 1114 measured what
that costs when a cell must be cloned or written back. **~8-11 ns a row per output column is the
engine's design, now priced** — that number is the result.

## 1117 — 🔶 the maintained per-type count's SITE LIST, from the code: **nine sites, two at `Vec` granularity**, and one of those is a restore (item 1042's seven were per-entry)

Item 1116 reproduced the 85x and named the fix (a global per-type count, O(1) per write, as TS
already has). The count must be `counts[t] = |{ live out_adj entries with etype == t }|`, because
`rebuild_csr` partitions on `a.etype` (the PRIMARY type) and `out_typed_flat(t)?.len()` is exactly
that.

Searching for `out_adj` STRUCTURAL MUTATIONS, not for function names:

```text
  +1  3705  add_edge / add_edge_with_id        -1  5244  delete_edge (dropped_etype captured)
  +1  6087  Undo::RestoreEdge (is_out guard)   -N  5616  delete_node_inner: mem::take a WHOLE Vec
  +1  6126  Undo::RestoreNode mirror entry     -1  5629  delete_node_inner: neighbour's mirror
  +N  6130  Undo::RestoreNode: out_adj[i] = out — a WHOLE Vec
  +N  6297  Builder load path (rebuilds anyway)     -0  6203  out_adj.pop() (already emptied)
```

⚠️ **The two `Vec`-granularity sites are what a per-entry hook misses, and one is a RESTORE.**
`Undo::RestoreNode` puts a deleted node's entire out list back by assignment, so a counter updated
only at `push` sites under-counts after a rolled-back `delete_node` — a WRONG typed count
thereafter, silently, on the undo path only. The existing `push_etype_entry` hook cannot be copied:
it maintains the OPT-IN edge-type index beside the per-entry pushes, where this counter must be
unconditional and must also track those moves.

**Implementation shape:** a `Vec<usize>` by etype (grown on intern, cloned with the store); deltas
at the seven live sites; **a `debug_assert` recomputing from `out_adj`** so a missed site fails
loudly across the 1,267-test suite and the fuzzers rather than answering wrongly — that assertion is
what makes the change safe, and it lands before any consumer. Then wire
`fastpath::typed_hop_count_from_size` and `fastpath::try_edge_label_count`, which end in
`out_typed_flat(t)?` and decline whenever the overlay is stale.

**NOT implemented this tick, deliberately** — nine sites, two at `Vec` granularity, with a wrong
answer on an undo path as the failure mode, is not a half-tick change. The list is now from the
code rather than from a note, which is the previous tick's lesson applied.

  per-type total cannot serve a per-node degree; that is `slice_degree`'s question (item 1101).
- `exec.rs:5084` — `for_each_typed_out` needs the **ENTRIES** (it visits neighbours), so its `?` is
  a real freshness gate and stays one.
- `exec/reverse.rs:203` — reads a **LENGTH**, and is the one that could.

**That site's `fwd` silently becomes 0 after any adjacency write** (`filter_map` drops every type
once `out_typed_flat` returns `None`), so the `fwd > 0 &&` guard skips its decline for the rest of
the session — the same defect 1118 fixed, in a different dress, and answer-equivalent so no test can
see it.

⚠️ **`live_etype_count` would restore it in one line and is deliberately NOT used.** The estimate
prices a forward alternative that is itself freshness-gated (`for_each_typed_out` returns `None` when
stale), so after a write the cheap forward sweep this guard would decline _in favour of_ may not
exist — and a correct `fwd` could decline the reverse seed into the GENERAL path, possibly slower
than what it replaced. **`fwd = 0` may be accidentally right.** Deciding it is a measurement on the
shape that function's own comment names (`age >= 77` = 92k seeds vs 80k forward F edges), not an
argument.

**Site ANNOTATED, behaviour unchanged.** The annotation records the staleness, names the fix and says
why it is withheld — because the risk is now the opposite one: with `live_etype_count` in the tree,
the next reader has an obvious-looking one-liner and no written reason to measure first.

## 1120 — ❌ the `fwd`-estimate one-liner is MEASURED NEUTRAL (not shipped); ✅ and the same probe prices the half item 1118 did NOT fix: a FILTERED typed count still pays **6x** after one write

Item 1119 named the fix (`live_etype_count` for `reverse_seed_decide`'s `fwd`, which silently
becomes 0 after any write) and withheld it pending measurement. Measured, on the shape that
function's own comment names — 200,000 nodes / 80,000 sparse `F` edges /
`MATCH (a)-[:F]->(b) WHERE b.age >= 77 RETURN count(*)`, min of 5:

```text
  FRESH 257.9 us    STALE 1556.9 (6.0x)    STALE+rebuild_csr 207.2
  alternated:  PRE (fwd broken) 1530.6 / 1536.8    POST (fwd correct) 1535.6 / 1525.1
```

**Identical — NOT SHIPPED.** Both branches cost the same once stale: `fwd = 0` skips the guard and
keeps the reverse seed; a correct `fwd` fires it and declines — into the general path, because the
forward sweep it prefers is ALSO freshness-gated. A route choice no test can police, with no
measured benefit, is not a change.

**🔶 THE 6x IS THE FINDING.** Item 1118's maintained count does NOT reach this shape:
`typed_hop_count_from_size` needs an unfiltered whole-graph hop, and an endpoint filter sends the
query through the walk, which loses `out_typed_flat`/`out_typed_csr` the instant the overlay goes
stale (rebuilt reference 207.2 vs 1556.9 stale). **So the cliff splits in two:**

- **GLOBAL per-type count** — FIXED at 1118 (0.347 → 0.003 ms) by maintaining one integer per type;
- **PER-NODE typed adjacency** — still **6x** on a filtered shape, unreachable by a global count.
  This is item 852's "only undisproven design", incremental per-type CSR maintenance, with the bar
  it must clear: `O(E + types × N)` amortized over fewer than 6 reads.

1118 took the half one integer per type could carry; the other half now has a 6x price on a named
shape instead of a general claim. The temporary probe was removed (851/852's pattern) and its
numbers live in `reverse.rs`'s annotation.

## 1121 — ⚠️ REVISES 852: its "6 to 27 stale reads" belongs to a query that NO LONGER HAS A PENALTY; on the shape that does, the break-even is **~2 reads**, stable across a 10x fixture range

852 refused an unconditional rebuild-at-commit hook at a 6-27 read break-even, measured with
`MATCH (a:P)-[:T0]->(b) RETURN count(*)`. **Item 1118 removed that query's penalty entirely**
(fresh 0.3 µs, stale 0.3, penalty 0.0 — it is answered from the maintained count), so 852's number
is now quoted for a shape that cannot produce it.

On item 1120's filtered endpoint predicate, swept (min of 5, break-even = `rebuild / (stale −
fresh)`):

```text
  nodes    edges    rebuild    fresh    stale   penalty   BREAK-EVEN
  200,000   80,000   2757.0     232.0   1548.9   1316.9     2.09 reads
  200,000  400,000   5254.6    1380.6   3811.4   2430.9     2.16
  400,000  400,000   8686.2    1462.2   5359.4   3897.2     2.23
  800,000  800,000  17189.3    2905.4  11626.8   8721.4     1.97
```

**1.97-2.23 across 10x of both axes** — rebuild and penalty are both ~O(E), so the ratio is a
property of the SHAPE, not the fixture, which 852's single row could not show.

**Does NOT license a commit hook.** 852's policy objection survives in form and a rebuild per commit
still loses on write-only workloads. What changes is the size of the bet: at 6-27 reads an
unconditional hook is a gamble, at **2** any serving workload that reads after a write has paid for
it. And 852's "depends on a future read count the store does not have" has an answer it did not
consider — **the store can know the PAST count.** Reads served since the last rebuild is a cheap
counter and a standard proxy; a hook gated on it costs nothing write-only and converges for
serving. NEXT THING TO TRY, now with a break-even to size it against.

⚠️ **A measurement error worth the entry:** the first sweep gave IDENTICAL numbers at three fixture
sizes (2634/2659/2678). `set -- $cfg` — **zsh does not word-split unquoted parameters** — so every
arm used the same defaults. The TELL: three fixtures differing 5x agreeing to 1% is the instrument,
not the result.

## 1122 — ✅ SHIPPED: the CSR re-arms at the QUERY BOUNDARY after 4 stale reads — **1.68x at ten reads per write, 2.74x at twenty**, nothing measurable below five

The design item 852's objection left open. 851 excluded a LAZY rebuild structurally; 852 refused an
UNCONDITIONAL commit hook because "the policy it would need depends on a future read count the store
does not have"; 1121 measured the real break-even at 1.97-2.23 reads. **The store cannot know the
future count but it can know the PAST one**, and `lnk_query` already holds `store_mut` — a mutable
borrow taken before any accessor has lent out a reference, which is exactly what 851's exclusion
turned on.

**The threshold is the change, and it is measured.** One write then `k` reads, min of 5:

```text
   k     PRE      T=2      T=3      T=4          then alternated x3 on T=4:
   1     1.5      1.6      1.5      1.5            k=1  1.5 -> 1.5   flat
   2     3.0      4.3✗     3.0      3.0            k=2  3.1 -> 3.0   flat
   3     4.5      4.6      5.8✗     4.5            k=3  4.5 -> 4.5   flat
   5     7.5      5.1      6.4      7.6            k=5  7.4 -> 7.6   +2.7% (reported)
  10    14.9      6.3      7.6      8.9            k=10 14.8 -> 8.8  1.68x
  20    29.6      8.4      9.4     10.9            k=20 29.6 -> 10.8 2.74x
```

Every threshold has a loss band where the rebuild fires unamortized (T=2: 1.43x at k=2; T=3: 1.29x at
k=3). **T=4 is the smallest with none above the noise floor.** The +2.7% at k=5 is break-even by
construction and is stated, not rounded away. A write RESETS the count, so small write batches never
accumulate into a rebuild — `k=1` flat is that measured.

**Teeth: 4 of 4 after two survivors got two DIFFERENT answers.**
⚠️ `no-reset-after-rebuild` survived because the line was **REDUNDANT** (`rebuild_csr` sets
`csr_fresh`, so the guard early-returns; only `invalidate_csr` returns to stale and it resets the
count itself) — **deleted, not tested.** A surviving mutant is sometimes the measurement saying the
code cannot matter.
⚠️ `ignores-fresh` survived because it is a **PERF GATE** — dropping the `csr_fresh` guard rebuilds
every 4th query on a store needing none, answer-neutrally, and `csr_fresh` is true either way. Added
a `#[cfg(test)]` `stale_reads()` accessor so the gate's only observable is assertable.

**Scope:** the hook is at `lnk_query`, so it covers both TS engines and every FFI consumer, NOT the
in-process Rust API `query_bench` uses — which is why the numbers come from a TS probe
(`rearm-probe.ts`, kept) and the bench groups are unchanged.

Rust 1269+13+725 pass; native 933 / gql 3117 / gremlin 918; fuzzers 13/0.

## 1123 — 🔶 item 292's blocker on caching the OPTIMIZED plan is AVOIDABLE: the optimizer already plans `Prop <op> Param`, so optimize-then-bind still seeds

`bench:usage`'s `read: point lookup` is **ts(+) 977.1k against engine(+) 455.4k** — reproduced. 291
exonerated the FFI boundary (8 ns) and accounted for the call; 292 named two avoidable items. The
first, verified against the code:

```text
  ffi.rs:626-630  lnk_query:    optimize_indexed(parse_cache::parse_for_run(…), store)
  ffi.rs:1127     prepared_run: let plan = crate::opt::optimize_indexed(plan, store);
```

**Parse is cached (228/229), optimize is not** — 295-330 ns of a ~3000 ns call, ~11% of the prepared
path's 2648 ns.

**292's blocker was bind-THEN-optimize, not the optimizer.** It recorded that parse substitutes
params so the plan depends on their VALUES. But `opt.rs:3805-3806` matches
`(Prop, Lit | Param)` — the optimizer plans a PARAM the same way it plans a literal. So optimizing
the prepared plan and binding AFTERWARDS still seeds, and that plan is param-independent and
text-cacheable — which is what `prepared_run`'s own comment already claims it does.

**Needs:** a STORE VERSION in the key (292 identified it; `Store::version()` exists at
store.rs:1771) because a cached plan seeking a dropped index is a WRONG answer. ⚠️ **And a trade
that is not free:** an optimized-once plan is no longer VALUE-specific — fine for a seek, but
`reverse_seed_decide` and `cost::estimate` both read values, so this is classic parameter sniffing.
**Measure that first:** a fixture where two param values want different plans, and what one plan
costs them.

Not built. ~11% of the prepared serving call, two lines, correctness key and risk both named.

## 1124 — ✅ item 1122's serving A/B RESOLVES clean (the flagged row was variance); ❌ item 1123's "blocker is avoidable" is REFUTED — a param-independent plan is a SCAN and costs **3.7x** on the selective value

**1122, `bench:usage` `engine(+)`, alternated ×2:**

```text
  read: point lookup      CTRL  490.0k/491.4k -> 452.0k/507.2k   the 452.0 did NOT reproduce
  read: 2-hop             CTRL  255.7k/257.7k -> 254.0k/255.7k   flat
  interleaved: w+point read      218.8k/216.5k -> 219.1k/219.5k   flat
  interleaved: w+traversal       180.3k/184.3k -> 188.3k/188.9k   +2.5%
  interleaved: append+link       264.7k/287.0k -> 281.4k/280.3k   within range
```

1123 logged the first POST point-lookup reading as PENDING, not as a regression. Correct both ways:
it was variance (second POST is the best of four), and it was not called variance before the data.

**❌ 1123 REFUTED.** It argued 292's blocker was avoidable because `opt.rs:3805` matches
`(Prop, Lit | Param)`, so optimize-then-bind should still seed. Measured on
`WHERE p.age >= $t`, 200,000 nodes, `age = i % 100`, range index, min of 5:

```text
  t = 99 (1%)   own plan 27.6 us    param-independent 101.9 us   3.7x WORSE   (plans DIFFER)
  t = 0  (all)  own plan 101.8      param-independent 101.8      (IDENTICAL)
```

**The param-independent plan costs what the SCAN costs** — it does not seek. Matching `(Prop, Param)`
collects a candidate KEY; the seek is then gated on SELECTIVITY, which needs the VALUE. Item 409
built that gate on purpose, so declining a param is the gate working.

⚠️ **292's blocker holds for a reason neither 292 nor 1123 stated:** not that parse substitutes
params, nor that the shape is unrecognisable — **the seek DECISION is value-dependent by design.**
Caching the optimized plan trades ~295 ns of optimize for **3.7x on the indexed selective read
`bench:usage` measures.** A `(text, version, param values)` key would hit only when a value repeats,
which the serving shape does not. The optimize cost is the price of value-specific planning.
Refuted for one probe rather than a plan cache plus a correctness key.

## 1125 — ❌ the 3-hop product's per-edge hash REFUTED BEFORE BUILT (items 355 + 495); 🔶 and THREE independent bodies now show the same **~110-150 ns residual** against a **41 ns** micro floor

`count 3-hop` (~300 ms vs native 4.7) takes the degree PRODUCT (1103), so its body was never ablated.
Hot line: `count += waysToA * dSide(graph, midOut ? e.toId : e.fromId)` — a string hash per MIDDLE
EDGE, with `e.to` memoized on the edge right there. Passing the vertex looks free.

**It is not.** ⚠️ **Item 355:** that swap is **1.21x WORSE on first touch** (203.4/171.3 against
247.0/127.1) because the box pays the same hash plus a memo write — _a memo helps a REVISITED element
and taxes a VISITED-ONCE one._ ⚠️ **Item 495** then measured it on the revisited position and got
**FLAT**, concluding: _"492 and 494 won by doing ONE LOOKUP INSTEAD OF TWO, not by the box being
cheaper. **Do not price a box swap that does not also remove a lookup.**"_ The `!needsC` branch
already hashes ONCE from the edge's stored id — resolving `e.to` would ADD a resolve, which is the
two-lookup shape 495 moved away from. No probe run; two items already ran it on both positions.

**Item 310's attribution of this loop is now two-thirds STALE:** it blamed "the `edgesOfTypes`
generator frame … the `Edge` property reads, and two hash lookups". Item 324 removed the generator
and item 1104's counters proved the fast path is taken **3,600,000 of 3,600,000** times; and this
branch does ONE hash, not two.

**🔶 THE REAL OPEN QUESTION, visible only across items:**

```text
  body                                in-situ/edge   micro floor
  GQL way-count sweep   (1104/1105)      190 ns         41 ns
  Gremlin multiplicity walk  (1109)      158 ns         41 ns
  GQL 3-hop degree product   (1125)     ~150 ns         41 ns
```

Three unrelated bodies, each **3.7-4.6x** a micro built on the engine's own shapes, and in each the
named suspects were refuted one by one (generator 324/1104; per-edge Map 24% at 1105; adjacency
allocation 3-4% at 1108; frontier representation 31.7/158 at 1109; box swap 355/495/1125).

**So the residual belongs to none of the loops.** Item 1105 saw the direction once — "a probe whose
working set is smaller than the engine's UNDERSTATES a cache-sharing cost" — and this is the third
confirmation. **Next instrument: not another ablation, but a micro that grows its working set to the
engine's and shows the floor rising to meet it.** If it does, three targets close at once.

## 1126 — ✅ the residual IS the heap: the SAME minimal body is **80.1 ns** synthetic and **140.0 ns** on a real graph — which CLOSES items 1104/1105, 1109 and 1125's shared target

1125 named the instrument: a micro that grows its working set to the engine's. Built. 200,000
vertices, degree 5, 1,000,000 edges, median of 9 dropping 3, under `timeout` + 16G cgroup cap:

```text
  ARM 1  synthetic heap, minimal body          76.7-80.1 ns/touch   (two runs)
  ARM 2  REAL graph, the SAME minimal body   135.9-140.0        1.75-1.77x, from the HEAP alone
  ARM 3  REAL graph, + per-edge degree read  345.9-353.6        ⚠️ bad model, see below
```

ARM 2 runs **no engine code** — iterate a vertex's adjacency `Set`, read `e.toId`, hash into a
200,000-entry `Map`, accumulate — over a real `Graph` (frozen properties, labels `Set` per edge,
`Map<id, Map<label, Set<Edge>>>` adjacency). **140 ns an edge.**

**That closes the shared target.** The three bodies cost 190 (GQL sweep), 158 (Gremlin walk), ~150
(GQL 3-hop product); a hand-written minimal body on the same data costs 140. The engine code is
worth 10-50 ns on top of an unavoidable 140 — **they are at their floor, and 41 ns was never the
floor.** Every individual refutation (324/1104 generator, 1105 Map, 1108 allocation, 1109 frontier,
355/495/1125 box swap) was right, and their sum could not find a missing 3-4x because there was
none. The remaining ratio is a DATA MODEL question — the dense integer-indexed adjacency CLOSED.md
already records as **refuted on DESIGN, not on perf.** Stop reading these rows as open targets.

⚠️ **ARM 1 is 80.1 where item 1104's equivalent read 41.2** — 2x, and the cause is the same effect:
1104 picked sets RANDOMLY (200,000 picks over 200,000 sets ⇒ ~63% touched), this walks each once. **A
smaller effective working set measured faster — the hypothesis confirming itself inside the
instrument.** 41 understated an already-understated synthetic floor, which is why the gap looked 4x.

⚠️ **ARM 3's 345.9 is a BAD MODEL, not a finding.** It exceeds the whole product's ~150 ns in situ,
which is impossible — `side()` reaches the bucket more cheaply than a double `Map.get` chain.
Recorded rather than dropped, since the number is in the output.

`packages/gql/working-set-probe.ts` is KEPT: ARM 1 vs ARM 2 is the floor any future per-edge claim
here should be judged against.

## 1129 — ❌ item 495's carried "28x apart" for native's per-anchor `COUNT { … }` is REFUTED: **1.3x**, flat across a 4x range of N, and the per-anchor DISPATCH is FREE

`query: 2-hop subquery item` is the widest ratio left on the clean sweep (ts 97.7 vs 5.8, **16.78x**),
and 495 left its native half open: "the whole-graph two-hop count in 2.7 ms and the per-anchor
`COUNT { … }` partition of the same traversal in 75.0 ms … **28x apart**." Measured on one store at
three sizes:

```text
  nodes    whole-graph 2hop   per-anchor COUNT{2}   COUNT{1}   one scalar/anchor
  200,000        3856.2            5106.0            953.2          965.0
  400,000        8526.4           11034.8           1940.5         1915.7
  800,000       18432.1           23071.3           4552.9         4221.4

  COUNT{2}/whole-graph  1.3x / 1.3x / 1.3x      COUNT{1}/one scalar  1.0x / 1.0x / 1.1x
```

**1.3x, not 28x, flat across 4x of N** — not a scale effect. Item 261's rule for the THIRD time this
session: _re-price a carried number before building against it_ (also item 852's break-even, whose
query no longer has a penalty, and item 1123's blocker, refuted at 1124).

**The per-anchor DISPATCH is FREE:** `COUNT { (n)-[:KNOWS]->(m) }` per anchor costs what
`RETURN n.age` per anchor costs (953/965, 1940/1916, 4553/4221) — the degree sum answers a one-hop
subquery and adds nothing over the cheapest one-row-per-anchor query. **The second hop is the whole
of it** (5.1-5.7x the first): 1,000,000 inner degree reads at ~4 ns each. No native target. The row's
ratio is the TS side, where 495 took the 1.25x available and item 1126's ~140 ns/edge floor says
what remains.

⚠️ **One arm was MISLABELLED and the label is corrected rather than the number buried:** I called
`RETURN n.age` the "EGRESS FLOOR" at 4.8-5.3 ns a row, but item 1111 priced native egress at **58 ns
a numeric row** — so that query takes a columnar path and measures no egress floor. It is still the
cheapest one-row-per-anchor query, which is the comparison that carries the conclusion; left

## 1130 — ✅ FOUR in-sweep "movers", ONE cause: the sweep run was globally inflated and its own NULL CONTROL said so; item 1128's comparison was incomplete

1128 isolated two high rows and concluded no regressions. **It checked the rows this session's
changes could reach plus the two that jumped out — not the whole board.** The rest:

```text
  row                                  baseline  sweep  ISOLATED
  count 2-hop                              75.7  101.3      74.8   (1128)
  query: distinct over a reversed hop      68.8   87.3      62.0   (1128)
  query: top groups by count                4.3    8.6       3.5   ← MISSED
  query: top distinct values (ffi)          0.4    1.0       0.4   ← MISSED, NATIVE side
  query: count distinct        CONTROL  3.1/0.4 3.4/0.4   3.1/0.4
```

All four isolate to baseline or better, and **the control is what makes it conclusive**:
`count distinct` isolated = 3.1/0.4 = its baseline in-sweep figure, so the isolated harness agrees
with the baseline and the SWEEP is what differs.

⚠️ **ONE cause, in the sweep's own instrument:** the spelling probe's **null control doubled, 12.5 →
24.9 ms**, in that same run. 1128 used that to say the flag SET was not comparable and stopped —
but it explains the board too: **the whole run was globally inflated**, so four unrelated rows
looked like movers for one reason.

**THE RULE: a sweep carries its own validity check. When the null control moves, no row-to-row
comparison with another run is admissible for ANY row — not just the flagged ones.** The spelling
probe's null control is the instrument for the whole run, not only for its own groups.

Does NOT change 1128's verdict — no regressions, now on four rows with a control pinning the
harness. Its three wins (`3-hop quantified` 2.02x, `var-length 1-3` 1.77x, `MIRROR` 1.68x) were
measured against an inflated run, so if anything understated.

**The lesson is the procedure: compare EVERY row, or compare none.** Checking only the rows a change
can reach finds the regressions you predicted and misses the ones you did not — which is the whole
point of a sweep over a targeted A/B. Two of four missed, one on the NATIVE side where no change
this session touched a distinct-values path.

## 1131 — 🔶 PRICED: the native Gremlin `.values(k).count()` shape is **22.8x** the same traversal's `count()`; the existing `count(prop)` arm cannot help; the O(1) route needs a fact that requires NO maintenance

```text
  V().outE('KNOWS').outV().count()                   58.5 us   a TALLY (edge count, O(1))
  V().values('name').count()                        136.9
  V().outE('KNOWS').outV().values('name').count()  1334.4     22.8x
```

Every fixture node carries `name`, so the answer is 1,000,000 and every row contributes.

⚠️ **`fastpath::try_frontier_count_prop` already answers `count(prop)` over a frontier and CANNOT
help here.** It is written well — `frontier_counts` then one `has_value_at` per DISTINCT vertex — but
`frontier_counts` itself walks the chain: 1,000,000 edge touches for `outE(T).outV()`, which IS the
1334 us. The gap is that **`count(*)` over this frontier is O(1) while `count(k)` is O(rows)**.

**The collapsing fact:** is column `k` present on every LIVE node? Then `count(k)` over any vertex
frontier = the frontier row count = a tally.

⚠️ **A maintained presence count per column is the WRONG design** and was rejected before being
written: its surface is every property write/delete/undo arm — strictly larger than the nine
adjacency sites item 1117 enumerated — for a far narrower shape. **The fact needs no maintenance:**
`present: Vec<bool>` already exists, so it is an O(nodes) SEQUENTIAL ~200 KB scan (plus liveness,
since a deleted node's bit may be false while every live node has the property), computed per query.

⚠️ **NOT MEASURED, and it is the number that decides:** the check's cost against the O(rows) random
walk it replaces. Three items this session (852, 1123, 495) were refuted by building against an
estimate. Prize if the check is ~10-20 us: **1334.4 → ~80 us, ~17x**; cost when it fails: ~1.5% on
top. Measure the check first.

## 1138 — ✅ FIXED a real emit bug (`planToGremlin` could not render a presence filter at all), then measured TWO open spelling gaps — one of which **item 1137 created**

⚠️ **`emit.ts` had NO `hasKey` arm**, so `planToGremlin` threw `unsupported: step hasKey` on any plan
containing a presence filter — and `has('k')` with ONE argument builds `hasKey`, not `has`
(`steps/filters.ts:34`). Both engines always EXECUTED it; only the emitter was blind. Since the
native engine is driven as `natG.gremlin(planToGremlin(plan))`, **a composed plan using `has(k)`
could not reach the native engine at all** — item 877's shape (a step the emitter cannot render is
one the differential path cannot see).

Fixed as `hasKey(...)`, NOT a chain of `has(k)`: the multi-key form is **ANY-of in both engines** (TS
`step.keys.some(...)`, Rust an `Or` of `PropertyExists`), so a chain would be ALL-of and silently
wrong. Verified in both rather than inferred from the name. Also note `has('age', 30)` emits
`has('age', eq(30))` — the implicit equality is rendered explicitly.

`packages/native/present-spelling-probe.ts` (new), 200k nodes / 200k edges, median of 9 dropping 3,
3 runs, both spellings asserted to return the same answer and TS asserted equal to native:

```text
  S2  out.values(age).count  104.5      1.5      [200000]

  ts: S1 172.0/189.8/189.0   S2 104.5/105.2/107.0
  ffi: S1 0.1/0.2/0.1        S2 1.5/1.5/1.5
```

⚠️ **GAP 1 — the TS engine has its own 1.64x**, `has` slower, stable. Separate implementation, not
inherited from the Rust side. OPEN.

⚠️ **GAP 2 — item 1137's claim does NOT generalize, and this corrects it.** 1137 measured T1/T2 at

## 1139 — 🔶 DIAGNOSED to one line: the TS 1.64x is `hasChain` admitting `has(k, pred)` and declining `has(k)`, which is a DIFFERENT step kind — the archetypal spelling bug

`executor/count-shortcut.ts`, `hasChain`: `if (step.kind !== 'has') return undefined;`. A
one-argument `has('age')` builds `{kind:'hasKey'}`, so this declines, every dependent rung declines,
and the query falls to the general stream. Instrumented, not inferred — the trace fired 5x for S1
(once per rep):

```text
  5 TRACE1139 hasChain declines on step kind=hasKey    <- S1 out().has(age).count()
  5 TRACE1139 hasChain declines on step kind=values    <- S2, which has its OWN hop-values route
```

S2 declines the chain too and is still 1.64x faster, so the gap is not "S2 is optimized" but "S1
reaches nothing". ⚠️ **This is exactly CLAUDE.md's archetype** — "recognized one spelling of a
predicate and scanned for another that meant exactly the same thing" — which historically cost
100-300x and always returned the right answer.

⚠️ **DO NOT just widen the `kind` check.** The consumers read `filters[i].key`/`.pred`, and **there
is no presence `Predicate`**: every variant in `ast.ts` reads a VALUE (eq/neq, 4 ordering ops,
between/inside/outside, within/without, 5 TextP ops). `dispatch.ts` evaluates `hasKey` as
`keys.some((k) => k in bag)` — presence, counting a stored present-null, the same `present_at` vs
`has_value_at` distinction that cost a mutant verdict at item 1136. Synthesising
`has(k, <always-true pred>)` would reintroduce it as a silent wrong answer on a present-null, since
every predicate drops missing-or-incomparable via the NaN path.

**Contained design (next tick):** split `rest` into single-key `hasKey` and `has` steps; when `rest`
is PRESENCE-ONLY (the measured shape) take a dedicated arm testing `k in bag` per candidate; leave
the MIXED case declining (correct, merely slow). ⚠️ Deliberately NOT adding a per-row branch to the
existing unrolled loops — this file records entering a call at ~65 ns a row (item 934) and the
unrolls exist to remove exactly that. OPEN.

## 1140 — ✅ SHIPPED **6.15x** on the TS `out().has(k).count()`: a `{op:'present'}` predicate, NOT the duplicated rung item 1139 designed — and the spelling pair is STILL unequal, now the other way

Item 1139 diagnosed the cliff (`hasChain` declines the `hasKey` that `has(k)` builds) and planned a
presence-only rung with its own copy of the vertex-driven loop. **The shipped fix is smaller and
reaches more:** a new `Predicate` variant `{op:'present'}`, one arm in `matches`, one conversion in
`hasChain` — three edits instead of ~40 duplicated lines, and every rung depending on `hasChain`
(edge-hop seed and start-filtered form included) gets it.

⚠️ **The accessor is `!== undefined`, NOT `!= null`** — the same distinction as the Rust engine's
`present_at`/`has_value_at` (item 1136). A property read is `undefined` only for an ABSENT key (the
numeric model converts a written `undefined` to `null`), so this IS `dispatch.ts`'s `k in bag` and a
stored present-null is KEPT. `!= null` drops present-nulls silently.

⚠️ **Multi-key `hasKey` DECLINES** — ANY-of in both engines, while this chain is a CONJUNCTION.

Checked before writing: the type checker found exactly ONE site needing the variant (`matches`), and
`seedForPred` has `default: return null` so a `present` pred cannot mis-seed the property index.

## 1141 — ✅ SHIPPED **3.45x**, and the TS spelling family CLOSES: a trailing single-key `values(k)` under a count folds to a presence filter, so the two spellings now agree within noise

Item 1140 left the pair 3.5x apart with `values` the slow side and recorded the family as open
(the doctrine is cost EQUALITY, not which side wins). Closed here, TS-side.

**Equivalence verified, not assumed** — on a fixture with a value, a stored present-null, an absent
key and a LIST:

```text
  values(k) rows = [1, null, [1,2,3]]   -> 3 rows, NOT 5
  values(k).count() = 3 = hasKey(k).count()
```

A list value is ONE row and a present-null IS emitted. Either going the other way would have made
the fold a wrong answer.

⚠️ **Two guards, neither a formality:** LAST STEP ONLY (`[values(k), has(x,1)]` applies `has` to the
emitted SCALAR, not the element — answers 0), and SINGLE KEY ONLY (`values(a,b)` emits one row per
present key, so its count sums over keys — `values(k,z).count()`=3 where `hasKey(k,z).count()`=2).
Sound at all only because every `hasChain` caller is a COUNT rung, so nothing downstream reads the
value.

## 1148 — ⚠️🔶 OPEN, PRE-EXISTING OPTIMIZER **WRONG ANSWER**: at `rewrite_fuzz` seed 383127, filter-pushdown through a `Join` turns 0 rows into 6 — and the remap arithmetic is CORRECT

Found by item 1147 running the fuzzer deeper than CLAUDE.md's documented 200000. Pre-existing
(pristine `opt.rs` fails identically). Reproduce:

```
LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEED=383127 cargo test --release -- --ignored dump_seed --nocapture
LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=500000 cargo test --release optimizing_preserves_rows_with_indexes
```

```text
  raw: []   optimized: 6 rows   <- the optimizer INVENTS rows
  RAW        Project / Filter{slot2.age<5} / Join{VarLength, Filter{slot3 bounds}}
  OPTIMIZED  Project /                       Join{VarLength, Filter{AND(slot0.age<5, slot3 bounds)}}
```

⚠️ **RULED OUT by reading the contracts** (so do not re-chase these): the remap arithmetic is
correct — `ir.rs` states right slot `j` becomes output slot `left.len() + j`, left is
`VarLength{Scan}` of width 2, so joined slot 2 IS right slot 0 (corroborated by the Project's slot 5
= right slot 3); `VarLength` is not under-counted (`width` and `plan_out_width` agree on `input + 1`;
exec's extra sink columns are `group_cols`, a `RepeatGroup` concern, not `path_need`); the
conjunction is not weakened (3VL `AND` commutes, and both engines short-circuit on FALSE in written
order per items 258/259).

**Suspects, in test order:** (1) `OptionalExpand{keep_source: true}` is LEFT-OUTER, so whether right
slot 0 survives null-padding on the second `OptionalExpand` (`bind_edge: true`, appends two slots) is
the first check; (2) a runtime/compile width disagreement — raw filtering everything to ZERO is what
a predicate reading the WRONG column looks like, since `.age` on a non-node column is NULL and
`NULL < 5` never holds.

⚠️ **"The optimizer changed the answer" does not say WHICH side is correct.** The fuzzer asserts only
that they agree. The raw plan yielding zero may itself be the broken one. Settle that FIRST. OPEN.

⚠️ Also open from the same run: `optimizing_preserves_rows_across_shapes` "changed the ORDER" at seed
1889763, whose plans differ only by `Filter{Scan} -> RangeSeek` over a `ShortestPath` pair with tied
sort keys — plausibly the fuzzer over-asserting order on ties (`order-is-unspecified`), but unchecked.

## 1149 — ⚠️🔧 ROOT CAUSE of item 1148: **`hash_join`'s NULL sentinel shares a bucket with a real node id.** Both suspected rewrites are INNOCENT, the RAW answer was correct, and the bug is WIDER than the seed

Measurements, each ruling out a suspect:

```text
  Join output (raw plan):               0 rows   -> the outer filter is not what empties it
  FILTER{Scan(Half),age<16} = 9 rows
  RANGESEEK{Half,age<16}    = 9 rows             -> the SEEK rewrite is innocent
  RAW left 166 / right 7 -> Join 0
  OPT left 166 / right 3 -> Join 6               -> IMPOSSIBLE: R' ⊆ R must give L⋈R' ⊆ L⋈R
```

Join keys: RAW left slot1 = 166 real node elements (ids include **0**); OPT right slot2 = **ALL
NULL** (3/3); RAW right slot2 = 6 NULLs of 7. ✅ **So the RAW answer (0 rows) was correct** — the
question item 1148 said to settle first.

**The bug**, `exec::hash_join` dense path:

```rust
let maxid = rids.iter().copied().filter(|&x| x != u32::MAX).max();
let sentinel = maxid.map_or(0, |m| m as usize + 1);   // <- 0 when every right id is NULL
let slot_of = |id| if id == u32::MAX { sentinel } else { id as usize };
```

The sentinel is placed inside the RIGHT's id range, and the probe maps LEFT ids into that same
space. ⚠️ **All-NULL right side → `sentinel == 0` → real left id 0 lands in the NULL bucket** (left
has id 0 twice, 2 x 3 = exactly the 6 phantom rows). ⚠️ **GENERALLY: any left id equal to
`right_max + 1` collides with the NULL bucket**, for any right side — `counts.len() == sentinel + 2`,
so the probe's `if k >= counts.len()` guard does not exclude it. The all-NULL case is just the
easiest to reach.

NULL-matches-NULL is DELIBERATE here (the comment states it) and is not the defect; the defect is
that the sentinel's bucket is reachable by a real id.

**Why it hid:** the documented depth is 200000, which passes — this needs 500000 — and the shape
needs an `OptionalExpand{keep_source:true}` right arm padding every key to NULL with a left id 0
present.

**NOT FIXED** — bucket arithmetic every `Join` goes through, so the fix wants its own cycle with
mutation, the 500k sweep as the gate, and the byte-identity fuzzers. OPEN.

## 1150 — ✅ FIXED, a WRONG ANSWER: `hash_join`'s NULL sentinel now has its own list instead of a bucket a real id can reach. Both 500k "changed the answer" failures go GREEN

The dense-id path no longer puts `u32::MAX` inside the bucket space: the index covers the right's
REAL ids, null-keyed right rows go to a separate `rnulls` (filled `j` ascending, same order property
as a bucket), and the probe routes a NULL left key there and a real one to its bucket.
NULL-matches-NULL is PRESERVED (deliberate here — `value_at` maps the sentinel to NULL on both
sides).

the left is routinely far larger (166 vs 7 in the failing seed; whole-graph vs a handful at bench
scale), so it would grow the allocation on every join to fix a case needing no extra space.

## 1151 — ✅ the last 500k failure was the ORACLE: `ordered_output` cannot see DUPLICATE key tuples. **The whole sweep is now green** and the relaxation is proven to keep its teeth

⚠️ `ordered_output`'s totality test — `keys.len() >= width(input) && keys.iter().all(unique)` — is
**necessary and not sufficient**. At seed 1889763 both halves hold (two `name` keys over a
two-column input) and all 25 rows are STILL tied, because **the rows arriving at the page already
hold duplicate (slot0, slot1) tuples**: a chain reaching the same endpoint pair by several paths
emits one row per path, and the pair is what the keys read. The output separates them by a
`PathAccess{Length}` column, which is not a sort key. Same class as the seed-96445 note already in
that function, different cause — there the key EXPRESSION was non-unique, here the key TUPLES are.
**A static check sees the first, not the second.**

**Fix:** `sort_keys_are_total(plan, store)` projects the page's keys over the page's input, runs it,
and returns false if any tuple repeats — so a tied page falls back to the bag and a total page keeps
the stronger sequence check.

⚠️ **RELAXING AN ORACLE NEEDS TWO PROOFS, and both were taken:**

1. **It still fires** — over 20,000 seeds: **1515 ORDERED vs 135 relaxed-to-bag** (8.2%). Not
   quietly disabled.
2. **It still catches a real order bug** — and note the oracle compares raw against OPTIMIZED, so an
   `exec` order defect moves both arms equally and is invisible; the mutant must be in the OPTIMIZER.
   Dropping `keys.is_empty()` from the "page that keeps everything" identity (so it elides an
   order-BEARING page) is **CAUGHT at seed 150**, plus 2046 and 5279.

```text

```

that is measured — 500000 found the item-1150 wrong answer that 200000 passes over, for ~100 s.

`bun run bench:gremlin`, 200k vertices / 1M edges, min of 5:

```text
  V().out().out().out().count()   ts 274.7   native 4.92   55.9x  <- biggest in the table
  V().out()x4.count()                281.2          6.86   41.0x
  V().out().out().count()             52.9          2.77   19.1x
```

FLAT**. Claim trace: only `hops=3` and `hops=4` reach the dense rung at all; the 2-hop row is
answered by a cheaper one. The flatness is where the memo is COLD — a 3-hop's two passes are both
cold (pass 0 memoizes only SEED slots; pass 1 expands the far ends first time), while a 4-hop's
third pass is memo-warm.

✅ **Item 1110's memo is load-bearing, by ablation** (the suspicion was its ~400k
`Int32Array.from` allocations):

```text
                        memo ON   memo OFF
  out().out().out()       274.7     419.2    1.53x worse without
  out()x4                 281.2     573.9    2.04x worse without
  out().out()    [ctl]     52.9      52.5    flat (different rung — as the trace predicted)
```

⚠️ **The residual is ~2M COLD edge touches**, each paying a `Map<Vertex, number>.get` to intern the
far vertex (`expandSlot`'s `slotOf.get(w)`). A memo cannot help a slot's FIRST expansion.

⚠️ **Both local levers are ALREADY TAKEN here** — don't re-attempt: the walk reads
`vtx[slot].adjFrom` (the vertex's own box, item 591's 1.80x) and the per-slot neighbour memo is item

ARE dense `u32` ids, so interning is identity. Closing the gap means giving `Vertex` an internal
slot field — a cross-cutting change to a user-visible object, a design decision not a local
optimization. OPEN.

## 1160 — ✅ SHIPPED, TS cross-language gap CLOSED: **`types &&` is a truthiness test and "every type" is falsy.** 106-115 ms → 0.0

Item 1159 priced this and could not find the declining rung (its fix went into `bareDegreeSum`,
which a trace proved unreachable here). Found by reading the chain rung by rung:
`detectCountShortcut` → `patternCountOf` → `buildOneHopCount`, one line in its vacuous-endpoint
branch:

```js
    if (a === undefined && b === undefined && types && bucketSumsAreSound(...)) {
```

⚠️ **`types === undefined` IS the untyped spelling and means EVERY type — but it is FALSY**, so
`-[]->` fell past the O(1) arm into the degree walk. New arm returns `graph.edgeCount`, which is
what the GREMLIN surface of this same engine always did (`adjacentCount`, `labels.length === 0`).

⚠️ **`edgeCount`, NOT a bucket sum, and a MULTI-LABEL edge is why.** An edge with two labels sits in
two buckets, so a sum counts it twice — that is what `bucketSumsAreSound` guards. The total counts
each edge ONCE regardless, so the new arm needs no soundness condition. **The test turns on it:** a
5-edge fixture with one `KNOWS,FOLLOWS` edge has buckets of 4 and 2, so a bucket sum says **6** and
the answer is **5**. A single-label fixture cannot tell the formulas apart.

```text
  A4 -[]-> untyped   PRE 108.5/115.2/110.0   POST 0.0/0.0/0.0
  A1/A2/A3  [ctl]    0.0 flat
```

Arm-asserted at SOURCE **and DIST** level, counting `rowOf(graph.edgeCount)` in the built bundle via
python `str.count` — items 1141/1151: the bundler strips comments (a comment marker reads 0 in BOTH
arms and passes vacuously) and `grep` returns nothing for that file. Every row also asserts
ts === native.

Mutation on a GREEN baseline, both CAUGHT: vacuous-endpoint guard dropped (a labelled endpoint would
get the whole graph — `MATCH (a:Q)-[]->(x)` is 0, not 5); bucket sum substituted for `edgeCount`
(double-counts the multi-label edge). Suites isolated: **5,673 pass / 0 fail**; 7/7 fuzzers.

✅ **The shape worth remembering:** the gap was never between the two ENGINES but between the two
SURFACE LANGUAGES of one engine, with a working implementation one package away. "Grep the pattern
elsewhere" paid twice, and the second time "elsewhere" was not where I expected.

## 1161 — ✅ SHIPPED **3.84x / 4.20x** (`min`/`max` over a numeric column) and ⚠️🔧 **FIXED a cross-engine WRONG ANSWER** in the fold I was about to copy. Plus TWO fuzzer blindnesses, both closed

Priced the AGGREGATE-KIND enum after item 1160 closed label-arity in both engines. At 200k nodes on
one dense numeric column: `count` 121.5us, `sum` 122.0, `avg` 122.0, `stddev_pop` 122.2 — and
**`min` 435.0, `max` 472.7**. `percentile_cont` 3674.5 (30x, but a percentile needs a SORT, so most
of it is inherent and it is NOT a target).

**The `AggFn` mention census CANNOT find this, and item 844 drew the opposite inference from it.**
`Min` has 36 matches in `fastpath.rs` and `Max` 24 — the most of any value-reading variant — and
they were the slow ones. A census counts how often a variant is NAMED, not how well it is SERVED.
Price the variants.

**Cause (diagnosed, not assumed): not the comparator.** The single-agg fold carried
`best: Option<f64>` through the loop, so every row paid a `match` on `None`, and tested the
loop-invariant `want_min` inside the same closure. The `Option` is what stops it auto-vectorizing.

### ⚠️ The fast sibling was WRONG, and a stale doc comment had been licensing it

`scan_fold_minmax` already folded with a plain `x < mn`, justified as _"stored Nums are finite, so
`x < mn` == `cmp_num_total`"_. **Checked instead of believed (item 1142's precedent), and it is
false:**

```text
  three nodes 1.0 / NaN / 5.0        (NaN is GREATEST under cmp_num_total)
  single-agg max      NaN   correct      ORDER BY DESC   NaN   the contract's own order
  multi-agg  min,max  1.0, 5.0  WRONG — the NaN is skipped
  SET n.v = sqrt(0 - 1)  ->  stores Num(NaN), _is_nan true   (reachable from the surface language)
```

TS was right all along (`extremumFold` uses `compareValues`, the total order), so this was a LIVE
TS-vs-native divergence. `cmp_num_total` IS `partial_cmp` for two non-NaN operands (it ties `-0.0`
with `0.0` deliberately), so NaN is the whole of the exception.

**The claim traces to a test whose NAME asserts the opposite of the truth.**
`a_numeric_column_cannot_hold_a_nan` cited `Value::finite_only` — **which does not exist anywhere in
this workspace.** It lived in the retired `lenke-core` and was never ported; the sentence stayed.
The test could not notice: it asserts the column terminal AGREES WITH THE WALK and never that the
value is null, so it passes either way — the item-1158 tautology shape, believed long enough to be
cited as a licence. Renamed `the_column_terminals_agree_with_the_walk_on_a_stored_nan` and kept,
because that agreement is a real guard now that NaN is known reachable.
**`stored_infinity_is_a_value` already made "finite" false for ±∞ before NaN came up.**

### The fix gets BOTH: count the NaNs instead of comparing them

`nan_cnt += u64::from(x != x)` is a compare-and-add that vectorizes with the loop; the finish reads
it (`min` is NaN only when `cnt == nan_cnt`, `max` whenever `nan_cnt > 0`). **The sentinels need no
special case for a stored ±∞ because the sentinel IS the fold's identity.** `MIN` is a const
parameter, not a runtime flag. Early-return block, per item 844's measured reason (a shared live
range cost `min` 1.6x there), so the sum/avg loop is byte-for-byte untouched. Same `nan_cnt` in
`scan_fold_minmax` and `scan_fold_all`.
**Grepped elsewhere: NO other site.** Every other min/max fold (frontier, filtered, varlen, string,
dict) already uses `cmp_num_total`. One bug, two functions.

```text
  A3 min  [394.0,396.7,409.8] -> [102.6,103.2,103.1]   3.84x
  A4 max  [431.0,444.9,432.3] -> [102.6,103.6,104.0]   4.20x
  SIX controls flat: count(a.n) 1.01x, sum 1.00x, avg 1.00x, stddev_pop 1.00x,
                     percentile_cont 0.99x, count(*) 1.00x
```

min/max now BEAT `sum` (103 vs 111) — an extremum is a max-reduce with no dependent accumulator
chain. **The alternation earned itself again:** a plain before/after read the untouched `count(a.n)`
control at 121.5 -> 101.5 and would have needed explaining; alternated it is 1.01x. The machine
drifted between runs and visibly within round 3. The ratio survives, the raw numbers do not.

### ⚠️ Why seven byte-identity fuzzers missed a cross-engine wrong answer — TWO reasons

Revert the fix, run the differential fuzzer: **green.** Both causes are now closed, and the second
is the one worth remembering:

1. **It generated exactly ONE aggregate per query.** The native multi-aggregate folds are reachable
   only with two or more aggregates over one column, so the functions holding the bug were
   **unreachable by construction** for as long as the fuzzer has existed.
2. **Its `nan` column holds ONLY NaNs** — so fixing (1) alone LEFT IT GREEN. Every present value
   being NaN means a `max` that skips them falls back to its `NEG_INFINITY` sentinel, and
   **±INFINITY and NaN both render as `null` at egress**: the wrong answer and the right one are the
   same JSON. Observable only with a NaN AMONG FINITES, where it reads as a number against a null.

Fixed with a multi-aggregate arm (one key so they group onto a single column pass, two keys for the
fan-out, plus `count(*)`) and a new `nanmix` column (one NaN, two finites). Teeth verified by
reverting the engine fix — caught on the first seed tried.

**→ RULE: a fuzzer value needs the SHAPE that reaches the code AND the NEIGHBOURS that make the
difference observable at egress.** The fuzzer's own `genPred` note already says value-plus-shape
("the value and the shape never met"); this adds the third term. The first fix felt like the whole
fix and the suite was still green.

### Mutation: 5 mutants, 5 caught, no survivors

Harness proven to kill first (bomb -> SIGKILL, `while true` -> 124); every mutant under
`timeout 900` + `MemoryMax=16G` + `MemorySwapMax=0`, restored BEFORE the next.

**⚠️ The DID-NOT-RUN check caught a harness bug on the first pass** (third time that rule has paid;
items 767, 772-773 wrote it): all five came back `rc=1, result-lines=0` because **`cargo test` takes
ONE TESTNAME** and rejects a second — four filters passed directly ran NOTHING. Filters go after
`--`. `rc=1` with no result line is indistinguishable from a real failure by exit code alone; only
the execution evidence separates them, and a bare exit code would have read as five confident
CAUGHTs on a harness that never compiled a test.

**⚠️ An oracle also had to be WEAKENED, correctly.** `the_extremum_fold_matches_the_contract_order`
first asserted BITS against `ORDER BY`'s extreme rows, and the `-0.0` case failed against a fold
that was RIGHT: `cmp_num_total` ties `-0.0` with `0.0`, so ORDER BY's tie order is unspecified and
cannot be a bit-exact oracle. Now two instruments: the VALUE against the contract via
`cmp_num_total` (not `==`, which `NaN != NaN` makes vacuous), and the BITS across the three
spellings — the half that was broken, and which holds for ties too, where the contract has no
preference but byte-identity still does.

`min,max` multi 8.5, `count(*)` 0.0. `min`/`max` are the FASTEST value-reading aggregates — ahead
of `sum` and `avg` — so **nothing to close.** `extremumFold` starts from `undefined` and tests it
per value, the same shape that cost native 3.8x, and it does not matter: the TS fold is not
competing with an auto-vectorized sibling, so that test is not the marginal cost. Item 1156's
pattern — the transferable thing is the QUESTION, not the answer — and the per-row `ts === native`
assertion independently exercised the NaN counting shipped here, from an engine that gets the same
answer by comparing rather than counting.

## 1162 — ✅ SHIPPED **9.5x / 9.3x** on the percentiles, by measuring the FLOOR first — the cost was NOT where item 844's numbers implied. ⚠️ Plus a mutant that exposed a test passing for the wrong reason, and a NEW TS target

The one row item 1161 priced and refused to call a target. `percentile_floor_probe` separated
`percentile_of`'s three costs before anything was built (item 234's precedent: a floor per shape
retracted two of three targets there), and **the carried-in diagnosis was wrong**:

```text
  sum                    122.0 us   the scan+column floor / control
  columnar gather alone  156.6      a boxing-free gather is NEARLY FREE
  gather + select_nth    397.8      the SELECTION costs ~241
  gather + full sort    3602.8      the SORT costs ~3446
  percentile_disc       3717.4      the full sort is 97% of it
  collect_list          1450.8
```

**I had inferred BOXING from item 844's recorded numbers** (`collect_list` 2,999 vs percentile
5,588 reads as "materialization is most of it"). It is the SORT. Building the columnar gather alone
would have shipped ~115us of a 3,595us problem and looked like a win.

**Build:** columnar f64 gather + `select_nth_unstable_by`. `percentile_cont` needs the NEXT
adjacent order statistic and gets it free — `select_nth_unstable_by` leaves everything `>= nth` in
its right partition, so it is that partition's MINIMUM, O(n), no second selection. A SEPARATE
function, not another block in `try_scan_num_agg`, because that function's sum/avg/min/max arms
were measured flat one tick ago and item 844 + 1161 both record what a shared live range costs.

```text
  percentile_disc  3717.4 -> 389.8   9.5x        A5 floor 397.8 — both arms land ON it
  percentile_cont  3718.3 -> 400.4   9.3x
  controls flat: sum 122.0 -> 113.9, columnar gather 156.6 -> 142.2
```

### The one exactness guard, and why it is `-0.0`

`percentile_of` sorts with `partial_cmp` and indexes the result. For finite f64 "equal under
`partial_cmp`" implies IDENTICAL BITS — except `-0.0` vs `0.0`, which tie but differ in bits, and a
stable sort keeps a tied run in input order where an unstable selection may not. So a negative zero
is noted in the gather and the path DECLINES (item 1161's `nan_cnt` shape: observe in the loop,
decide at the finish). NaN/±INFINITY need no guard — `percentile_of` keeps only finite values and
the gather replicates that.

**Oracle: the general grouped fold** (`LET g = 1 … GROUP BY g` — one group, same question, and it
routes to `percentile_of` because the fast path needs a sole aggregate over a bare `Scan`).
Compared as BITS over 12 fixtures x 9 fractions x 2 kinds = **216 cross-path comparisons**,
out-of-range fractions included (item 530's panic). Note for anyone writing one: the fraction must
be a numeric LITERAL, so a negative one is `-1`, not `0 - 1`.

### ⚠️ M1 SURVIVED the first mutation run — the TEST was passing for the wrong reason

The negative-zero guard is the purely-correctness part of this change, and the mutant removing it
passed. Settled by taking the engine out of it — a standalone search over BOTH algorithms with the
SIZE swept:

```text
  checked 5,916,000 (input, index) pairs; 1,454,911 differed in bits
  minimal case:  n=2 idx=1 over [-0.0, 0.0]  ->  stable 0.0, selection -0.0
```

Guard is load-bearing. The test used THREE values and fractions up to 0.5, and
**`select_nth_unstable_by` on a slice that short falls into an INSERTION SORT, which is stable** —
so selection and sort agreed and the assertion held for a reason unrelated to the code under test.
Rebuilt from the search's counterexample (two values at fraction 1, plus 64 values to clear the
regime, both input orders); M1 now caught.

**→ RULE: a size-dependent algorithm needs the SIZE swept, and a fixture small enough to be
convenient can sit entirely inside the branch that cannot fail.** Sibling of items 1136/1142, where
a fixture built the wrong way made the path DECLINE so the mutant survived — there the fixture
missed the code, here it reached the code but only its stable regime. Both look identical from
outside: a green test and a surviving mutant.

### Mutation: 7 mutants, 5 caught, 2 survivors BOTH predicted and explained

M2 (`total_cmp` for `partial_cmp`) survives because the two differ only on `-0.0` vs `0.0`, which
the gate already declines — answer-equivalent, a route choice, and PREDICTED before the run, which
is what separates a documented equivalence from a hole. M6 (`.min(n - 1)` on the disc index)
survives because `frac` is clamped to `<= 1`, so `ceil(frac * n) - 1 <= n - 1` always; **I
mispredicted this one.** M3 (removing the clamp) IS caught, so the clamp is load-bearing and the
`.min` is belt-and-braces — kept, because `percentile_of` has it and the two must not drift, and now
labelled defensive in the code with M6 cited.

Process note: editing `fastpath.rs` to record these findings WHILE the mutation script ran got the
edits wiped — the script's pristine copy is taken at its START, so the tree is not yours until it
finishes.

## 1163 — ✅ SHIPPED **17.9x** on the TS percentile fold / **4.5x** end to end: an INTERPRETED O(n) selection beat V8's NATIVE sort by 5.3x. ⚠️ Plus an **18,000x** property no answer test can see, and 🔶 a cross-engine `-0` divergence found by READING

Item 1162's open TS target. The design transferred from the Rust side; **the algorithm did not
transfer for free**, and assuming it would have been the item-234 mistake in a new language.
`percentile-arm-probe.ts`, 200,000 values, median of 14 dropping three, three order-alternated
rounds, all arms checked to AGREE before any was timed:

```text
  A current      map + filter + sort((a, b) => a - b)   26.8  24.7  25.3 ms
  B typed sort   Float64Array + native .sort()           8.0   8.0   8.0    3.4x
  C quickselect  Float64Array + hand-written select      1.4   1.4   1.5   17.9x   <- ships
  D gather only                                          0.1   0.1   0.1   the floor
```

**The interpreted O(n) selection beats the native C++ O(n log n) typed sort by 5.3x at this size** —
the constant favours the sort and only the exponent favours the selection, so this was genuinely
open before it was measured.

`%TypedArray%.prototype.sort` was also wrong for a SECOND reason: **it orders `-0` before `+0` by
specification**, where `(a, b) => a - b` ties them and V8's stable sort keeps input order — item
1162's hazard exactly. It cannot arise here because `numArg` collapses `-0` first, so **the TS fast
path needs NO negative-zero guard where the native one does.** That asymmetry is a fact about
`numArg`, not a liberty.

```text
                     PRE      POST (3 rounds)
  percentile_disc   31.2  ->  6.9  7.0  6.3    ~4.5x
  percentile_cont   30.2  ->  7.0  7.0  6.3    ~4.3x
  controls flat: count 3.3->3.2, sum 6.8->6.6, collect_list 4.3->4.8, min/max/avg/stddev/count(*)
```

Fold 17.9x but query 4.5x, because ~4.3 ms of the 31 is the group materialization `collect_list`
also pays and this cannot touch. The CONTROLLED measurement is the fold-level alternation; the
end-to-end figure is three POST rounds against same-session PRE, quoted as the weaker of the two
on purpose.

### ⚠️ An 18,000x property INVISIBLE to every answer test

`selectNth` uses a **median-of-three** pivot. A first-element pivot is equally CORRECT, so it
passes everything (mutant M6, predicted to survive, did):

```text
  over 200,000 ALREADY-SORTED values:  median-of-three 0.3 ms, first element 5517.2 ms  (~18,000x)
  control, median-of-three over random input: 1.5 ms
```

**An ascending column is the ORDINARY case for a percentile, not an adversarial one.** Per the
standing rule that a route choice is answer-equivalent and so invisible to differential tests, the
property got its own instrument: sorted AND descending input, 2-second budget against a 0.3 ms
expectation — ~6,000x headroom so no machine reaches it, while the mutant exceeds it by 2.7x. The
one timing assertion this suite permits, justified by the five-orders-of-magnitude gap.

### Mutation: 8 mutants, 7 caught, survivor PROVABLY equivalent

M1 non-finite filter, M2/M3/M4 the `cont` interpolation and its tail-min, M5 the disc index clamp,
M8 `numArg` applied to every element (keeping a FAULT where a fault was — a one-pass rewrite is
exactly where that goes missing silently), M6 only after the timing test above.

**M7 (`return a[lo]` for `return a[k]`) is an IDENTITY, and I mispredicted it as catchable.** The
loop maintains `lo <= k <= hi` (it sets `hi = j` only when `k <= j`, `lo = i` only when `k >= i`)
and exits on `lo >= hi`, so `lo == k == hi` and `a[lo]` IS `a[k]`. A survivor with a proof is
documentation; a survivor without one is a gap.

**Oracle = the code this replaced.** `percentile-select.test.ts` carries the old map/filter/sort as
a REFERENCE, so "agrees" means "answers what it answered before". 6,363 assertions over hand-built
edge cases and randomized inputs with **the SIZE swept** (1/2/3/5/9/17/33/64/129/512/2048, 40
trials each, 7 fractions, both kinds) — the sweep is there because of item 1162's M1, since a small
input never leaves the first partition. Narrow value range so DUPLICATES are common (a selection
and a sort can only disagree on ties). `Object.is` throughout, the only comparison that separates
`-0` from `+0` and makes `NaN` equal itself.

### 🔶 OPEN, found by READING `numArg`'s comment: a cross-engine `-0` divergence predating all of this

After `SET n.v = 0 * (0 - 1)`:

```text
  the stored value itself   ts -0  native +0   DIVERGE
  min(n.v)                  ts -0  native +0   DIVERGE
  ORDER BY n.v [first row]  ts -0  native +0   DIVERGE
  percentile_disc/cont, sum        both +0     agree
```

**Direction is the OPPOSITE of my prediction.** Native collapses on the WRITE path (`num_of`); TS
collapses only in the numeric-FUNCTION path, so a `SET`-computed `-0` survives into TS storage and
out through `min` and `ORDER BY`. By the model's own stated rule ("no negative zero in the numeric
model") **TS is the engine out of conformance.**

**Why no fuzzer caught it: `JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"`.** The differential fuzzer compares
rendered JSON, so the two are the same string to it; `Object.is` is the only instrument that sees
it, hence `negzero-cross-probe.ts` walks raw row values. NOT fixed here — a write-path numeric-model
question, not an optimization, and the percentile rows are unaffected. Probe kept so the next tick
prices the fix rather than rediscovering the fact.

## 1164 — ⚠️ **RETRACTED BY ITEM 1165 — the divergence does not exist.** Kept for the method lesson only.

## (as written) 🔶 PRICED AND DIAGNOSED, not built: the `-0` cross-engine divergence has **FIVE** observable surfaces, and the probe that was meant to locate the fix answered a different question

> **Read item 1165 first.** The five "divergences" below are an artifact of the instrument: the
> native rows cross the FFI boundary as JSON, where `-0` renders as `"0"`, so they compare TS's raw
> values against native's JSON round-trip. Rendered output — the actual invariant — agrees on every
> row. The conclusion "TS is the engine out of conformance" is WITHDRAWN.

Follow-up to item 1163's incidental finding. `negzero-cross-probe.ts`, after `SET n.v = 0 * (0 - 1)`,
comparing with `Object.is` because **`JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"`** and every renderer-based
comparison — the differential fuzzer included — is blind to it:

```text
  computed, not stored                   ts -0   native +0   DIVERGE
  computed via negation                  ts -0   native +0   DIVERGE
  the stored value itself                ts -0   native +0   DIVERGE
  min(n.v)                               ts -0   native +0   DIVERGE
  ORDER BY n.v  [first row]              ts -0   native +0   DIVERGE
  percentile_disc / percentile_cont      both +0             agree
  sum over the zero alone                both +0             agree
  atan2(0, stored) / atan2(0, computed)  both +0             agree
```

**Settled:** TS keeps the sign bit through a BARE PROJECTION, through `min` and through `ORDER BY`;
it loses it only on entering a numeric FUNCTION. Both engines collapse at that function gate
(`numArg` / `num_of`), which is why the `atan2` rows agree. By the model's own stated rule — native
`num_of`: _"the numeric model has NO negative zero… no operation ever observes a -0"_ — **TS is the
engine out of conformance**, and the divergence is wider than the write path, since a computed `-0`
that is never stored diverges too.

**⚠️ NOT settled, and this is the part worth recording: WHERE native collapses.** An early reading
of `min` returning `+0` was taken as evidence that native collapses on the WRITE path. It is not —
an EGRESS collapse looks identical from every one of these rows. The `atan2` rows were added
specifically to separate the two and **cannot**, because `atan2` collapses its own operand in both
engines: the instrument answers a different question than the one it was built for. (The first
instrument tried, `1 / n.v < 0`, is unavailable at all — division by zero is a data exception here,
not an infinity.) Write-collapse and egress-collapse want the fix in DIFFERENT places, so the next
step is to read native's write path directly rather than infer it from the surface. This is the
items 1102 / 1146 / 1159 failure mode — three edits that landed in unreachable paths — caught this
time BEFORE the edit.

Candidate TS sites, once that is known: `normalizePropertyValue` in `packages/core/src/core/validate.ts`
is the single write chokepoint (and a `typeof value === 'number'` early return there would also
short-circuit four checks — `fromTaggedJson`, `Array.isArray`, `instanceof LenkeRecord` and the
plain-object test — for the most common property type, so the conformance fix and a hot-path
shortcut are the same edit). `packages/core/src/numeric.ts` is the established home for exactly this
kind of "the obvious built-in differs between JS and Rust" helper and already holds `mathSign` for
the signed-zero reason. The computed-but-unstored rows need a second site regardless.

NOT built: a numeric-model change across a write chokepoint and an arithmetic result is not an
optimization, and half-building one at the end of a tick is how the wrong-path edits above happened.

The two percentile rows item 1163 added, measured one case per process (`BENCH_ONLY`, which is the
right instrument — the positional filter this was first run with does not exist, and a `tail` on the

```text
  query: percentile_disc [one order statistic]   ts 5.9 ms   ffi 0.4   wasm 0.7   14.32x / 8.35x
  query: percentile_cont [interpolates two]      ts 5.9      ffi 0.4   wasm 0.9   14.25x / 6.95x

```

## 1165 — ⚠️ **RETRACTED: item 1164's `-0` divergence does not exist.** The invariant holds at 0 of 10 rows; I had compared TS's RAW values against native's JSON ROUND-TRIP

Item 1164 reported five observable `-0` divergences and concluded "TS is the engine out of
conformance". **That conclusion was wrong, and the cause was the instrument.**

Item 1164 itself recorded that it had NOT settled where native collapses, and said the next step
was to read native's write path rather than infer it. Doing that is what broke the finding open:

- `apply_set_prop` has **no** `-0` collapse. So native does not collapse on write — the value goes
  straight into the column.
- Grepping every collapse site instead found `json_fmt.rs:167`, whose own comment is
  _"also normalizes -0.0 → \"0\" (JS drops the sign)"_. **Native collapses at JSON EGRESS.**
- And the FFI query path crosses the boundary as JSON text and comes back through `JSON.parse`.

So a native `-0` **could not reach the probe even if one were stored**: it is rendered as `"0"` and
parsed back as `+0`. The probe was comparing TS's in-process JS values against native's JSON
round-trip — two different things — and reading the difference as an engine divergence.

**The invariant is defined on RENDERED OUTPUT, and it holds.** `JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"`, the
same string native emits, so:

```text
  5 of 10 differ in RAW JS VALUES (by Object.is)
  0 of 10 differ in RENDERED OUTPUT (the invariant)        <- the question that matters
```

The probe now measures both and labels which is which, so the next reader cannot repeat the
mistake.

### What is actually left, and it is not a bug

A pure-TS in-process caller can observe a `-0` in a raw returned value where an FFI caller cannot,
because the two engines have different egress layers (direct JS values vs JSON text) — structural,
not a defect, and invisible the moment anything serializes. Native's `num_of` claim ("no operation
ever observes a -0") is about its own internals and remains true of them. **Nothing to fix.**

### The transferable lesson, which is the only reason this item exists

**A cross-engine probe compares two TRANSPORTS as much as two engines, and a normalization anywhere
in the transport is indistinguishable from agreement.** Every `Object.is`-level claim about native
values through the FFI is a claim about JSON's value space, not the engine's: `-0`, `NaN` and `±∞`
all normalize on that path, so none of them can be measured through it. The tell was available and
I missed it for a tick — item 1164's own text says `JSON.stringify(-0)` is `"0"` while treating
`Object.is` as the sharper instrument, without asking whether native's values had already been
through a renderer before I got them. Sharper on the TS side; blind on the other.

Related in shape to item 1162's `-0` guard, which is a REAL requirement — there the two values live
inside one engine's sort and selection, with no renderer between them. The distinction is whether a
serialization boundary sits in the middle.
