### Item 1229 — item 1228's attribution CONFIRMED by a discriminating test; the `ne` fix is a TRADE, not a win, so it is priced and NOT taken; and a separate 11.9x cliff found (OPEN x2)

Item 1228 recorded the `ne` arm's 2.3-3.2x periodic-vs-random as "the misprediction signature".
That was an attribution, not a measurement, and a second explanation fit the same three numbers:
with `k = i % 100` the rows passing a range form long CONTIGUOUS runs of ids, so everything
downstream reads `data[id]` sequentially, while random values make the same reads a GATHER.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, built rather than argued (`ne_arm_mechanism_probe`): a count with TWO
exclusions. Item 1213's two-pass trick handles exactly one, so `<> a AND <> b` falls to the general
branchy arm — a branchy predicate with NO gather and no materialization.

```text
  shape                                       periodic    random   ratio
  count, TWO exclusions [branchy, NO gather]     608.8    1254.7   2.06x   <- branchy, no gather
  projection, range only [gathers, no ne]        444.3     447.1   1.01x   <- gathers, not branchy
  sum, range only [gathers, no ne]               247.5     251.2   1.01x   <- gathers, not branchy
  count, ONE exclusion [1213 two-pass]            51.2      51.4   1.00x
```

The data-dependence tracks the EXCLUSION and not the gather: a branchy predicate with no gather is
2.06x data-dependent, and two gathering shapes with no exclusion are FLAT. **Item 1228's
attribution stands, and now it is measured.**

### The fix is a TRADE, so it is not taken

Making the exclusion closures non-short-circuit — `(v >= lo) & (v <= hi) & (v != x)` — removes the
data-dependence and costs on predictable data. Three order-alternated rounds, binaries
hash-asserted (PRE `e9dd2914`, POST `7ac31902`):

```text
  row                        PRE periodic  PRE random  POST periodic  POST random
  sum, ONE exclusion                269.5       852.2          348.6        358.2
  projection, ONE exclusion         455.5      1066.6          547.6        551.7
```

So the WORST case improves 1.93-2.38x and the BEST case degrades 1.20-1.29x, because `&` always
evaluates three compares where `&&` exits early on a column whose predicate outcome runs in long
blocks. Controls (the range-only rows, the two-pass count, the unfiltered projection) are flat.

NOT SHIPPED. The standing instruction for this work is to optimize WITHOUT REGRESSIONS, and a
measurable 1.20-1.29x loss on a real (if synthetic) distribution is a regression, whichever way the
average goes. It is a product call — a 2.4x data-dependent cliff is arguably worse than a 1.3x
constant, and no real column is a perfect repeating ramp — so it is recorded here with its numbers
for whoever makes it, rather than taken unilaterally.

⚠️ WHY THREE TERMS AND NOT TWO: item 1228 refuted `&&` -> `&` on the two-term RANGE closure in this
same function (flat), and `projection, range only` is 1.01x data-dependent, so LLVM evidently
if-converts a two-term chain and does NOT if-convert a three-term one. That is a threshold in the
compiler, not a property of the predicate, which is why the same rewrite is worth nothing at two
terms and 2.4x at three.

### A SEPARATE, UNAMBIGUOUS TARGET: the one-vs-two exclusion cliff is 11.9x

```text
  count, ONE exclusion [1213 two-pass]     51.2 us
  count, TWO exclusions [general arm]     608.8 us     11.9x
```

Item 1213 answers ONE exclusion as two vectorized passes (a range count minus the excluded value's
count) and k > 1 falls all the way back to the fully general arm, which walks `bounds` and
dispatches `num_pred` per row. Extending the trick to k exclusions is k+1 vectorized passes, is
exact (counts are integers, so there is no association-order question), and has NO trade of the
kind above — both arms are branchless. That is the next target.

⚠️ AND THE SUM EQUIVALENT IS BARRED, which is worth stating so it is not attempted: `sum(range)
minus the excluded value times its count` is arithmetically exact but changes the ASSOCIATION ORDER
of a floating-point reduction, and byte-identity across the two engines is a hard invariant here.
The count is safe for exactly the reason the sum is not.

### Item 1230 — the `ne` trade is WORSE than its two points suggested: the predictor copes with runs of 10, so the "best case" is five regimes out of six (REFUTED as a lever)

Item 1229 priced making the exclusion closures branchless as a trade — worst case 1.93-2.38x
better, best case 1.20-1.29x worse — and asked how often each occurs. Two points cannot answer
that, and the question matters because the predictable case is NOT merely synthetic: a column of
sorted ids, or timestamps inserted in order, gives a filter long predictable runs exactly as a
periodic one does.

So the RUN LENGTH was swept — the number of consecutive rows whose predicate outcome is the same —
holding the value range, the selectivity (~49%, where misprediction is maximal) and the row count
fixed, so only the ORDER changes (`ne_predictability_curve_probe`):

```text
  regime                         PRE sum / proj      POST sum / proj
  sorted (one block per value)    274.0 /  463.7      335.5 /  539.4
  blocks of 1000                  432.3 /  475.4      339.8 /  543.0
  blocks of 100                   271.1 /  466.5      344.6 /  539.3
  blocks of 10                    280.6 /  474.2      346.7 /  545.3
  periodic i % 100 (corpus)       273.3 /  469.7      341.7 /  539.5
  random                          885.1 / 1079.9      345.7 /  537.8
```

**THE BRANCH PREDICTOR COPES WITH RUNS AS SHORT AS 10.** Every regime from sorted down to blocks of
ten is within noise of the periodic figure, and only a genuinely SHUFFLED column pays the penalty.
So the current `&&` form wins on five of the six regimes and the branchless form wins on one.

REFUTED AS A LEVER. The POST column is admirably flat — it does remove the data-dependence — but it
buys that by making every predictable case pay what it currently avoids. Item 1229's framing of
"worst case versus best case" was right arithmetically and misleading in proportion: the best case
is the ordinary case, not the lucky one. Reverted and closed; the numbers are here so the trade is
not re-priced from two points again.

⚠️ ONE ROW IS UNEXPLAINED AND SAID SO RATHER THAN SMOOTHED: `blocks of 1000` reads 432.3 us on the
PRE sum against ~271-280 for both its neighbours, which no account of run length predicts. It
reproduces within the run but has not been isolated, and nothing here depends on it.

WHAT THIS LEAVES, unchanged and still the better target: the one-vs-two exclusion cliff at 11.9x
(item 1229). Extending item 1213's two-pass trick to k exclusions is branchless in BOTH arms, so it
carries no trade of this kind at all.

### Item 1231 — k exclusions as k+1 vectorized passes: 8.65-17.6x, flat across fixtures, and no crossover up to k=32 (DONE)

Item 1213 answered ONE exclusion as two vectorized passes (count the range, subtract the excluded
value's own count); `if let [x] = c.ne.as_slice()` admitted exactly one and everything beyond fell
to the fully general arm, which walks `bounds` and dispatches `num_pred` PER ROW. Item 1229 measured
that as a cliff: one exclusion 51.2 us, TWO exclusions 608.8 — **11.9x for one more literal**. The
gate is now `!c.ne.is_empty()` and the trick runs k+1 passes, which is the same soundness argument
with no dependence on k.

200,000 nodes, min of 7, binaries hash-asserted (PRE `7b4e8eba`, POST `f6eed0a4`):

```text
  k   PRE periodic   PRE random   POST (both)   gain periodic / random
  0         28.2         28.2          27.8     control — the `ne.is_empty()` branch
  1         50.8         50.6          49.9     1.02x / 1.01x — item 1213's arm, unchanged
  2        624.8       1269.0          72.2     8.65x / 17.57x
  4        779.1       1429.2         116.7     6.67x / 12.25x
  8       1042.6       1729.1         206.0     5.06x /  8.39x
 16       1615.0       2365.5         384.4     4.20x /  6.15x
 32       2194.8       3122.3         741.0     2.96x /  4.21x
```

POST IS FLAT ACROSS THE TWO FIXTURES AT EVERY k (1.00x) where PRE was 1.42-2.03x data-dependent —
that is the signature that the rewrite replaced a branchy pass with vectorized ones, not merely that
it got faster. Answers identical between arms at every k.

⚠️ NO CROSSOVER, AND IT WAS MEASURED RATHER THAN CAPPED ON A GUESS. k+1 passes each cost something,
so for large enough k one branchy pass must eventually win — that is the obvious objection, and the
honest answer is a sweep. POST's slope is ~23 us per exclusion against PRE's ~50-60, so POST's cost
grows MORE SLOWLY and the lines never cross; at k=32 it is still 2.96-4.21x ahead. No cap was added,
because adding one would have been an arbitrary number defended by nothing.

⚠️ TWO THINGS ARE NEW AT k > 1 AND BOTH ARE WRONG ANSWERS IF MISSED:

- **Duplicates must be subtracted once.** `k <> 73 AND k <> 73` reduces to `ne = [73, 73]`, and
  `canonical_num_conj` does not deduplicate (the general arm is idempotent in `ne`, so it had no
  reason to). Dedup uses `contains`, i.e. `PartialEq` on `f64` — the SAME `==` the counting pass
  uses, so a signed zero cannot slip between them. NaN cannot appear: `canonical_num_conj`
  declines a NaN literal outright.
- **An exclusion outside the range must be skipped**, or it subtracts rows the range count never
  included.

TEETH: four mutants, all compiled. THREE SURVIVED before the test existed — dedup removed, the
`inside` gate removed, and a `break` after the first pass — i.e. nothing tested k≥2 exclusions, a
repeated exclusion, or an out-of-range exclusion, which are exactly the three things that are new.
All four now fail, three by exactly one test (the new one) and the sign flip by six.

CONTROLS: the range-only count and a STRING bound, flat in both arms. `query_bench`'s worst rows are
`counts|filtered` 1.13x and `gremlin|has age>50` 1.10x — both the single-bound scan path this change
does not touch, and both re-measured ISOLATED at PRE 28.0-28.2 against POST 27.9-28.1, flat. That is
the bimodal row item 1225 recorded, behaving as recorded.

⚠️ NO CORPUS ROW EXERCISES k≥2 EXCLUSIONS, which is how an 11.9x cliff sat unmeasured until item
1229 went looking. Same gap item 1221 found and closed for the bare filtered count; this one is
still open.

THE SUM EQUIVALENT REMAINS BARRED: `sum(range)` minus `excluded value x its count` is arithmetically
exact but changes the ASSOCIATION ORDER of a floating-point reduction, and byte-identity across the
engines is a hard invariant. The count is safe for exactly the reason the sum is not.

### Item 1232 — the exclusion corpus gap closed, and TS has NO cliff: 82.3x at k=1, narrowing to 43.1x at k=4 (DONE, instrument only)

Items 1213, 1229 and 1231 are an arc about filtered counts with `<>` exclusions, and the whole of it
happened without a corpus row — which is exactly how an 11.9x cliff survived until item 1229 went
looking. Three rows added at k = 1, 2 and 4, isolated per process with `BENCH_ONLY`, 200,000 nodes:

```text
  workload                          ts     ffi    wasm    ts/ffi   ts/wasm
  count + filter, 1 exclusion      4.6     0.1     0.4     82.28x    12.46x
  count + filter, 2 exclusions     5.1     0.1     0.4     64.26x    14.15x
  count + filter, 4 exclusions     5.6     0.1     0.5     43.14x    10.29x
```

**TS HAS NO CLIFF.** 4.6 → 5.1 → 5.6 ms is a smooth ~0.5 ms per exclusion, so the TS engine never
had the step the Rust engine did and needs no equivalent of item 1231. The ts/ffi ratio NARROWS with
k (82.3 → 64.3 → 43.1) for the same reason: after item 1231 the Rust side grows ~23 us per exclusion
where TS grows ~500.

82.3x at k=1 is the widest gap in this corpus — wider than the 38.6x item 1221 found for the bare
filtered count — and it is the same cause, not a new one: ~19-28 ns a vertex of general predicate
machinery, which item 1222 established is DATA LAYOUT (item 805's walk-plus-read pairing) and not
closure overhead. So these rows price the shape; they do not open a new TS lever.

⚠️ AND ITEM 1231'S TRICK CANNOT TRANSFER TO TS, which is worth recording so it is not attempted.
k+1 vectorized passes is cheap over a COLUMNAR store: each pass is a contiguous `f64` sweep at ~0.15
ns a row, so the k=4 case costs 116.7 us in the Rust engine. In TS every "pass" is a full
object-graph walk at ~19 ns a vertex — the bare filtered count row measures 3.8 ms — so five passes
would be ~19 ms against the 5.6 ms a single compiled predicate costs today. The trick is a property
of the storage, not of the predicate, and in TS it would be ~3x WORSE.

No engine change. `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1233 — the corpus ranked by ts/ffi gap, and the WIDEST one (2675x) is REFUTED as a TS target: it is schemalessness, not a missing path

TS has had no win since items 1197/1198, and every TS target examined since has traced back to item
805's layout. Rather than guess at another, the whole corpus was ranked by gap — "price the
variants" applied to the bench instead of to an enum. 62 rows parsed:

```text
     2675.30x  ts     4.6  ffi   0.0   query: min boolean [short-circuits]
      156.96x  ts     5.1  ffi   0.0   count + prop filter ~49%
      107.14x  ts     3.5  ffi   0.0   count + prop filter ~2%
       73.87x  ts     4.1  ffi   0.1   count + filter, 1 exclusion
       68.02x  ts   330.8  ffi   4.9   count 3-hop
       61.64x  ts     4.9  ffi   0.1   count + filter, 2 exclusions
       55.80x  ts   366.8  ffi   6.6   count 4-hop
       51.08x  ts   235.2  ffi   4.6   count var-length 1-2 hops + end filter
       49.81x  ts   237.9  ffi   4.8   count var-length 1-2 hops
       49.57x  ts    41.0  ffi   0.8   traverse 1-hop + filter
  ...
        0.20x  ts   183.9  ffi 925.6   query: project the edge [ts lazy]
        0.11x  ts     6.2  ffi  55.2   query: project 3 columns
        0.04x  ts     5.7  ffi 148.5   query: project the element [ts lazy]
```

THE TOP ROW IS 17x WIDER THAN THE NEXT and its name says `[short-circuits]`, which reads exactly
like a missing TS fast path. It is not one.

`try_scan_bool_agg`'s own header states the soundness argument, and the operative words are the
last three: "`bool::cmp` gives `false < true` ... so **over a boolean column**: `min` is `false` the
moment ANY present `false` is seen — nothing later can beat it". The guarantee comes from
`Column::Bool` — the storage itself proves the column holds only booleans.

THE TS ENGINE HAS NO SUCH GUARANTEE, and its own total order is why. `typeRank` in `executor.ts` is
`Num(0) < Str(1) < Bool(2) < Temporal(3) < List(4) < Record(5) < Map(6) < Null`, matching the native
`Value::rank`. Booleans rank THIRD, so a later row holding a number or a string is SMALLER than any
boolean — seeing `false` bounds nothing. In a schemaless store, knowing the column is boolean-only
requires the very scan the short circuit exists to avoid. The same argument kills the `max` twin:
nulls are skipped by aggregates, so the ceiling is a Map at rank 6, and seeing `true` bounds nothing
either.

REFUTED as a TS target. The 2675x is the cost of being schemaless, and closing it needs TYPE
INFORMATION per property key — a schema sketch maintained on write — which is a structural change to
`@lenke/core` and a product decision, not a fast path. (`defineNode` exists but is host-side
validation only, so it does not supply this today.)

WHAT THE RANKING LEAVES, and the picture is consistent: every remaining wide TS row is STRUCTURAL
and already recorded.

- the filtered-count family (156.96x, 107.14x, 73.87x, 61.64x) — item 805's walk-plus-read
  pairing, priced and declined at 1.08x end to end; items 1221, 1222 and 1232 are the arc.
- the hop-count family (68.02x, 55.80x, 51.08x, 49.81x, 49.57x) — item 1193 recorded the TS 3-hop
  as a closed form needing a dense per-edge-type degree array.

So TS's gaps are not missing paths; they are two data-layout decisions, each with its own recorded
entry. That is worth knowing before the next tick goes looking for a third.

⚠️ AND THE BOTTOM OF THE TABLE IS WORTH AS MUCH AS THE TOP: `project the element` is 0.04x — the TS
engine is **25x FASTER** than native there, and `project the edge` 0.20x (5x faster). Both are marked
`[ts lazy]`. A ranking that only reads the head would miss that the comparison runs both ways.

No engine change (instrument and analysis only).

### Item 1234 — three Rust targets examined: two REFUTED by existing records, one PRICED with up to ~89 ms of headroom and the reason it is an IR change (OPEN, diagnosed)

Item 1233 pointed away from TS, so the Rust corpus was ranked by ABSOLUTE cost. Three candidates,
in the order they presented themselves.

**1. `project the edge` at ffi 925.6 ms — REFUTED before measuring, by the row's own comment.**
It is the largest single number in the corpus and the TS side is 5x faster, which reads like a
renderer problem. `bench.ts` says otherwise, and item 289 settled it: "the ts-vs-ffi gap on any
row-returning query is the JSON CARRIER — the same fixture with the same work and ONE row out runs
30.8x the OTHER way. Anyone reading these four rows as a renderer comparison should read
`queryArrowIpc` and item 289 first." Reading 925.6 ms as a Rust target is the exact mistake that
comment exists to prevent.

**2. The nested/k2 group counts at 147-152 ms — REFUTED as GUARD rows.** `nested count :label`
152,460 us and `nested-group count` 147,687 against `repeat-group count`'s 783 is 189x, carrier-free
(one row out), and the biggest absolute cost in the Rust corpus. But these rows exist to GUARD a fix
that already landed: "863,818us -> 146,402us once the walk got a counting sink of its own; ~665ms
means the lists came back and ~860ms means the rows did." Today's 147,687 is that guard holding. The
residual is genuine path enumeration over a nested unit with a reversed hop, and the group's own
header already warns "the win may simply not be there".

**3. `RepeatGroup`/`NestedGroup` lack `PathNeed` entirely — PRICED, and this one is real.**

```text
  repeat-group control      70849.4 us    (RETURN size(b))
  repeat-group + path      104343.0 us    (RETURN path_length(p))     +33493.6, 1.47x
  repeat-group unread       15418.2 us    (nothing reads the lists)   <- THE FLOOR
  varlen control            15535.4 us
  varlen + path             25167.3 us    +9631.9, 1.62x
```

`opt.rs`'s `mark` descends to set `PathNeed::CountOnly`, and its match arm names exactly two
producers: `ShortestPath` and `VarLength`. `RepeatGroup` and `NestedGroup` have NO `path_need` FIELD
in the IR, so they cannot be marked and always materialize their chains.

THE PRIZE IS BOUNDED BY A ROW THAT ALREADY EXISTS. `repeat-group unread` at 15,418 us is what the
same traversal costs when nothing reads the group's lists — so the list-building alone is
70,849 - 15,418 = ~55,431 us, and `+ path` adds another ~33,494 on top. A shape that reads ONLY
`path_length(p)` needs neither the lists nor the chain, which puts the headroom at up to ~89 ms
against today's 104,343. The precedent for the size is `VarLength`'s own marking, recorded in
`opt.rs`: 58,891us -> 22,662us at 599,998 rows, 2.6x.

WHY IT IS NOT A ONE-TICK CHANGE, stated so the next tick budgets for it rather than discovering it:

- a new `path_need` field on TWO `ir::Plan` variants, which touches every construction site
  including `reverse.rs` and the fuzzer's generators;
- threading it through two separate walkers (`NestedGroup` has its own, not `run_varlen`);
- the correctness argument `opt.rs` spells out — "marking under an operator that MATERIALIZES the
  path is a wrong answer ... that is exactly what the raw-vs-optimized fuzzer caught at seed 632",
  so the allow-list must stay a whitelist and the suppression must be proved, not assumed;
- `rewrite_fuzz`'s generator must be WIDENED to emit these shapes with path reads, or the fuzzer
  passes for the same reason an empty test does (CLAUDE.md records two historical rewrites that
  needed exactly this).

No engine change this item. The value is three targets examined, two closed with their reasons, and
the third priced against a floor that already exists in the corpus.

### Item 1235 — `RepeatGroup` gets `PathNeed`: 1.37x / −29.4 ms, and the three-sided mutation story is the result (DONE)

Item 1234 priced this and warned it would not be a one-tick change. It was smaller than that warning
implied, for a reason worth recording: `exec`'s `RepeatGroup` arm ALREADY routed through
`var_length`, which already honours `count_only`, with a hardcoded `PathNeed::Full` and a comment
saying "`RepeatGroup` has no `path_need` of its own yet, so it materializes". The walker support was
there; only the field was missing.

The change: a `path_need` field on the `RepeatGroup` IR variant, carried through the three `opt`
rewrites that rebuild one, defaulted to `Full` at the lowering and in the fuzzer's generator, passed
by `exec`, and `RepeatGroup` added to `set_path_need`'s allow-list beside `ShortestPath` and
`VarLength`.

REACH FIRST, per item 1216's rule — and it matters doubly here, because a marking rewrite changes no
ANSWER when it fails to fire:

```text
  repeat-group + path                              RepeatGroup  CountOnly
  [CTL] repeat-group, lists READ                   RepeatGroup  Full
  [CTL] varlen + path (marked before this change)  VarLength    CountOnly
```

COST, `query_bench` at 599,998 rows, binaries hash-asserted (PRE `6500e7c6`, POST `2bff735f`):

```text
  row                       PRE        POST      delta
  repeat-group + path   108491.9     79101.5   -29390.4   1.37x
  repeat-group control   70992.5     73619.9    +2627.4   (lists read, stays Full)
  repeat-group unread    14823.6     17487.8    +2664.2   (rewrite-guard row)
  repeat-group head(b)   79191.7     78338.7     -853.0
  varlen + path          24738.7     22862.1    -1876.6   (marked before this change)
  nested-group count    148229.2    147430.6     -798.6
```

READ IT IN ABSOLUTE TERMS, which is the honest frame when baselines differ by 7x: the target moved
−29,390 us while the largest control movement was +2,664, an ORDER OF MAGNITUDE apart, and the
drift runs BOTH ways (`varlen + path` got 1,877 us faster). A ratio table alone would put the
target's 1.37x uncomfortably near `repeat-group unread`'s 1.18x and obscure that.

Row counts identical in every arm (599,998 and 239,994 on the probe) — `CountOnly` suppresses the
chain COPY, never a row. And `repeat-group unread` at 17.5 ms is nowhere near the ~82,000 us its own
comment names as the signal that the unread-bindings rewrite has stopped firing, which matters
because this change edits that rewrite.

### ⚠️ THE MUTATION STORY IS THREE-SIDED, AND THE SURVIVOR IS THE INTERESTING ONE

```text
  suppress the chain regardless of what reads it   CAUGHT  (1 test; the wrong-answer direction)
  take RepeatGroup off the allow-list              CAUGHT  (by the new plan test, named)
  reset the flag in an earlier rewrite             SURVIVED
```

The survivor is NOT a gap. `optimize_indexed` runs `set_path_need` LAST, after
`drop_unread_group_binds`, so a reset inside an earlier rewrite is overwritten and cannot change
behaviour. Carrying `path_need` through those rebuilds is therefore DEFENSIVE rather than
load-bearing — correct to do, since the pass order could change, but not something a test can
pin today. Recording why a mutant survived is worth as much as recording that one died.

The second mutant is the one that mattered: a marking rewrite is ANSWER-EQUIVALENT, so no
correctness test can see it stop firing — exactly the "a perf gate needs its own test" case. The new
test asserts the PLAN: size-only reads (`path_length`, `cardinality`) are `CountOnly`; element reads
(`nodes`, `edges`) stay `Full`; and a query reading no path at all stays `Full`.

⚠️ AND THE TEST FAILED FIRST ON A CYPHERISM OF MINE. I wrote `relationships(p)`; `gql.rs` says
plainly that "the ISO GQL name for the edge list is `edges`; the Cypher-ism `relationships` is NOT
accepted". The panic was inside `parse().unwrap()` — the parser being right, and this repo's first
standing rule catching me.

### Open

`NestedGroup` is still unmarked and is the larger of the two (`nested-group count` 147.4 ms). It
calls `nested_group`, a SEPARATE walker with no `path_need` parameter at all, so it needs the walker
work this item did not: the field alone is not enough there. `opt.rs:455`'s `RepeatGroup` to
`VarLength` flatten also still hardcodes `Full`, so a marked group that flattens loses its mark —
harmless today because marking runs after that rewrite, and worth fixing if the order ever changes.

2,065 Rust tests green; `rewrite_fuzz` at `LENKE_OPT_FUZZ_SEEDS=500000` green in 100.1 s; all seven
cross-engine fuzzers green; `clippy -D warnings` and `bun run check` each 0.

### Item 1236 — a path bound over a NESTED group is a WRONG ANSWER in the Rust engine: every accessor is null, and binding a path changes the TS row count (OPEN, pinned)

Item 1234 named `NestedGroup` as the larger remaining `PathNeed` target (`nested-group count`
147.4 ms) and item 1235 did `RepeatGroup`. Checking whether marking the nested one was worth
anything found something else: there is nothing to mark, because there is nothing being built.

`exec/nested.rs` contains NO `Lineage` at all, and the plan for a nested group with a path variable
is a bare `Project { NestedGroup { .. } }` — no path-tracking wrapper. So the accessors have no
lineage to read, and they do not say so.

```text
  case                        ts                      native
  no path, count              2                       2                 AGREE
  no path, endpoints          {n:1}, {n:3}             {n:1}, {n:3}      AGREE
  path BOUND, never read      3 rows                   2 rows           DIFFER
  path_length(p)              1, 1, 1                  null, null       DIFFER
  cardinality(p)              3, 3, 3                  null, null       DIFFER
  nodes(p)                    real element maps        null, null       DIFFER
```

TWO SEPARATE DEFECTS, and the controls are what make them separable:

- **The walkers agree with no path mentioned** — same count, same endpoints. The nested traversal
  itself is not in dispute.
- **Merely BINDING a path changes the row count, on the TS side only.** Native answers the same 2
  rows as the no-path control; TS answers 3. Binding a path should not change which rows exist.
- **Every accessor is NULL in the Rust engine** — a silent wrong answer rather than an error.
- The SAME accessors over a FLAT group and over a var-length hop AGREE, so this is specific to
  the nested walker.

⚠️ NOT A REGISTRY CANDIDATE, and the registry says why: "There is deliberately NO `value` axis, and
`accept` refuses a value divergence whatever the registry says. If the engines disagree about the
answer to a determinate question, that is a bug in one of them, and no entry may excuse it." Pinned
in `nested-group-path-conformance.test.ts` so it cannot change silently while the direction is
decided — four tests, including the two agreements that make the divergence diagnostic.

⚠️ THE FUZZER GAP THAT HID IT IS AN INTERSECTION, which is why neither arm caught it.
`differential-fuzz.test.ts` generates a named path over a quantified group — but its unit is FLAT,
`MATCH pp = (a:T)((x)-[:E]->(m)){q}(b:T)`, a single hop. Item 244 added nested UNITS to a different
arm, the one that reads no path. So paths-over-flat-groups is covered, nested-units is covered, and
their INTERSECTION is not. Closing it is a one-line change to the named-path arm's unit — which
would turn the fuzzer RED immediately, so it is recorded rather than done unilaterally.

THE FIX IS A DIRECTION CHOICE, not a bug fix with one answer:

- build lineage in the nested walker, matching `VarLength`/`RepeatGroup` (and then `PathNeed`
  becomes meaningful there, which is where this started); or
- refuse the shape with `E_NOT_IMPLEMENTED`, which is what the engine already does for a
  label/property/`WHERE` on a nested group's inner nodes — consistent, and better than a null;
- and separately, decide which engine is right about the row count, since binding a path moves
  TS from 2 rows to 3.

So item 1234's priced ~89 ms headroom for `NestedGroup` is NOT available as stated: the operator
does not build the chain that `CountOnly` would suppress. The performance item is blocked behind a
correctness decision.

### Item 1237 — the row-count question ANSWERED: TS is wrong, and it is worse than a count — with a path bound it answers a DIFFERENT QUERY (OPEN, pinned; direction chosen)

Item 1236 left two questions and the direction for both was asked for rather than assumed. The
answers: build lineage in the nested walker, and investigate the cardinality before deciding. This
is that investigation, and it settles it against TS on evidence rather than on preference.

The identifying step was the one item 1236 skipped: "3 rows versus 2" names no row, so the EXTRA ROW
had to be identified. Projecting the pattern's endpoint does it. The unit is `(x)->(m)<-(y)`, so the
endpoint is `y`.

```text
  case                          ts                       native
  endpoint, NO path             {1}, {3}                 {1}, {3}        AGREE
  endpoint, path BOUND          {2}, {2}, {4}            {1}, {3}        DIFFER
  inner lists, path BOUND       sx:null, sy:null x3      sx:1, sy:1 x2   DIFFER
  WALK  mode, path bound        3 rows                   18 rows         DIFFER
  TRAIL mode, path bound        3 rows                   2 rows          DIFFER
  exactly TWO reps, path bound  0 rows                   0 rows          AGREE
```

THREE SYMPTOMS, ONE CAUSE. With a path bound, TS's endpoints are `{2, 2, 4}` — the MIDDLE nodes,
not `y` — its group bindings go NULL, and it admits a row at node 4 that TRAIL excludes. It has
stopped treating the unit as nested and ends at `m`.

⚠️ THE DECISIVE EVIDENCE IS MODE-INSENSITIVITY, not the count. With a path bound TS returns THE SAME
THREE ROWS under `WALK` and under `TRAIL`. `WALK` permits edge reuse and `TRAIL` forbids it, so on
this fixture no correct implementation can answer identically — and native does not, giving 18
against 2. A cardinality argument can be waved away as a semantics preference; an implementation
that cannot tell two path modes apart cannot.

HAND ENUMERATION AGREES WITH NATIVE. Fixture `1->2`, `3->2`, `3->4`, all `KNOWS`; unit
`(x)-[:KNOWS]->(m)<-[:KNOWS]-(y)`; default TRAIL. One repetition: from 1, `1->2` then `2<-3`
(`2<-1` would reuse `e1`), giving endpoint 3; from 3, `3->2` then `2<-1`, endpoint 1, while
`3->4` then `4<-3` reuses `e3`. From 2 and 4 there are no out-edges. Two repetitions: every
continuing edge is already used. So exactly TWO paths, ending at 1 and 3 — native's answer, and
both engines agree on it until a path is bound.

AND THE STRUCTURAL ARGUMENT POINTS THE SAME WAY: binding a path NAMES the match, it does not filter
or multiply it, so cardinality must not change. Native answers 2 with and without; TS answers 2
without and 3 with, so TS is inconsistent with ITSELF, independent of which number is right.

### Where this leaves the two items

- **TS's nested-group-with-path handling is the larger defect** — wrong endpoint slot, dropped group
  bindings, and blind to the path mode. Item 244 already found TS's nested close test "read the RAW
  cursor position, true only for a single-level unit"; this looks like the same organ.
- **The Rust side's direction is settled: build lineage in `nested_group`.** The row-count answer
  matters because it fixes the design — lineage is per PATH, and native already emits the right
  2 paths, so the walker needs to record the chain it is already walking rather than to change what
  it walks.
- Item 1234's ~89 ms `PathNeed` headroom for `NestedGroup` remains blocked behind that lineage work,
  which is now a well-specified job rather than an open question.

Pinned in `nested-group-path-conformance.test.ts` (five tests now), including the two AGREEMENTS and
the mode-insensitivity pair, so none of it can change silently.

### Item 1238 — the nested-group wrong answer is FIXED: lineage built in `nested_group`, verified by HAND because the usual oracle is itself wrong (DONE)

Item 1236 found every path accessor returning NULL over a nested subpath group; item 1237 established
TS is wrong on the same shape. The chosen direction was to build the lineage, and this does it.

THE FIX IS SMALL BECAUSE THE WALK ALREADY KNOWS THE CHAIN. `M::steps` holds one
`StepRec { source, edge, target }` per hop in traversal order — `bind_nested` already reads it for
the group's inner lists. So `nested_group` now records what the walk already knows rather than
changing what it walks, which matters: item 1237 established the ROWS are right (both engines agree
with no path bound) and only the path was missing. A k-hop path is the first hop's SOURCE followed by
every target, with the edges in parallel; a zero-hop match is the seed node alone.

### ⚠️ THE DIFFERENTIAL FUZZER CANNOT VERIFY THIS FIX

The usual oracle for a Rust answer here is the TS engine, and item 1237 showed it is WRONG on this
shape — comparing against it would REJECT the correct result. So the expectations are hand-enumerated
from the fixture (`1->2`, `3->2`, `3->4`, all `KNOWS`; unit `(x)-[:KNOWS]->(m)<-[:KNOWS]-(y)`;
default TRAIL):

```text
  path A:  1 -(e1)-> 2 <-(e2)- 3     nodes 1,2,3   edges e1,e2
  path B:  3 -(e2)-> 2 <-(e1)- 1     nodes 3,2,1   edges e2,e1
```

so `path_length` (hops) is 2, `cardinality` (nodes + edges) is 5, and the element lists are 3 and 2.
The engine now answers exactly that. TS answers 1 hop / 2 nodes / 1 edge — a straight contradiction
of the hand count, which is item 1237's finding seen from the other side.

### ⚠️ MUTATION FORCED THE TEST TO ASSERT IDENTITY, NOT SIZE

With size-only assertions, two of four mutants SURVIVED the whole suite:

```text
  first node dropped            CAUGHT
  edges dropped                 CAUGHT
  first node is the TARGET      SURVIVED  -> then CAUGHT
  chain REVERSED                SURVIVED  -> then CAUGHT
```

Both survivors preserve every count, so only element IDENTITIES separate them. Path A runs 1,2,3 and
path B runs 3,2,1, so asserting BOTH ENDS pins both: the target-instead-of-source mutant moves `head`
to 2, and the reversal moves `last` to 2. All four now fail with exactly one failing test. A
size-only test here would have been the "passes for the same reason an empty test does" case.

```text
  nested group + PATH read                 661704.0 -> 758129.2   1.13x
```

### Item 1239 — `NestedGroup` gets `PathNeed`: 1.12x, which recovers item 1238's correctness cost down to ~1.02x (DONE)

Item 1234 priced this and item 1236 found it unavailable — there was no chain to suppress. Item 1238

`RepeatGroup`, with one extra piece: the nested walker now has to choose a REPRESENTATION, not just
skip a copy.

`CountOnly` records `Lineage::elem_counts` — the `(node, edge)` pair per row — and leaves `values`
and `edges` empty, which keeps the offsets equal so every row's span is empty. That is what
`elem_counts`'s own doc requires: "non-zero offsets over an empty `values` is an out-of-range slice,
not a compact encoding", because `gather` rebuilds through `path_at`.

REACH FIRST, and it matters because a marking rewrite changes no ANSWER when it fails to fire:

```text

  nested group + path                              NestedGroup  CountOnly   <- new
  [CTL] repeat-group, lists READ                   RepeatGroup  Full
  [CTL] varlen + path                              VarLength    CountOnly
```

### Item 1240 — the TS nested-path defect FIXED by one guard, and the fuzzer gap that hid it is CLOSED with teeth proven (DONE)

Item 1237 left TS answering a different query once a path was bound over a nested group: the endpoint
was the unit's MIDDLE node, the group's lists came back null, and WALK and TRAIL returned the same
rows. Three symptoms, and they share one cause.

```js
const singleVarlen = path.segments.length === 1 && path.segments[0].rel.quantifier !== undefined;
if (path.pathVar !== undefined && singleVarlen) yield* allWalk(...);
else if (path.pathVar !== undefined)            yield* walkSegments(..., { pathAcc });
```

`allWalk` advances ONE HOP PER REPETITION, so it is right only for `(a)-[:R]->{m,n}(b)`. But a
MULTI-ELEMENT unit is also a single segment — the compiled `CSegment` is `{ rel, node, unit? }` and
the unit's `elems` hold the hops beyond the first — so
`((x)-[:E]->(m)<-[:E]-(y)){1,2}` took that branch and stopped after one hop. That single wrong
branch produces all three symptoms: it ends at the first hop's target (the middle node), it knows
nothing of the unit so it binds none of its variables, and its one-hop walk cannot express the
difference between the path modes.

THE GUARD NOW TESTS WHAT IT MEANT TO: `unit === undefined || (unitIsFlat(unit) && unit.elems.length
=== 1)`. The no-path case has always used `walkSegments`, which handles the unit correctly — both
engines agreed on the rows whenever no path was bound — so the fix is to let the bound-path case
take the same walker with its `pathAcc`.

(The first attempt reached for the AST's `unitRest`/`nested`/`innerQ`, which do not survive
compilation and do not typecheck. `CSegment` is the compiled form; that is the field set to read.)

AFTER THE FIX, every case from items 1236/1237 AGREES, and on the hand-enumerated values:

```text
  case                          ts            native
  path_length(p)                2, 2          2, 2
  cardinality(p)                5, 5          5, 5
  size(nodes(p)), size(edges)   3/2, 3/2      3/2, 3/2
  endpoint, path BOUND          {1}, {3}      {1}, {3}      (was {2},{2},{4})
  inner lists, path BOUND       sx:1, sy:1    sx:1, sy:1    (was null)
  WALK  mode                    18 rows       18 rows       (was 3)
  TRAIL mode                    2 rows        2 rows        (was 3)
  row count with vs without     2 and 2       2 and 2       (was 3 and 2)
```

### ⚠️ THE FUZZER GAP IS CLOSED, AND ITS TEETH ARE PROVEN

Item 1236 identified the gap as an INTERSECTION: the named-path arm generated a FLAT one-hop unit,
and item 244's nested-UNIT arm reads no path. So both halves were covered and their overlap was not
— which is exactly where the wrong answer lived, in BOTH engines. The arm now picks among a flat
unit and two multi-element ones.

Adding it before this fix would have turned the fuzzer red; adding it after is the guard. VERIFIED
BY MUTATION, which is the only way to know a generative test does anything:

```text
  fix applied    5 seeds  ->  5 pass, 0 fail
  fix REVERTED   3 seeds  ->  0 pass, 3 fail
```

So the arm catches precisely the bug it was added for, rather than being coverage that happens to be
green.

### The arc, closed

```text

  1237  TS proved wrong by MODE-INSENSITIVITY, not by cardinality
  1238  native lineage built, hand-verified (TS was the wrong oracle)
  1239  PathNeed for NestedGroup, 1.12x, cost of correctness down to ~2%
  1240  TS's one-line cause fixed; fuzzer intersection closed with teeth
```

Rust tests green; 943 TS tests green; all seven cross-engine fuzzers green; `clippy -D warnings` and
`bun run check` each 0.

### Item 1241 — grepping item 1240's bug CLASS found one more wrong answer, and the obvious fix for it was a 1.19x regression (DONE)

Item 1240's defect was a guard testing a weaker condition than it meant: `segments.length === 1`
standing in for "a single HOP". That is a CLASS, so it was grepped. Eight single-segment guards
exist in the TS executor; `hop-projection`'s is already protected (`plainUnnamedRel` ->
`plainRel` requires `quantifier === undefined`), and reading the rest one by one is slower and less
reliable than asking the engines.

So the unit shapes were SWEPT across query forms instead — 3 units (flat, reversed, two-hop) x 12
forms (counts, endpoints, aggregates, group lists, anchored ends, WALK, `{0,2}`, with and without a
bound path). **One divergence of 36, and on the FLAT unit — the shape item 1240's fix does not
touch:**

```text
  MATCH p = ((x)-[:KNOWS]->(m)){1,2} RETURN size(x) AS x
    ts:     x = null, null, null
    native: x = 1, 1, 1
```

Row counts agreed, so the rows were right: `allWalk` binds the endpoint and the Path and NONE of the
unit's group variables. Item 1237 saw the same symptom for nested units; routing those away fixed
them, and left this.

⚠️ **THE OBVIOUS FIX WAS A REGRESSION, AND MEASURING IT IS WHY IT IS NOT IN THE TREE.** `allWalk`'s
doc says it serves "a single quantified segment (`p = (a)-[:R]->{m,n}(b)`)" — a plain quantified HOP
— so excluding every unit looks like the principled change, and it does fix the bug. It also costs
**1.19x** on `MATCH p = ((x)-[:KNOWS]->(m)){1,2} RETURN path_length(p)`, a shape whose answer was
ALREADY CORRECT. Reverted.

THE FIX THAT SHIPPED binds the group variables inside `allWalk` instead — the same two lines every
other walk site uses:

```js
const withGroups =
  unit && unitExposes(unit) && unitIsFlat(unit)
    ? bindGroupVarsFlat(binding, unit, walk.verts, walk.edges)
    : binding;
```

Only the FLAT branch is needed, because the caller's guard sends a non-flat unit to `walkSegments`.
After it the sweep is **0 of 36**.

COST, three order-alternated rounds (min of 5 per round, 20,000 nodes, degree 3):

```text
  flat group + path                 234.1 -> 262.1   1.12x
  flat group + path, lists read     239.1 -> 270.2   1.13x   (was WRONG before: null)
  [CTL] plain quantified hop        243.5 -> 243.0   1.00x
  [CTL] flat group, NO path           5.7 ->   5.7   1.00x
```

1.12x, controls flat. AND IT IS THE ENGINE'S EXISTING POLICY, not a new tax: `walkSegments` already
binds exposed group variables unconditionally, so the no-path case has always paid this and
`allWalk` was the inconsistent one. The guard is `unitExposes`, so a unit that NAMES no variables
still skips the work.

⚠️ A FUZZER FAILURE IN THIS RUN IS THE KNOWN ONE. `FUZZ_SEED=1558963448` hit

exhaustively, and item 1236's gap was precisely an intersection (paths over flat groups generated,

So it was widened and committed: 9 pattern families (var-length directed/undirected/multi-type, flat
/ two-hop / reversed / inner-edge-var groups, ANY SHORTEST, fixed two hops) x 6 projection forms x

THE LESSON, which this file has in other words at items 1209 and 1222 and now has in the sharpest

### Item 1243 — the fused hop PROJECTION gets a branchless compaction, 2.33x, and the lever is NOT the one item 1224 found (DONE)

`try_fused_hop_project` serves `MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->(b) WHERE b.k <op> <lit> RETURN b.k` by streaming
the per-type CSR and collecting the surviving target ids. Its bound test was the one items 1224 and
1227 hoisted out of the COUNT twin — `bounds.iter().all(|&(op, t)| num_pred(op, data[j], t))` — and
this arm still paid it per edge.

**The obvious read was that item 1224's 5.28x would repeat here, and that read was wrong.** Item
1224's own ranking rule says to price the removal against the loop's PER-ELEMENT cost, and this
loop's element cost includes a `Vec::push`, which cannot be masked the way a `count += 1` can. So
the PRE probe swept SELECTIVITY before anything was built, and the sweep said something the
dispatch story does not explain at all (200,000 nodes, degree 4, random ages):

```text
  project, ONE bound, k > 98 (selective)      1844.5 us
  project, ONE bound, k > 50 (half)           6544.0
  project, ONE bound, k >= 0 (everything)     5503.2
```

**The half-selective spelling is SLOWER than the one that keeps every edge**, while pushing half as
many survivors. No amount of survivor work orders those three that way; a mispredicted branch per
edge does. The dominant cost was the BRANCH, not the dispatch — a different lever that happens to
live in the same loop.

### Both levers, and what each is worth

The operator is now matched once (ten `match` arms, a single bound dispatched directly and two or
more reduced to a range through `canonical_num_conj`, exactly as the count twin does), and the
compaction is branchless in the new `hop_num_survivors`:

```rust
if n == out.len() {
    out.resize(n * 2, 0);
}
out[n] = nbr;
n += usize::from(present[j] & cmp(data[j]));
```

A `Vec::push` cannot be masked because the write's ADDRESS depends on the predicate. What CAN be
masked is the INDEX: write the candidate unconditionally and advance the cursor by the mask, so a
rejected edge is overwritten by the next one. The buffer still ends up proportional to the SURVIVORS
(rounded to a power of two), not to the edge count — which is the property this whole arm exists
for, so the branchless form is not bought back with the memory the general path was avoiding.

Three alternated rounds, binaries hashed per arm and reproduced (item 1219), min of each:

```text
  row                                         PRE      POST    ratio
  project, ONE bound, k > 98 (selective)     1898.6   1613.1   1.18x
  project, ONE bound, k > 50 (half)          6590.7   2831.1   2.33x
  project, ONE bound, k >= 0 (everything)    5433.8   4894.8   1.11x
  project, TWO bounds, 50 < k < 90           7385.1   2709.3   2.73x
  [CTL] hop COUNT, one bound                  768.1    770.8   1.00x
  [CTL] SCAN project, one bound                436.1    435.0   1.00x
```

**THE `k >= 0` ROW IS THE INTERNAL CONTROL THAT SPLITS THE TWO LEVERS, and it is why the mechanism
is established rather than assumed.** That predicate is true for every edge, so its branch never
mispredicts and only the dispatch removal can reach it: 1.11x. The 2.33x lands exactly where the
branch is maximally unpredictable. Both external controls — the count twin (already hoisted at
1224/1227) and a scan projection (never enters this arm) — are flat to within 0.4%.

### The route is asserted, because a fastpath route is answer-equivalent

`fused_hop_project_is_reached` asserts `try_fused_hop_project(..).is_some()` for one bound, two
bounds and an equality — item 1235's lesson, and the reason it is a PLAN assertion: no output can
reveal that the arm stopped firing.

### ⚠️ Four of the ten arms were reachable and UNASSERTED, which only mutation found

Five mutants, each on a fresh copy under `timeout 600 systemd-run --user --scope -q -p
MemoryMax=16G -p MemorySwapMax=0`, the cap's teeth proven first with an allocator bomb (137) and a
bare spin loop (124). Four were caught at once. The fifth — swapping the
`(lo_incl, hi_incl) = (true, false)` arm's `<` for a `<=` — **SURVIVED the entire 1330-test suite**:
nothing anywhere asked this path for a `>= lo AND < hi` range, so four of the ten arms were
reachable with no assertion behind them.

`fused_hop_projection_matches_general` now asserts all ten bound shapes, with the fixture's scores
placed so the four inclusivity combinations answer DIFFERENTLY (bounds ON a boundary value: 20 and
60 against scores 10/20/30/60/90). With bounds off a boundary the four would agree and the
assertion would be decoration. All five mutants are now caught; the range one fails that test alone.

### ⚠️ A harness bug nearly turned four caught mutants into "does not compile"

The verdict's compile-error detector matched `^error:` — which also matches cargo's own
`error: test failed, to rerun pass ...`. The first run therefore reported four mutants as compile
failures when they were being CAUGHT by named tests. Items 767 and 772-773 are the same shape in
the other direction; the rule stands and gets a third instance: **read the result lines before the
exit code, and make sure a diagnostic pattern cannot match the thing it is meant to distinguish
itself from.**

### The TypeScript engine has no twin for either lever, and that is checked, not assumed

TS compiles its hop predicate to a closure through `compilePredicate` (`executor/hop-projection.ts`),
so the per-row operator dispatch this item removed does not exist there. The branchless half is a
branch-prediction effect with no JS analogue — `n += keep ? 1 : 0` is not reliably branchless
through the JIT. The TS filtered-hop gap is data layout and was priced and declined at item 805.

```text
  1.48x  44775.30 -> 66377.10   query/gql    | scan node | best_us
  1.33x  69248.20 -> 91854.60   query/gql    | distinct node | best_us
  1.17x 146999.70 ->171757.70   query/gql    | hop node, NO distinct | best_us
```

**THE SWEEP REFUTES ITSELF, and the row that does it is `scan node`.** A bare node scan has no hop
and no filter, so `try_fused_hop_project` cannot be reached by it under any plan — and it moved
1.48x, more than three of the four "targets". A control moving as far as the targets is item 762's
giveaway, and item 737 already priced this exact failure (a phantom 1.66x from in-sweep
interference, refuted at 25.2 against 24.7 by an isolated A/B).

So the two flagged groups plus that control went on an isolated three-round alternated A/B, binaries
hashed per arm and each reproducing exactly across its three rounds (`4b31c15c` for PRE,
`289d81e9` for POST):

```text
  row                                   PRE(min)   POST(min)  ratio
  query/perrow | element r             272639.8   276531.1   1.01x
  query/perrow | element p              67492.0    66559.6   0.99x
  query/gql    | scan node              63030.1    62357.4   0.99x   <- the control
  query/gql    | distinct node          90320.6    89175.4   0.99x
  query/gql    | hop node, NO distinct 174526.5   172853.7   0.99x
```

Every flag is gone and the control sits with them at 0.99x. **No regression.**

⚠️ ONE DETAIL WORTH KEEPING, because it is the opposite of what item 737 observed: the isolated PRE
readings are HIGHER in absolute terms than the sweep's (63030 against 44775 for `scan node`), since
this harness ran two groups per arm rather than one row. That is why the ratio is the claim and the
absolute number is not — and why the arms must alternate. Item 747's correction stands: a full sweep
is not inherently untrustworthy and remains the regression pass it exists for, but a cell it flags
is a QUESTION, never a verdict.

### Item 1244 — the widest TS gap re-ranked in ABSOLUTE terms, and the remaining `count 3-hop` cost priced to the byte (CONFIRMED, no change)

A `ts,ffi` sweep was run to pick a TypeScript target (72 comparable rows). **Ranking by ratio
picks the wrong row, and by a factor of 60.**

```text
  ratio        ts    native  shape
  2578.10x    5.5       0.0  query: min boolean [short-circuits]
  2383.65x    5.3       0.0  query: top-k by boolean [short-circuits]
    63.26x  302.5       4.8  count 3-hop
    51.88x  338.2       6.5  count 4-hop
```

The two 2000x rows are native fast paths finishing in under a microsecond, so the ratio explodes
while the ABSOLUTE headroom is 5.5 ms. `count 4-hop` at 52x is 331 ms of headroom — sixty times
more. Items 1235 and 1239 established reading a ratio in absolute terms when the baselines differ;
this is the same rule applied to target SELECTION, where it reorders the list rather than
re-describing one row.

### Two levers retracted on evidence ALREADY IN THE TREE, before either was built

1. **Pass the `c` VERTEX to the d-side instead of its id** (`sideOfVertex(e.to, ..)` for
   `side(graph, e.toId, ..)`, so the adjacency comes off `v.adjFrom` as a field read instead of a
   keyed `Map.get`). `sideOfVertex` already exists as its own function for exactly this reason — but
   **item 355 measured it: first touch is 1.21x WORSE** (the same hash plus the memo write). The
   endpoint memo lives on the EDGE, and this loop visits each middle edge exactly ONCE, so `e.to`
   is cold every single time and the cold cost is all this row would ever get. Item 355's note
   already says five of six call sites have that property; this is a sixth.
2. **Memoize the d-side degree per `c`** — refuted at item 310 by its own unreachable control
   moving as far as the target (1.063x against 1.052x, both disjoint).

### What the remaining cost IS, priced independently

The recorded diagnosis says the gap is spread across three components: the `edgesOfTypes` generator
frame, the `Edge` property reads, and two hash lookups. Re-checked, component by component:

- **The generator frame is GONE everywhere**, not just where item 324 measured it. That fix landed
  inside `edgesOfTypes` itself, which returns the `Set` directly for both single-bucket cases, so
  all 17 call sites inherit it — this one included.
- **The `Edge` property read is already the cheap one.** The ungated arm reads `e.toId`, a stored
  string, never `e.to`; that is items 140/218's choice and lever 1 above is why it stays.
- **The two hash lookups are the whole of what is left**, and they are both inside one statement:
  `side` does `graph.edgesFromByLabel.get(c.id)` and then `bucketSize`'s `byType.get(types[0])`.

The arithmetic closes it. The fixture is 200,000 vertices at five edges each, so the middle-edge
loop runs **1,000,000** times:

```text
  measured per middle edge      302 ns   (302.5ms / 1e6)
  two string-keyed Map.gets     380 ns   at item 194's ~190ns each
  native per middle edge        4.8 ns
```

**Two keyed lookups at the measured rate already exceed the row's entire per-edge budget.** So they
are not one component of three — after items 324, 140/218 and 355, they are essentially the whole
cost, and the per-edge work left to shave is bounded by roughly nothing. Native does the same work
in 4.8 ns an edge because it indexes a dense array.

This is therefore a CONFIRMATION of item 300's verdict rather than a new finding: the remaining gap
needs the dense integer-indexed adjacency the TS graph does not expose, and the figure to attach to
that decision is **~63x on `count 3-hop`, 302 ns against 4.8 ns per middle edge**. Item 300's
original 7.30x pricing and item 350's 26x re-pricing both predate items 324 and 355; this is the
first time the residual has been attributed to a specific pair of instructions.

⚠️ WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS, so the next pass does not re-derive it: nothing that keeps a
string-keyed adjacency. Every route from an edge to its target's degree goes through one of two
string maps — id -> vertex, or id -> bucket map — and both cost the lookup this row cannot afford.
A route that wins has to carry a dense ordinal on the EDGE, which is the CSR by another name.

### Item 1245 — the TS hop extremum folds PER ROW where it could fold per DISTINCT ENDPOINT: 2.90x priced, and TWO wrong premises caught on the way (PRICED — BUILT BY ITEMS 1246/1247, see item 1295)

`MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN min(x.name), max(x.name)` is 131-165 ms in TS against
native's 2.4-3.4 (item 1244's sweep). This item diagnoses it and prices the fix. **It was not yet
built when this entry was written** — item 1246 then wired the per-endpoint fold into
`detectMultiHopAggregate` and item 1247 extended it to the single-aggregate rung after 1246 created
a spelling inversion. Item 1295 confirmed the rung is live (the accepted shape reads 80.5 ms against
692.9 for a spelling the gate refuses, 8.6x). What follows is the pricing and, more usefully, the
two premises that had to be discarded first.

### ⚠️ WRONG PREMISE 1: "there is no ungrouped hop aggregate detector"

The detector index at the top of `executor/shortcuts.ts` lists `detectNodeAggregate` (one, scan),
`detectMultiNodeAggregate` (two or more, scan) and
`detectGroupedNodeAggregate`/`detectGroupedHopAggregate` (grouped) — and nothing for the ungrouped
hop. **That comment is incomplete.** `detectHopAggregate` and `detectMultiHopAggregate` both exist
and are wired in `executor.ts`. A new detector written on the strength of that comment would have
added a second claimant for a shape that already has one, into a ladder whose own notes record a
branch ahead of a hot dispatch costing the shape it does NOT claim 1.12x (items 418, 469).

### ⚠️ WRONG PREMISE 2: "fold over the distinct endpoints and it gets faster"

The licensing algebra is real and extremum-specific: **min/max over a multiset equals min/max over
its distinct support**, so ~200,000 distinct endpoints can answer what ~1,000,000 edges are asked.
`count(*)` cannot (it needs the multiplicity) and neither can `sum`/`avg`.

Priced in ONE process on the bench fixture (200,000 nodes, 1,000,000 edges, min of 7) before any
detector was written — `packages/native/src/hop-extremum-price.ts`:

```text
  A engine (general path)            173698.3 us
  B per-edge fold          [CTL]     336675.0        1.94x WORSE
  C per-distinct-endpoint fold       186070.9        1.07x WORSE
  D C + universal-label shortcut      59851.6        2.90x BETTER
```

All four answers agree. **C on its own is a REGRESSION**, and a detector built from the premise
would have shipped 1.07x slower with correct answers — the exact bug class `bun run spelling`
exists for, invisible to every correctness test.

What makes D work is the second half, not the first: C still resolved `e.from` per in-edge to test
the start label. When the start label is carried by EVERY live node, a non-empty bucket already
proves a qualifying edge and nothing has to be resolved. `vacuousLabel` has been exported for this
since item 167, and native's `for_each_typed_out` makes the identical test.

### What the gap actually is, stated precisely

The claiming rung was identified by ELIMINATION rather than by reading, each arm rebuilding the
dists:

```text
  BASELINE (all rungs)                       149.8 ms
  multiHopAggregate DISABLED                 654.3        4.37x slower -> it CLAIMS the shape
  hopAggregate DISABLED  [CTL, expect flat]  188.7        1.26x        -> see the caveat below
```

So `detectMultiHopAggregate` claims it and is already worth 4.37x. The residual is narrower than
"no fast path": that detector reduces the aggregate to a hop PROJECTION (`synthRet`) and folds the
projected rows, so it still emits one row per EDGE and takes ~1,000,000 fold steps where 200,000
would give the same extremum. Its `idempotent: allExtrema` flag is NOT this optimization — it only
decides self-loop safety across two undirected walks. Item 481's far-driven walk is adjacent prior
art (118 ns a row against 375) and explains why the measured ~150-174 ns a row sits between them.

**The open lever:** fold once per distinct FAR endpoint instead of once per row, admitted only when
every aggregate is `min`/`max`, every argument reads only the far variable, and the start label is
absent or vacuous. Everything else must fall through — C's number is what happens otherwise.

### ⚠️ Two instrument failures, both caught, both worth the rules they produce

1. **A VOID run is not a NULL result.** The first elimination run invoked `bun run bench` from the
   repo ROOT, where that script does not exist (it is `packages/native`'s). Every arm emitted
   nothing, which reads exactly like "disabling the rung changed nothing". The script had asserted
   that the MUTATION applied (`grep -c` on the sed) and never that the MEASUREMENT produced a row.
   Items 767 and 772-773 are the same family in the other direction; this is the third variant, and
   the probe now prints `NO ROW EMITTED - the measurement is VOID, not a null result`.
2. **The control moved 1.26x when it should have been flat.** Disabling the SINGLE-aggregate rung
   cannot change which rung answers a two-item projection, yet the row read 188.7 against 149.8.
   Either single-arm noise or item 762's call-site redistribution. It does not threaten a 4.37x
   conclusion, but it DOES price this instrument's drift at ~25%, so nothing small may be read off
   it — the in-process A/B/C/D probe above is the instrument for the fix itself.

### Item 1246 — the TS hop extremum folds per DISTINCT ENDPOINT: 1.17-1.68x, after FIVE guard bugs and a control regression that was the INSTRUMENT (DONE)

Item 1245 priced this and deliberately did not build it. The fold now lives in
`executor/hop-endpoint-extremum.ts` and `detectMultiHopAggregate` consults it before its per-row
walk.

`min`/`max` over a multiset equal `min`/`max` over its distinct support, so a one-hop extremum whose
arguments read only the far endpoint folds once per DISTINCT endpoint (~200,000) instead of once per
row (1,000,000 on the bench fixture). Admitted only when every accumulator is an extremum
(`allExtrema`, already computed for its self-loop meaning), every argument's `freePredicateVars` is
exactly the far variable, the hop is directed and plain with no edge variable, and — at RUN time,
because it is a property of the GRAPH — the start label is absent or `vacuousLabel`.

`foldFor` and the compiled argument closure are REUSED, not hand-rolled. **Item 1245's 2.90x was an
upper bound measured with an inlined property read and a raw `<`**, which would diverge from the
general path on NaN and cross-type ordering; the shared fold is what keeps this byte-identical, and
it is the whole of the difference between that figure and the one below.

A five-cases-in-one-process A/B showed BOTH controls 1.03-1.07x SLOWER with disjoint ranges —
`count(*), max(x.name)` (declines: a `rows` acc) and `min(a.name), max(a.name)` (declines: reads the
start variable). Neither can reach the fold.

1. ~~The wrapper branch~~ — REFUTED. `primed !== null` inside the returned closure is one check per
   QUERY. Returning the BARE walk closure to a declining shape did not help.
2. ~~Module code layout~~ — REFUTED. Moving the fold to its own module did not help either. (The
   move was KEPT and its header records why, so it is not tidied back inline.)

**An ablation settled it:** the same code present but admitting NOTHING put every row back on its
PRE reading, controls included. So the controls slowed only when the primed path RAN — inline-cache

inside one process. That is item 762's rule, which CLAUDE.md states, and the remedy it prescribes:
ONE SHAPE PER PROCESS. The rule was available and two hypotheses were tested before it was applied.

Re-measured with `AB_CASE` selecting a single case, one process per case, three alternated rounds,
each arm's SOURCE and BUILT DIST asserted:

```text
  row                      PRE(min)   POST(min)  ratio   ranges
  string  min+max over x   172103.6   102530.9   1.68x   disjoint
  dict    min+max over x   162378.2   101760.0   1.60x   disjoint
  number  min+max over x   115825.8    98793.4   1.17x   disjoint
  [CTL] count(*) + max     132930.4   136406.7   1.03x   OVERLAPPING - flat
```

⚠️ **The `number` row is 1.17x, not the 1.43x the in-process run reported.** Its PRE reads 115825 in

### ⚠️ The mutant that SURVIVED the whole suite

Four mutants under `timeout` + cgroup cap. Three were caught at once; `reach-always-true` — every
endpoint treated as reached, qualifying edge or not — **SURVIVED exit 0**, because every existing
fixture gives every vertex a qualifying in-edge, so "always reached" answered correctly everywhere.
Item 1242's lesson in a new place: the suite had no fixture where the refusal and the admission
DIFFER.

`packages/gql/src/hop-endpoint-extremum.test.ts` is built so each refusal answers differently: two
ISOLATED vertices hold the global extremes (so folding an unreached endpoint moves both `min` and
`max`), one vertex is reached only by the WRONG edge type, m2 carries a SECOND in-edge so

the start label from the one source that reaches two endpoints. 7 tests, and all four mutants are

### ⚠️ FIVE GUARD BUGS IN FIVE TICKS — two silent, three loud

Recorded together because three were the SAME guard failing three different ways, and the silent ones
are the dangerous class: both surfaced only because a RESULT looked wrong, not because the guard
spoke.

| #   | guard                | bug                                                                               | how it surfaced             |
| --- | -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| 1   | dist carries the arm | `packages/gql/dist/*.js`; the build emits `dist/esm/index.mjs`                    | SILENT `dist=0`             |
| 2   | dist carries the arm | `grep -c` on ONE file prints a bare count, so `awk -F: '{s+=$2}'` summed nothing  | SILENT `dist=0`             |
| 3   | arm is its own code  | the marker was the DEFINITION, which had moved to the new module                  | loud, exit 3                |
| 4   | dist carries the arm | `grep -c` prints `0` AND exits 1, so `                                            |                             | echo 0`made it`"0\n0"` | loud, exit 6 |
| 5   | mutant was applied   | an INSERTING mutant leaves the anchor in place, so the anchor count was unchanged | loud, `SED CHANGED NOTHING` |

THE RULE, item 1219's extended one step: **verify an assertion can FAIL before trusting that it
passed.** Asserting the arm's SOURCE is not enough when the harness reads a BUILT dist; an assertion
that cannot fail is indistinguishable from one that holds; and a mutant's change-detection must
watch what the mutation REMOVES, not what it adds. The dist check is now strict in both directions —
PRE must build a dist WITHOUT the change and POST one WITH it — which is also what catches an
nx-cached build serving the wrong artifact.

Gates: 39/39 test tasks green, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green, `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1247 — item 1246 CREATED an equivalent-spelling inversion, found by grepping its own pattern: asking for ONE aggregate cost 1.42x asking for TWO (DONE)

Item 1246 wired the per-endpoint extremum fold into `detectMultiHopAggregate`. `detectHopAggregate`
runs EARLIER in the ladder and claims every ONE-item projection, so it kept the per-row walk — and
the result was the bug class this repo is organised around, introduced by the previous item:

```text
  RETURN min(x.name)                 145333 / 147313 / 149023 us
  RETURN min(x.name), max(x.name)    102463 / 105407 / 106737        1.42x FASTER for asking MORE
```

200,000 nodes / 1,000,000 edges, one shape per process, three alternated rounds, disjoint by a wide
margin. **This file's own note warns the single-aggregate row is bimodal ACROSS BUILDS (125-180 for
one source)**, which is why the two spellings were alternated WITHIN one build rather than compared
across two — a cross-build comparison here can read disjoint by luck.

Two spellings of one question, costing differently, both answering correctly: no correctness test
can see it, which is what `bun run spelling` exists for. It was found by the loop's own rule —
**grep the pattern elsewhere** — applied to item 1246 itself rather than to older code.

### The fix, and what it measured

`withPrimedEndpointExtremum` wraps the single rung's walk the same way, with the same refusals
(`fold === undefined` excludes the percentiles outright, and `EXTREMA.has(name)` is what admits only
`min`/`max`).

```text
  row                                     before     after    ratio
  RETURN min(x.name)                     145333.3   99284.2   1.46x
  [CTL] RETURN min(x.name), max(x.name)  102462.6  104534.2   1.02x  flat, within its 102-107 band
```

The single spelling is now slightly CHEAPER than the pair, which is the natural ordering — one
accumulator against two. The inversion is gone rather than reduced.

- `eslint(complexity)`: `detectHopAggregate` hit **37 of 35** with the wiring inline. The file

### Teeth

All four of item 1246's mutants are caught through this rung too (they live in the shared module). A
