### Item 1248 — the UNDIRECTED hop extremum, 3.89x, and the self-loop correction items 480-483 built does NOT apply to it (DONE)

Item 1246 declined `-[:T]-` with a stated reason: it "has its own self-loop arithmetic (items
480-483) that this has not been measured against." **That reason was wrong, and the argument for why
is the whole of this item.**

The counting paths need that arithmetic because a loop sits in BOTH adjacency maps and `expand`
yields it once, so an undirected degree would double-count it. This fold asks something weaker: _is
x reached at all_, as a BOOLEAN, and then folds x's value ONCE. A loop makes the answer true through
either bucket, and `min`/`max` do not depend on how many times a value would have arrived. So an
undirected hop is the UNION of the two buckets with nothing subtracted — simpler than the directed
case rather than harder.

Priced first, one shape per process (item 762's rule), on the 200,000-node / 1,000,000-edge fixture:

```text
  undirected min+max      338746.1 us     3.23x the directed pair
  grouped by far prop     664932.1        6.35x the directed pair   <- OPEN, see below
  directed min+max        104755.9
```

The undirected row is ~2x structural (it visits both directions), so 3.23x left real headroom. After
admitting it, three alternated rounds:

```text
  row                        before     after    ratio
  undirected min+max        338746.1   87051.7   3.89x
  [CTL] directed min+max    104755.9  107041.5   1.02x   flat
```

### The fixture had to be able to tell the directions apart

`hop-endpoint-extremum.test.ts` asserts the undirected answer DIFFERS from the directed one:
`-[:KNOWS]-` reaches every endpoint of a KNOWS edge, the two SOURCES included, so `max(x.k)` is
**51** (s2) rather than the directed **30** (m3). An undirected arm that silently behaved like the
directed one would pass a weaker fixture. The isolated extremes (-999/999, no edge either way) stay
out, and a self-loop case asserts a looped vertex is reached once and folded once — the correction
that is NOT needed, pinned so nobody adds one.

Five mutants, all caught, including one specific to this item: never consulting the opposite bucket,
which makes an undirected hop under-reach.

### ⚠️ OPEN, priced: the GROUPED hop extremum at 664932 us, 6.35x the directed pair

`MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->(x) RETURN x.city, min(x.age)` — the largest remaining gap in this family and
the biggest absolute number measured in it. The same identity licenses it: each distinct endpoint
belongs to exactly ONE group when the key reads only the far endpoint, so `min`/`max` per group is
per-group idempotent and the fold can run once per endpoint into that endpoint's group.

NOT built here, and the honest reason is scope rather than doubt: it needs group-key evaluation and
a group map inside the endpoint walk, which is a different shape of change from the three scalar
accumulators this file now carries. The rung to extend is `detectGroupedHopAggregate`. **Before
building it, confirm the rung actually claims the shape** — item 1245 lost a tick to a stale
detector-index comment, and the `ORDER BY` in the priced query above has not been checked against
`sortsOnOutputOnly`.

Gates: 21 projects green, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green, `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1249 — `ORDER BY` on a grouped aggregate cost 2.15x (hop) and 11.90x (node) because BOTH rungs refused it outright (DONE)

Item 1248 recorded the grouped hop extremum at 664932 us and told the next pass to check that
query's `ORDER BY` against `sortsOnOutputOnly`. **Doing so first showed the `ORDER BY` was HALF the
number**, so that figure was an overstatement by 2.1x — priced on a spelling I had not validated.
The corrected gap for the grouped extremum itself is **313718 us**, and the ordering is its own
defect:

```text
  HOP   RETURN x.city AS c, min(x.age) AS lo              313718.8 us
  HOP   ... ORDER BY c                                    670623.3        2.14x
  NODE  RETURN x.city AS c, min(x.age) AS lo                8038.1
  NODE  ... ORDER BY c                                     94934.9        11.81x
```

Eight groups do not take 357 ms to sort, let alone 87. **ELIMINATION found the cause**: with the hop
rung disabled the UNORDERED spelling went 313718 -> 702617 (it reaches the rung) while the ORDERED
one did not move at all (it never did). `detectGroupedHopAggregate` and
`detectGroupedNodeAggregate` both refused `proj.orderBy.length > 0` outright and fell to the general
path, which sorts one row per input ELEMENT.

**The refusal was not an oversight**, which is why the fix is a resolver and not a deleted line. The
single-row aggregate rungs admit an `ORDER BY` for free through `sortsOnOutputOnly` — ordering one
row is a no-op. These two return one row per GROUP, so admitting it means SORTING. The `count(*)`
tally sibling already does exactly that through `sortGroupRows`, whose own note carries the
argument: the sort is over the GROUPS, at most what the query returns.

### Both rungs, because fixing one would have been item 1247 again

The node twin shares the hop rung's body AND its refusal — found when a `return slots.map(...)`
anchor matched TWICE. Fixing only the hop would have left a sibling inversion, which is exactly what
item 1247 had to come back and repair. Measured after, three alternated rounds, one shape per
process:

```text
  row                        before     after    ratio
  HOP   ... ORDER BY c      670623.3  312337.7   2.15x
  HOP   no order   [CTL]    313718.8  306399.3   1.02x  flat
  NODE  ... ORDER BY c       94934.9    7977.3  11.90x
  NODE  no order   [CTL]      8038.1    7950.8  1.01x  flat
```

Ordering is now within 2% of not ordering on both rungs — the spellings have CONVERGED rather than
merely narrowed.

**BOTH SPELLINGS of a key resolve**, which is why this reuses the tally's `colSortsOf` rule instead
of `outputColumnSorts`: that one matches an output NAME only, and item 1062 measured the asymmetry
it creates at 3.8x on `bun run spelling`. A key may name any output column or BE the grouping
expression, and a test asserts `ORDER BY x.city` answers exactly what `ORDER BY c` answers.

### NULL sorts LAST in both directions, verified rather than assumed

The first DESC expectation written here was wrong — NULLS do not move to the front. Three spellings
were checked (the alias, the key expression, and a filtered variant that routes differently) and all
agree: null last. That is `compareSort`'s policy, which `sortGroupRows` uses rather than re-deriving
one, so the fast path cannot drift from the general path on it.

### ⚠️ Teeth, and the SIXTH guard bug — the first to give a FALSE SURVIVED

`grouped-aggregate-order.test.ts` asserts ROW ORDER with `toEqual` on the full array, never a
multiset: the defect this guards is not a wrong row SET but a sort that silently does not apply. The
fixture's first vertex carries the LAST city alphabetically, so a rung returning groups in discovery
order fails rather than passing by luck.

Four mutants, all caught: the sort never applying, DESC dropped, any unresolved key silently sorting
by the group key, and duplicate output names no longer declining.

**But the first run reported `sort-never-applies` as SURVIVED, and it was a harness lie.** Run
directly, the test failed 3 of 5; the root runner exited 1. The cause: `local out=$(cmd)` followed
by `local code=$?` captures the exit status of the **`local` builtin**, not the command. Item 1246's
script happened to write that assignment without `local` and worked; adding it here produced a false
SURVIVED — **the dangerous direction**, since it invents a test gap and sends you writing redundant
tests for a phantom. Declare first, assign second.

Two further anchor failures were caught rather than mis-scored: two mutants matched the tally's
`colSortsOf`, whose lines are textually identical, and one re-anchored mutant turned out VACUOUS
(adding an unused name to a Set), whose survival meant nothing. The rule stands and has now cost six
instances: **verify an assertion can FAIL before trusting that it passed**, and for a mutant, that
its survival could only mean a missing test.

Gates: 21 projects green, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green, `bun run check` 0 (after extracting
`keyedClausePred`, since admitting the sort pushed `detectGroupedHopAggregate` to 36 of the 35
complexity cap — the cap has been right in this file every time).

### Item 1250 — adding `ORDER BY` to a working reachability query made it THROW, and this one is not a slowdown (DONE)

Items 1247 and 1249 found `ORDER BY` costing 1.42x, 2.15x and 11.90x on rungs that refused it.
Grepping that refusal across the executor turned up one more — `detectReachableShortcut`, the
unbounded var-length + DISTINCT rung — **and there the consequence is not a cost at all.**

Falling off that rung sends an UNBOUNDED pattern to the general path, which enumerates TRAILS and
dies on the trail budget. 3,000 nodes / 15,000 edges:

```text
  MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->*(x) RETURN count(DISTINCT x) AS c        OK     58 ms, 1 row
  ... ORDER BY c                                              THROW  E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
  MATCH (a:P)-[:T]->*(x) RETURN DISTINCT x.n AS n             OK     29 ms, 3000 rows
  ... ORDER BY n                                              THROW  E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
```

**Two spellings of one question where one ANSWERS and the other FAILS** — and on the count form the
`ORDER BY` is a NO-OP, because one row is already in order. The user is told to "add a tighter
bound" for a query that worked before they sorted it. That is worse than any of the cost gaps above.

### The fix

`reachSortApplier` resolves every `ORDER BY` key to one of the rung's own output columns — by name,
or by BEING that column's expression — and sorts `runReach`'s rows. The name half is the tally's
argument (item 190): an output column's value is already computed, so nothing is left unevaluated
and no raise can be swallowed. The expression half is there because `outputColumnSorts` matches
names ONLY and item 1062 measured the asymmetry that creates at 3.8x — here it would be
answer-versus-error, which is worse than 3.8x.

After, on the same fixture: the count form answers in 46 ms, the rows form in 37 ms against the
unordered 39 ms — the sort of a reached SET is free next to the BFS, and both key spellings return
identical rows.

### ⚠️ `ORDER BY` with a WINDOW still declines, and still throws — recorded, not hidden

`runReach` applies `skip`/`limit` ITSELF, so a sort layered on its output would slice BEFORE
ordering and return the WRONG ROWS. Declining is therefore correct rather than lazy:

```text
  ... RETURN DISTINCT x.n AS n LIMIT 5                        OK     5 rows
  ... RETURN DISTINCT x.n AS n ORDER BY n LIMIT 5             THROW  E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
```

**That leaves the top-N-reachable shape erroring, which is the most natural query of this family.**
It is not fixed here for a stated reason rather than an unstated one: `ReachSpec` carries
`skip`/`limit` as `CountValue`, which may be a PARAMETER, while `SortPlan` needs plain numbers — so
moving the slice inside needs parameter handling and its own test surface, and this item had already
run long. A test PINS the throw, so a future fix has an assertion that must flip rather than a
comment to notice.

### Teeth

`reach-order.test.ts` asserts ORDER rather than row sets, and carries its own control: the
unordered spelling is asserted NOT to be ascending, because if BFS order happened to be sorted the
ordering test would pass with no sort at all and prove nothing. Three mutants, all caught — the sort
never applying, PAGING admitted (which would slice before sorting), and an unresolved key silently
taking the first output column.

Gates: 21 projects green, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green, `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1251 — `ORDER BY … LIMIT` over unbounded reachability: the gap item 1250 recorded, closed, and its pinned test FLIPPED (DONE)

Item 1250 admitted `ORDER BY` on `detectReachableShortcut` but declined a WINDOW, for a correctness
reason: `runReach` applies `skip`/`limit` itself, so a sort layered on its output would slice BEFORE
ordering and return the wrong rows. That left the top-N-reachable shape — the most natural query of
the family — still throwing:

```text
  ... RETURN DISTINCT x.n AS n LIMIT 5                  OK     5 rows
  ... RETURN DISTINCT x.n AS n ORDER BY n LIMIT 5       THROW  E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
```

The window is now ordered FIRST and sliced SECOND: `specWindow` hands the spec NO window when a
sort is active, and `reachSortApplier` does both in that order. All three forms answer — `LIMIT`,
`DESC LIMIT`, and `OFFSET … LIMIT` — and the first five are the five SMALLEST rather than the first
five the BFS happened to reach.

**A PARAMETERIZED window works rather than declining**, which is the one design choice worth stating:
`LIMIT $k` cannot be resolved when the shape is COMPILED because the value lives in `params`, and
`outputColumnSorts` declines exactly that case for exactly that reason. But this sort runs inside
the per-QUERY closure, where `params` exist, so `resolveCount(limit, params)` resolves it there.
Declining would have sent it back to the general path, which THROWS on an unbounded pattern — so
the choice is between resolving at run time and leaving a parameterized top-N broken.

### ⚠️ THE PINNED TEST FLIPPED, which is what the pin was for

Item 1250 wrote `expect(() => …).toThrow()` for the window case and said in the audit that a future
fix would have "an assertion that must flip rather than a comment to notice." Applying this change
made that test FAIL — the query stopped throwing — and the test now asserts the sorted, sliced
answer. **A recorded gap with a failing assertion attached is worth more than a TODO**, and this is
the first time in this run that mechanism has paid off.

### Teeth

Three mutants, all caught, and the first is the wrong-answer risk this change introduces:
`slice-before-sort` (the spec pages itself again, so `runReach` slices before the order exists),
`window-ignored` (the slice is dropped after sorting, so `LIMIT` returns everything), and
`offset-ignored`. The `LIMIT 5` case asserts the five smallest, so slicing the BFS-order prefix
fails rather than passing with five plausible rows.

`detectReachableShortcut` hit 36 of the 35 complexity cap again, and `specWindow` is the extraction
— the fourth time in this run that cap has pushed back and been right.

Gates: 21 projects green, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green, `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1252 — a WRONG ANSWER in the TS reachability shortcut, found by looking for the Rust engine's version of items 1247-1251 (DONE)

Five items of `ORDER BY` work had all been TypeScript, so this went looking for the same defects in
NATIVE. What it found instead was a **wrong answer in TS**, and native being right.

The divergence probe said native THROWS `E_RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` on unbounded reachability where TS
answers — which looked like a missing native fast path. It is not. Native HAS the shortcut
(`varlen_distinct_endpoint_count`) behind a soundness gate:

```rust
fn set_reachability_is_exact(mode: PathMode, max: u32) -> bool {
    match mode { Walk => true, Trail => max <= 1, Simple | Acyclic => false }
}
```

Its comment records why, from `fastpath_fuzz` seed 3249 (item 68): the BFS permits EDGE reuse, so it
computes WALK reachability, while a TRAIL forbids it. **TS had no such gate.**

### The wrong answer, and its own oracle

One node, one self-loop — the smallest graph where walk and trail reachability differ. A 2-hop
TRAIL needs two DISTINCT edges and only one exists, so `min >= 2` matches NOTHING:

```text
  MATCH TRAIL (x:P)-[:R]->{2,}(y)  RETURN count(DISTINCT y)    1   <- WRONG (the shortcut)
  MATCH TRAIL (x:P)-[:R]->{2,9}(y) RETURN count(DISTINCT y)    0   <- correct (enumeration)
  MATCH TRAIL (x:P)-[:R]->{3,}(y)  RETURN count(DISTINCT y)    1   <- WRONG
  MATCH TRAIL (x:P)-[:R]->{3,9}(y) RETURN count(DISTINCT y)    0   <- correct
```

The BOUNDED spelling cannot reach the rung (it requires `max === null`), so it is an independent
ORACLE for the same question — and the two disagreed. `ReachSpec` records only `minZero: boolean`,
so `{2,}` was executed as though it had no lower bound at all.

Swept across all four modes on that fixture, exactly ONE cell was wrong: `TRAIL` at `min >= 2`.
SIMPLE and ACYCLIC decline the rung (it requires the default mode) and agree with their oracles;
`->*` and `->+` are correct because for an UNBOUNDED max with `min <= 1` walk-reachability and
trail-reachability COINCIDE — remove the cycles from any walk and a trail remains.

### The fix, and why declining is right

`reachQuantifierIsExact` admits an unbounded max with `min <= 1`, which is native's condition
expressed for a rung that only ever sees unbounded patterns. `{2,}` now declines to enumeration,
which THROWS on a cyclic graph — and that is the correct trade twice over: **a wrong answer is worse
than an error**, and native throws on the identical query, so this CLOSES a cross-engine divergence
rather than opening one.

### Teeth, in both directions

Two mutants, both caught. `min-bound-unchecked` re-introduces the wrong answer. `over-declines-min-1`
is the opposite failure — refusing `min <= 1` would disable the `->*` / `->+` shapes items 1250 and
1251 serve, and a test asserts those still answer, because declining too much would otherwise make
the correctness test pass for the wrong reason.

### ⚠️ Still open, measured: WALK unbounded THROWS where the BFS is exact

The rung requires the DEFAULT mode, so an explicit `MATCH WALK (x)-[:R]->*(y)` declines and
enumerates — and a WALK over a cyclic graph has infinitely many paths, so it throws on a ONE-NODE
graph whose answer is plainly 1. Native's gate says `Walk => true`: the BFS is exact there, more
clearly than for any other mode. Admitting it is a separate change (the rung's mode check guards
SIMPLE and ACYCLIC too, which need their own argument), and it is left priced rather than attempted.

Gates: 21 projects green, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green, `bun run check` 0 (after extracting
`reachQuantifierIsExact` — the fifth time the complexity cap has pushed back in this run).

### Item 1253 — CI red from a test I wrote: a THROW assertion that depended on how fast the machine exhausts a budget (DONE)

Item 1252 went green locally and **failed in CI**, on a test item 1250 had added:

```text
  ✗ ORDER BY over unbounded reachability (item 1250)
      > an ORDER BY the rung cannot resolve declines rather than answering wrongly   [5087.84ms]
```

5087 ms against bun's default 5000 ms test timeout. It was not asserting anything — it was TIMING
OUT. The test asserted `expect(() => …).toThrow()`, where the throw came from the general path
EXHAUSTING THE TRAIL BUDGET on a 400-node cyclic fixture. That takes about a second on this machine
and longer on a slower runner, so the verdict depended on hardware speed.

**A test whose outcome depends on how fast a budget is exhausted is not a test.** The claim being
made — "an unresolvable `ORDER BY` declines, and declining does not produce a wrong answer" — is a
claim about the ANSWER, and asserting it through a resource error was a category mistake: the error
is incidental to the fixture's size, not to the behaviour.

Rewritten against its own three-node acyclic CHAIN, where `->*` enumeration finishes in
microseconds, asserting the rows and their order instead — plus the resolvable spelling, which must
agree, since that agreement is what makes the decline invisible in the answer. The file went from
950 ms to **110 ms** and no longer touches the budget at all.

⚠️ THE WIDER LESSON, which this run has now paid for twice in different clothes: item 1250 recorded
that declining "still throws" as the honest state of the engine, and that was true — but encoding it
as a TEST made the engine's resource limit part of the test's contract. A limit is allowed to move;
a correct answer is not. Assert the invariant, not the symptom.

Checked for siblings: no other test added in items 1246-1252 asserts a throw, so this was the only
one of its kind.

Gates: 21 projects green, `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1254 — closing the fuzzer gap that let item 1252's wrong answer through, with its teeth PROVEN by reverting the fix (DONE)

Item 1252 fixed a wrong answer that seven fuzzers had passed over. This finds out why and closes it.

**Two hypotheses, and the first was REFUTED by measurement.** The fuzzer's fixture places its
self-loop at a vertex that HAS an in-edge (`4 -> 5`, loop on `5`), and the fixture's own note argues
the placement is safe under every mode it pairs with an unbounded quantifier. So the fixture looked
inadequate — `4 -> 5 -> 5` is a legal 2-hop trail, so walk and trail would never diverge there.
Checked directly, running the PRE-1252 code against the fuzzer's own extracted fixture:

```text
  :F ->{2,}  = 2   against its bounded oracle {2,9} = 1    DIFFER
  :F ->{3,}  = 2   against {3,9} = 0                       DIFFER
  :E ->{2,}  = 4   against {2,9} = 4                       agree
```

**The fixture was always adequate.** My reasoning about the in-edge was wrong: a loop reached at hop
2+ from elsewhere still separates walk from trail.

**The real gap was the PAIRING.** The generator's unbounded arm emits `+`, `{1,}` and `{2,}` — and
only ever with `RETURN count(*)`. `count(*)` cannot reach `detectReachableShortcut` at all:
`reachCount` refuses `first.star` and requires `count(DISTINCT <endpoint>)`, and the rows form
requires a `DISTINCT` projection reading only the endpoint. So `{2,}` was generated, and the rung
that mishandled it was never the rung that answered.

Two arms added, pairing the same quantifiers with `count(DISTINCT b)` and with
`RETURN DISTINCT b.n ORDER BY x`.

### ⚠️ Teeth PROVEN by reverting the fix, not assumed

CLAUDE.md's rule for a generative test is that a mutant must be shown to be caught, because "a
generative test whose teeth were never verified is worse than no test, because it is believed."
Item 1252's gate was reverted and the widened fuzzer run three times with random seeds:

```text
  before item 1254:  passes with the bug present (that is how 1252 shipped unnoticed)
  after,  run 1:  0 pass 1 fail
          run 2:  0 pass 1 fail
          run 3:  0 pass 1 fail
```

3 of 3 on fresh seeds, where the same bug previously survived every run.

of all, and native says so outright (`set_reachability_is_exact`: `Walk => true`). WALK is now

```text
  SIMPLE    400               THROW E_RESOURCE…      DIFFER (pre-existing)
```

`Simple | Acyclic => false`, so a TS that answered where native throws would OPEN a divergence on a
large cyclic graph — exactly what the table above shows for the TRAIL and SIMPLE rows today. A free
perf win is not worth buying a divergence.

That gate declines an UNBOUNDED trail pattern, so native throws on `MATCH (x)-[:R]->*(y) RETURN

### Item 1258 — a 29,253 ms query on a ONE-NODE graph: the `min >= 2` frontier walk had no level cap (DONE)

Item 1257's parity sweep recorded that native ANSWERS `MATCH WALK (x)-[:R]->{2,}(y)` where TS
throws, and called native right. It is right — and it took **29,253 ms on one node with one
self-loop**, against 0 ms for the bounded `{2,9}` and for `->*`.

The `min >= 2` regime walks the frontier level by level and unions the levels in `min..=max`. Its
loop was `for hop in 1..=max`, exiting only on an EMPTY frontier — and a cyclic graph never empties
one. With `max = u32::MAX` for an open bound that is **4.29 billion levels over a one-edge graph**.
The answer was correct the whole time; only the cost was absurd.

### `min + n` is exact, not a heuristic

If `y` has a walk of length `h >= min`, take the SHORTEST such walk and suppose `h > min + n`. A
walk with more than `n - 1` edges must repeat a node, so it contains a cycle of length `c <= n`;
excising that cycle leaves a walk of length `h - c > min` — still qualifying, and shorter,
contradicting minimality. So the smallest qualifying length is at most `min + n`, and level-sets
past that can contribute no node the union does not already hold.

A BOUNDED pattern is untouched: `max` is the smaller of the two whenever it is real.

Verified against a BOUNDED oracle (wide enough to be exact) on six shapes — self-loop, 2-cycle,
3-cycle, chain, lollipop, two joined cycles — at `min = 2` and `min = 3`: **12 of 12 agreed**, and
the 29,253 ms case now answers in **0 ms**.

### ⚠️ A PURE TEST FOR A PERF FIX, because reverting the cap changes no answer

Removing the cap is ANSWER-EQUIVALENT — it only makes the query spin — so no result assertion can
see it, and item 1253 is why this is not a timing test (a verdict that depends on machine speed is
not a verdict). The arithmetic is extracted as `level_cap(min, max, nodes)` and gets a truth table:
open bounds capped at `min + n`, real bounds untouched, the cap never exceeding `max`, and no
overflow at `usize::MAX`.

Alongside it an ANSWER guard the truth table cannot give: a lollipop at `min = 2` reaches `{b,c,d}`
= 3, where a cap of `min + 1` would union `S_2 ∪ S_3` = `{c} ∪ {d}` = 2. Three mutants — cap
removed, cap too tight, cap ignoring `max` — all caught.


### ⚠️ I ARGUED THE CLOSED EXPLANATION COULD NOT COVER THIS, AND THE MEASUREMENT SAID OTHERWISE

The ingest family is closed as a CONSTANT FACTOR (item 312: `JSON.parse` + allocation + freeze,
`addVertex` withdrawn at 7.4%, `addEdge` ~85%). My argument against it: pg-text and csv are **not
JSON**, and they have the WORST ratios — if `JSON.parse` dominated, the JSON formats would be the
slowest, not the fastest. That reasoning is wrong, and phase attribution is what showed it.
200,000 nodes / 1,000,000 edges, min of 5:

```text
  split('\n')                      32 ms
  + tokenize, DISCARD               61
  + tokenize and BUFFER             78      <- what `decode` actually does
  full deserialize               3385
  ---------------------------------------
  APPLY phase                    3306      97.7% of the total
```

**The parse side is 78 ms of 3385.** The two-phase buffering item 1244 flagged as a candidate —
`decode` tokenizes every line into a `string[]` and holds them all before applying — costs **17 ms**,
not the seconds the gap is made of.

Split further, which confirms item 312 rather than contradicting it:

```text
  addVertex x200,000      181 ms   (0.91 us each)    5.5% of apply
  addEdge   x1,000,000   2398 ms   (2.40 us each)    73% of apply
```

So TS's apply cost is essentially FORMAT-INDEPENDENT, and the ratio spread comes from the other
side: **native's parse speed varies by format** (pg-text 353 ms, graphson 1198), so the format
native parses fastest shows the biggest ratio. The ordering I read as evidence of a TS pathology is
a fact about the Rust decoders.

### What this means for target selection

The five largest absolute gaps in the whole field are one closed finding wearing five hats. The
sixth row — `count 4-hop` at 337 ms — is item 300's dense-adjacency target, re-confirmed and priced
to a specific pair of instructions at item 1244.

⚠️ AND A LIMIT OF THIS INSTRUMENT, worth stating because it nearly misdirected the next tick: a
TS-vs-native sweep ranks TS gaps and **cannot rank a RUST-side improvement at all** — native is the
fast column by construction. The open Rust target (the remaining conditional-increment sweeps in
`fastpath.rs`, from item 1219) does not appear anywhere in this table, and choosing from this table
alone would have retired it by omission. Rust work needs the Rust bench as its instrument.

Enumerated while here, since item 1219's "eleven more" is stale: **13 conditional-increment sites
remain, 7 are already branchless.** Most of the 13 are DELIBERATE — the three string sites keep

### Item 1260 — `IS NOT NULL` is ~4x slower than Gremlin's `has(k)` for the same question, and a probe that measured the WRONG PATH three times before the route check caught it (OPEN, priced)

Item 1259 nominated the two PRESENCE-count sweeps as the Rust target. Pricing them found something
bigger and a different kind of defect:

```text
  GQL   scan  WHERE age IS NOT NULL     890.3 us      GREM  scan  has('age')   228.9 us   3.89x
  GQL   hop   WHERE b.age IS NOT NULL  1216.5         GREM  hop   has('age')   286.4     4.25x
```

200,000 nodes / 800,000 edges, identical answers. Two spellings of "count the elements carrying
`k`", ~4x apart — the defect class this repo is organised around.

**The cause is a predicate SHAPE mismatch.** `has(k)` lowers to `PropertyExists`, which the
fast-path matchers accept; `IS NOT NULL` lowers to `IsNull { negated: true }`, which they do not, so
it falls to the general path.

### ⚠️ THE OBVIOUS FIX WOULD BE A WRONG ANSWER

`ir.rs` is explicit: `PropertyExists` is true for a PRESENT value "regardless of that value", and it
is "the one predicate that separates an absent property from a present `Null` … which
`<var>.<key> IS NOT NULL` cannot." The masks genuinely differ — `PropertyExists` is
`present || nulls`, `IS NOT NULL` is `present` ALONE — so accepting one as the other would miscount
any column storing a present-null.

The route is available but needs the mask to follow the spelling, not the site. On a `Column::Num`
the two coincide (a present-null promotes the column to `Gen`, which the matcher's own comment calls
load-bearing at exactly one line), so the scan numeric path could accept the spelling outright; the
hop path serves ANY column type and would need `present` alone for the `IS NOT NULL` form. Pinned
with an assertion that a fix must FLIP — the mechanism that has paid off three times in this run
(items 1251, 1255, 1257).

### ⚠️ THE PROBE MEASURED THE WRONG PATH THREE TIMES, and each was a different fixture trap

Worth recording in full, because the timings looked perfectly reasonable throughout.

1. **First value null → a `Gen` column.** The fixture nulled node 0, so the column had no kind to
   infer and was built as `Gen`; every numeric fast path declined. The bounded CONTROL read
   **765.4us against 26,056** and I nearly wrote that up as "a present-null costs 34x".
2. **Any null → still not `Num`, via the Builder.** Moving the null off node 0 did not help. A
   `Column::Num` `accepts` a `Null` in place ("no de-opt"), but that describes mutation, not the
   build path — so the with-nulls arm could not be constructed at all this way, and the
   `has_nulls` branch it was meant to price stayed untested. Added a column-representation
   assertion to the probe, which is what said so.
3. **And the shape never reached the target anyway.** A route check printed the plan:
   `Filter { pred: IsNull { negated: true } }`, and
   `try_fused_hop_present_count reached: **false**`. All the earlier numbers were the general path.

THE RULE, which items 1185 and 1242 both state and this is a third instance of: **verify the route
before trusting the time.** Three rounds of plausible measurement priced a function that was never
called, and the one-line `is_some()` check settled it instantly. A probe that cannot say WHICH code
it ran is measuring the engine, not the change.

That is the third harness-shape error in two items, all the same family — the harness not mirroring

### ⚠️ THE MUTATION RUN FOUND A WRONG ANSWER IN THIS CHANGE

`masks-merged-hop` survived while only the SCAN half of the semantic test existed. Writing the hop

The premise was wrong. `has_value_at`'s own note says why: "for every typed variant the `present` bit
IS this question; only `Gen` keeps its null in `data` and has to look." So `present` alone is the
right mask for a TYPED column and the wrong one for `Gen`, where a present-null has `present = true`
and its null lives in the value. `IS NOT NULL` now DECLINES a `Gen` column — the de-optimized
representation takes the general path rather than making the sweep read values.

### The two surviving mutants, explained rather than patched

  source-side `IsNull { slot: 0 }` is pushed BELOW the `Expand` onto the `Scan`, so the Filter above

  `nulls` half.

### Item 1262 — `NOT (k IS NULL)` is the SAME question and was ~4x slower; canonicalized in the optimizer, not the matcher (DONE)

Item 1261 admitted `IS NOT NULL` to the presence fast paths. Grepping that defect class for other

```text
  scan  NOT (age IS NULL)   844.8 us   against  IS NOT NULL  222.2    3.80x
```

### Fixed in `normalize_pred`, and the reason is the repo's own rule

`Not(IsNull { negated })` now canonicalizes to `IsNull { negated: !negated }`. **Not in the
matcher** — CLAUDE.md states that speed is a property of the optimized PLAN rather than the surface
syntax, so two spellings that canonicalize to one plan cannot differ, and every consumer benefits
rather than the two presence sweeps alone. The rewrite sits in the `Not` arm that already folds
double negation and `NOT (l = r)`.

⚠️ SOUND BECAUSE A NULL TEST IS TOTAL, which is exactly why this is safe where that arm's ORDERING
rewrite is not. `ir.rs`: a null test is 2VL — "`NULL IS NULL` is TRUE, not NULL" — so the predicate
never yields UNKNOWN and `NOT` of it is its exact complement. The NaN hazard that sank
`NOT (x >= 2)` (TRUE where `x < 2` is FALSE, which is why that rewrite is equality-only) cannot
arise: there is no comparison here to be unordered.

After, all three spellings within 5%, controls flat:

```text

  scan NOT (IS NULL)    229.8  (3.67x)  hop NOT (IS NULL)    293.3  (4.22x)
```

### Item 1263 — item 1262's TS presence target REFUTED, and the "far walk is 4x" it led to is the fixture's ingest order (RETRACTED)

Item 1262 closed with a target: TS is 44x / 166x native on a presence count (`scan IS NOT NULL`
9751.6 µs, `hop IS NOT NULL` 48408.1 against native's 222.2 / 290.9), "comparable to the largest
query-side gaps in the field", never ranked because the cross-engine sweep has no presence row.
Both halves of that framing are now refuted. No code change beyond three comment corrections.

### Presence is not the variable — rows KEPT is

The control is the one `CLOSED.md` already names for this question (item 570: `WHERE true` is THE
control for "why is the filtered version slower"). `IS NOT NULL` keeps all 800k rows; `age > 50`
keeps 392k, so the comparison item 1262 drew was between two different amounts of work. A bounded
predicate that keeps the SAME rows settles it:

```text
  shape                      kept        ms
  hop IS NOT NULL            800,000    46.3
  hop age >= 0               800,000    45.6     <- the same, within noise
  hop age > 50               392,000    26.5
  hop age > 999                    0     4.1
  scan IS NOT NULL           200,000     8.9
  scan age >= 0              200,000     8.9     <- the same, exactly
```

So there is no presence-specific gap in TS, and nothing to fix for `IS NOT NULL` there. The cost
decomposes cleanly instead: ~4.1 ms for 800k hops plus the predicate (≈5 ns an edge), and ~53 ns
per row KEPT on top. A bare `count(*)` is ~0 ms, an O(1) tally. **Adding a presence row to
`bench.ts` would have measured selectivity, not presence** — so it is not added.

### The 4x that remained, and why it is not in the code

What the control did expose is a 4x between the two ENDS of one hop — 46.1 ms filtering the far
endpoint against 10.7 ms filtering the start — which is exactly the asymmetry `farOnlyHopCount`
exists to have removed (item 137). Four spellings ruled out the obvious gate: the start label is
vacuous here, so `pa` is undefined and `farWalkFits` is satisfied, and all four read ~40 ms.

**Route verified before the time was trusted** (items 1185, 1242, 1260) and without instrumenting
anything. A predicate that keeps NOTHING costs a vertex walk its 200k visits and an edge scan its
800k, which are far apart enough to tell apart:

```text
  far   keeps NONE    4.1 ms        start keeps NONE    4.6 ms
```

Both are ~20 ns a vertex, matching item 164's 29 ns/vertex. So `farOnlyHopCount` IS running, and
the entire gap sits in the survivor degree sum: 200k identical `degreeOfTypes` calls, 6.1 ms
through `adjFrom` against 42.0 ms through `adjTo` — 30 ns against 210 ns for the same function.

Not caching: `Vertex.adjFrom` and `adjTo` are the same `??=` accessor over the same map shape. The
cause is allocation order. The fixture emitted `from = k % N` (sequential) and `to = (k*7919) % N`
(a permutation), so the reverse index's per-vertex `Set` objects were created in scrambled order
and reading `.size` is a pointer chase to a random address — which caching the BOX does not help,
because the box is not the scattered thing.

The control that settles it: ingest the same graph with the edge list sorted by TARGET. Same
degrees, same answers, only the order changed.

```text
                           far filter   start filter
  edges in SOURCE order       45.4 ms       10.3
  edges in TARGET order       13.7          44.5
```

It FLIPS. No code-side cause can do that, so "the far walk is slower" does not exist.

### ⚠️ The bench's own two rows carry a stale claim, and one inflated number

`traverse 1-hop + start filter` says the two rows are "a different COST CLASS: a start-only
predicate can be decided once per vertex and multiplied by that vertex's degree, so it scales with
the vertex count where the row above scales with the edge count." True when item 114 wrote it;
item 137 gave the far side the same per-vertex walk and the comment was never updated — so it has
been stale for ~1100 items, and it is the explanation a reader would have reached for first.

And `graphDoc` scatters BOTH endpoints, which puts both rows in the worst-case locality regime.
Min-of-3, alternated rounds, same graph size and the same answers throughout:

```text
  fixture                      far filter   start filter
  bench-like (both scrambled)     42.4 ms       38.5
  source-ordered                  39.8           9.8
```

The scatter is kept — it is the shape a reloaded snapshot has, and it prices both ends alike — but
the TS column should not be read as pure interpreter cost. A source-grouped ingest, which is what
a CSV or an export sorted by subject produces, is 3.9x cheaper on the side being filtered.

next to the code it would have changed: the rejected lever on `farOnlyHopCount`'s header, and a
note on each of the two bench rows.

### Item 1264 — a numeric `IN` / `=`-OR-chain count had no streaming arm at all: 12.1x, and the first implementation of it was a 2.4x REGRESSION (DONE)

Pricing the predicate-spelling enum that paid at items 1261 and 1262 found the one CLAUDE.md names
by hand as a historical 100-300x class: "`k = $a OR k = $b` vs `k IN [$a, $b]`". `num_conj_on_slot`
admits `PropertyExists`, a `Compare` against a Num literal in either operand order, and AND-chains
of those on one key — and neither `Expr::Or` nor `Expr::In`, because it returns a CONJUNCTION of
bounds and a disjunction has no such shape.

### The control is what made it a finding rather than a selectivity reading

On a contiguous set, `k IN [1,2,3]` selects the IDENTICAL rows as `k >= 1 AND k <= 3` — same
answer, one spelling a disjunction and the other the AND-chain the fast path already took. That
equivalence is the whole instrument; item 1263 had just retracted a target for comparing two
spellings that kept different numbers of rows. 200,000 nodes / 800,000 edges, all three answering
6000:

```text

  scan IN [1,2,3]                0.85 ms     0.07     5.90
  scan = 1 OR = 2 OR = 3         0.84        0.07     5.82     12.1x
  scan >= 1 AND <= 3             0.03        0.03     5.03     <- the control
  [CTL] scan age >= 0            0.03        0.03     4.72
  [CTL] hop rows (untouched)     3.55/0.78   3.54/0.77
```

So this is a NATIVE gap — TS shows 1.17x between the same spellings and is not the lever here.

### k VECTORIZED PASSES, not one k-term closure, and no arity cap

Item 1231's rule applied in a new place: k passes that each auto-vectorize beat one closure
carrying k terms, because a third term stops LLVM vectorizing (item 451 named the mechanism, item
1229 measured the cliff — one exclusion 51.2µs, two 608.8). `k IN {v..}` is the sum of k equality
passes, and `sweep_num_count(|x| x == v)` already is that primitive; the k-exclusion arm in the
same function does exactly this and has no cap either.

A cap was still looked for rather than assumed, because k passes must eventually lose to the
general path's single pass. It is not in range — the general path grows with k too, so the route
wins at every arity tried, with identical answers at every k:

```text
  k          2      4      8     16     32     48     64
  before  0.709  1.131  1.735  2.752  4.735  6.557  6.766   ms, 200,000 nodes

```

(k=1 is flat at 0.147/0.148 — a one-element list is not a disjunction after normalization, so it
is an in-shape control. See the open target below: 0.147 for a single `=` is itself wrong.)

### Item 1265 — `Eq` does have a range form, and pairing it changes nothing, because the optimizer never sends a bare `=` to that arm (REFUTED; the real target identified)

Item 1264 recorded this on its way out: a single `k = v` count reads 0.145 ms where
`k >= v AND k <= v` — strictly more work — reads 0.035, and `try_stream_num_count`'s pairing match
says `CompareOp::Eq | CompareOp::Ne => None`, "Eq/Ne have no range form". The reasoning was right
and the conclusion was wrong.

### The spelling gap is real, and the controls killed the first two explanations

200,000 nodes, min of 9, three alternated rounds, the two spellings answering an identical 2000:

```text
  age = 50                   0.145 ms      [CTL] age >= 50              0.034
  age >= 50 AND age <= 50    0.035         [CTL] age >= 20 AND <= 80    0.035
                               4.1x        [CTL] age <> 50              0.029
```

`<> 50` is ALSO unpaired and is fast, so "unpaired implies slow" is false. `>= 50` keeps 50% of
rows and is fast, so it is not branch prediction either. `Ne` genuinely has no range form — `x <> t`
is a union of two ranges and `NaN <> t` is TRUE where `x < t || x > t` is false for NaN — but `Eq`
does: `x = t` is exactly `x >= t && x <= t` for every f64 pair, NaN (both FALSE) and `±0.0` (equal
under all three operators) included.

### ⚠️ So the pairing was implemented, and measured EXACTLY ZERO change

`age = 50` read 0.145 before and 0.145 after. The arm is not reached. One route probe settled in
one run what three rounds of timing could not — the rule from items 1185, 1242, 1260 and 1261,
which I had just written up and then failed to apply BEFORE building:

```text
  MATCH (a:P) WHERE a.k = 50 RETURN count(*)
    PLAN: Project { Aggregate { IndexSeek { label: "P", key: "k", value: Num(50.0) } } }
    -> agg child is NOT a Filter

  MATCH (a:P) WHERE a.k >= 50 AND a.k <= 50 RETURN count(*)
    PLAN: Project { Aggregate { Filter { Scan { "P" }, And(Ge, Le) } } }
    -> num_count=true
```

A bare equality is rewritten into an **`IndexSeek`**, so it never becomes a `Filter` over a `Scan`
and `try_filtered_count`'s whole chain — including the arm I changed — is unreachable for it. The
pairing is reverted: a change that cannot be shown to move anything is not kept, however sound.

(A prediction was falsified on the way, which is what exposed this. `canonical_num_conj` folds
`= 50 AND > 0` to the range `[50,50]`, so a REDUNDANT conjunct should have been FASTER than the
bare `= 50`. It measured 0.150 against 0.145 — no fold, because `normalize_pred` drops the
redundant conjunct first and hands back the bare equality. The model was wrong about the optimizer,
not about the range arm.)

### The real target, now located

`IndexSeek` is a SCAN-FALLBACK node by design (`opt.rs`: "predicate becomes a scan-fallback
`IndexSeek`/`RangeSeek`"), and `index_seek_ids` scans the label and filters when no index exists.
What is missing is the COUNT: `count(*)` over a `Filter(Scan)` has a streaming arm and `count(*)`
over an `IndexSeek` materializes an id vector first. That is the 4.1x, it is worth the same on
every unindexed `k = v` count, and it is the next target rather than this one.

Gates: not applicable — reverted, nothing shipped from this item but the measurement.

### Item 1266 — the CI red on `a1e38108` is a PRE-EXISTING rare-seed divergence, ruled out structurally and then by replay

`a1e38108` went red on the differential fuzzer ("20000 random queries render byte-identically"),
one commit after item 1264 changed native count answers — so the suspicion was reasonable and it is
wrong. Seed and query from the CI log:

```text
  FUZZ_SEED=3835470458
  MATCH (t:T) OPTIONAL MATCH (t)-[:E]->(n WHERE ((true > {a: n.nu, b: '0'}.zz)
    AND ((NOT n.nu) IS NOT NULL))) RETURN t.n AS x, n.n AS y ORDER BY x, y

    ts:     ok  [{"x":3,"y":null}, … 6 rows]
    native: err E_INVALID_VALUE
    (the fuzzer's own label: "an evaluation-order difference, but no registry entry covers this shape")
```

**Ruled out STRUCTURALLY first** (the rule from `gremlin-fuzz-families`: rule a suspect out by
structure, not by counting failures). The query has NO aggregate, so `try_filtered_count` — the only
caller of the function item 1264 touched — is never invoked. Then confirmed by replay, the same seed
against both arms:

```text
  post-1264 (marker 3)   FAIL
  pre-1264  (marker 0)   FAIL, identically
```

So it is the OPEN item 1226 family — a faulting predicate under an OPTIONAL hop, where TS keeps the
left rows with `y` null and native fails the whole query. A passing test in the same CI run names it
("OPEN: an OPTIONAL hop makes the TS side NON-EMPTY, so the known fault divergence is not
registry-covered"), and the conformance decision is still outstanding.

Frequency, 8 fresh random seeds locally: **8 pass, 0 fail.** So the gate is rarely red rather than
broken, which is also why items 1259-1264 all went green through it.

⚠️ NOT REGISTERED, DELIBERATELY. The repo has a divergence registry for exactly this, and adding an
entry would encode the item 1226 conformance call — which is the open question, not a side effect of
clearing CI. A registry entry would also mask a genuine future regression in that shape. Left red
and reported instead.

### Item 1267 — `count(*)` over an unindexed equality seek asked for the ids it then threw away: 4.75x (DONE)

Item 1265 located this after chasing the same 4.1x into the wrong function. A bare `k = v` is
rewritten into an `IndexSeek`, never becomes a `Filter` over a `Scan`, and so reaches none of
`try_filtered_count`'s streaming arms — while its own explicit range spelling does. Two spellings of
one question, one of them 4x.

`try_scan_count` is where a count answered from a size or a cheap enumeration lives (`Scan`,
`Expand`, `EdgeScan`), and it sent everything else to `_ => return None`. `IndexSeek` is now an arm.

### ⚠️ The first version of that arm measured NOTHING, and said why

`super::index_seek_ids(..).len()` — skip the general aggregate's Batch gather, take the length —
read **0.140 ms against 0.145**, inside noise. So the cost was never the Batch: it is the seek
MATERIALIZING a `Vec<u32>` of matches, a push per hit through the label's id list, when a count
needs no id at all. `seek_eq_num_count` sweeps the typed column instead, reusing item 1264's
`stream_eq_set_count` with a single value.

### Measured, two stores, min of 9, three alternated rounds per arm

```text
  NO index on the key                    PRE      POST
    = 50  (the IndexSeek)              0.133 ms  0.028     4.75x
    [CTL] >= 50 AND <= 50              0.032     0.032     the Filter(Scan) spelling
    [CTL] <> 50                        0.027     0.026
    [CTL] bare count(*)                0.002     0.002
    [CTL] = 50 PROJECTED               0.301     0.306     still materializes, by design

  HASH INDEX on the key
    = 50  (the IndexSeek)              0.036     0.036     unchanged, and that is the point
    [CTL] = 50 PROJECTED               0.225     0.217
```

The REAL index is asked first, so only the scan fallback is replaced: a hash bucket is O(matches)
and a sweep is O(label), and the indexed row must not get slower. It did not move.

⚠️ A FIRST PASS SHOWED THE TWO UNTOUCHED CONTROLS DRIFTING ~10% in the same direction (0.032 ->
0.035, 0.301 -> 0.334), which is this file's documented layout hazard — an arm costing a shape it
never runs. A second alternated pass settled it as between-run drift: the controls came back
IDENTICAL (0.032/0.032, 0.026/0.026, 0.306/0.309, 0.217/0.217). Worth the extra pass, because at
~10% the first reading could not tell the two apart.

### ⚠️ The tests did not reach the code, twice, for two different reasons

Mutation is what exposed both. `label-ignored` — pass `&None` where the seek's label belongs —
SURVIVED, and so did two others, while all three tests passed.

1. **The fixture was too small to route.** Five nodes plan as a `Filter(Scan)`, not an `IndexSeek`.
   Fixed by building 200 nodes AND asserting the plan IS an `IndexSeek`, so it cannot go vacuous
   again silently.
2. **Still unreached, and this is the one worth remembering.** The answer tests in this file use
   `run(&parse(q), &st)` — the PARSED plan. The optimizer never runs, so the rewrite this whole item
   is about does not exist in what the test executes. Confirmed by printing from inside the arm:
   **no output at all.** All three tests now run `opt::optimize_indexed(..)` first.

That is the third harness-shape error in this run of items (1260's assertion called the wrong plan
node, 1264's list was desugared below the check it was aiming at, this one ran an unoptimized
plan). The rule generalizes past "verify the route": **verify that the TEST takes the route**, and
for anything the optimizer does, that means running the optimized plan.

A third mutant, `cross-type-literal-accepted` (default a non-numeric literal to `0.0`), survived on
a fixture with no zero cell — answer-equivalent there. A `k = 0` node makes it a wrong answer, and
the node is asserted in its own right rather than left as a silent trap.

### Teeth: 5 mutants, 3 caught, 2 explained

```text
  label-ignored                  CAUGHT  an_unindexed_equality_count_matches_the_general_path
  count-off-by-one               CAUGHT  (3 tests, including both new ones)
  cross-type-literal-accepted    CAUGHT  an_unindexed_equality_count_matches_the_general_path
  index-preference-removed       SURVIVES — answer-equivalent COST choice. Sweeping an indexed
                                 key returns the same count; only the time differs, and no
                                 assertion can see it. Its guard is the measured indexed row above.
  nan-decline-removed            SURVIVES — equivalent: `x == NaN` is false for every cell, and
                                 `index_seek_ids` returns empty for a NaN value at its first line,

```

Route pin checked both ways: PRE fails ("count(*) over an IndexSeek must reach try_scan_count"),
POST passes, for the indexed and unindexed store alike.

### Left undone, deliberately

A `Str`/`Dict` column under an unindexed `k = 'v'` seek materializes ids the same way and is
presumably the same 4x. It needs its own measurement and its own equality argument (`Arc<str>`
compare, dict code resolution), so it is recorded rather than guessed at.

And a cost-model question these numbers raise: at 1% selectivity the unindexed SWEEP (0.028) now
beats the INDEXED seek count (0.036), because the index path builds a bucket `Vec` and binary-searches
the label per candidate while the sweep is vectorized. For a far more selective value the index must
win. Neither end is measured, so the preference stays "index first" — but it is now a known
unmeasured assumption rather than an obvious one.

### Item 1268 — two TS suspicions refuted by the right estimator, and a 1.84x spelling spread found and located (measurement only)

Four native items in a row (1261, 1262, 1264, 1267) left the TS side unexamined, so this prices the
TS twin of item 1267's question: does the TS engine seed an index for a filtered count, and is any
spelling of an equality count left out?

### It does seek, and every equality spelling reaches it

200,000 nodes, `age` with 100 distinct values, `min`-of-9 over three alternated rounds:

```text
  shape                  no index   HASH INDEX
  = 50       (count)       3.158      0.205
  {age: 50}  (count)       2.998      0.207
  = $p       (count)       3.305      0.209
  IN [50,51] (count)       5.717      0.552
  [CTL] bare count(*)      0.001      0.000
```

So the clause, inline and PARAMETER spellings all seed, and they agree within 2% — the
equivalent-spelling invariant holding in TS, measured rather than assumed.

### ⚠️ REFUTED: `<> 50` is NOT slowed down by creating an index

That first pass read `<> 50` at 4.134 unindexed against 7.303 indexed and looked like a 1.77x
REGRESSION from merely creating an index the predicate cannot use — which would have been a real
bug. It is an artefact of `min`-of-N on a bimodal series, which is precisely what this repo's TS
estimator rule exists for. The series:

```text
  unindexed  21.6 16.2 8.5 8.4 8.8 4.1 4.2 4.1 3.9 3.9 3.8 3.8 3.9 3.9
  INDEXED     4.2  4.3 4.1 4.0 3.9 3.8 3.6 3.6 3.7 3.7 3.7 3.7 3.7 3.8
```

The unindexed arm's first five reps are the JIT tiering up; `min` over 9 reps caught one low rep in
one arm only. With 14 reps, the first three dropped, the MEDIAN of the rest, min over three
alternated rounds:

```text
  <> 50        unindexed 3.930   INDEXED 3.725    flat (indexed marginally FASTER)
  [CTL] > 50   unindexed 3.970   INDEXED 3.873    flat
  [CTL] = 50   unindexed 3.493   INDEXED 0.146    23.9x — the index works
  [CTL] bare   unindexed 0.001   INDEXED 0.001
```

No regression. Three rows that the wrong estimator would have mis-signed, one of them as a bug.

### ⚠️ REFUTED: a TS `IN [..]` count is NOT linear in k, so item 1264's design does not transfer

Native's membership count is k VECTORIZED PASSES, which wins there because each pass vectorizes.
In TS there is nothing to vectorize, so the same shape would be pure k-fold cost — worth checking
before assuming the fix is symmetric. It is already a single pass:

```text
  k            1      2      4      8     16     [CTL] >= 1 AND <= 16
  ms         5.942  5.484  5.872  5.253  5.220        5.036
```

Flat. So the TS engine does one scan with a membership test, which is the right design for it, and
the lever that paid 12.1x natively does not exist here.

### FOUND: three spellings of one question, 1.84x apart — and the cause is already written down

The k=1 row is the tell: `IN [50]` costs what `IN [16 values]` costs. Measured in ONE PROCESS
(item 762: a two-process A/B flatters whichever arm it likes), 14 reps / drop 3 / median, min over
three rounds, all four answering an identical 2000:

```text
  {age: 50} inline          3.195 ms   [3.23 3.20 3.21]
  age = 50                  3.358      [3.39 3.36 3.36]
  age IN [50]               5.884      [6.37 5.89 5.88]
  age = 50 OR age = 50      5.885      [8.67 5.88 5.92]   <- IN and OR are one shape
  [CTL] age > 50            4.006      [7.14 4.01 4.01]
  [CTL] bare count(*)       0.001
```

LOCATED, not just measured. All of these DO reach `buildNodeCount` — the node-count rung admits a
clause `WHERE` deliberately, and its comment says why ("tallying one while declining the other
would create exactly the equivalent-spelling gap the probe exists to catch"). What differs is the
per-vertex evaluation, and the per-vertex numbers name it exactly:

```text
  3.358 ms / 200,000 = 16.8 ns a vertex      (= 50)
  5.884 ms / 200,000 = 29.4 ns a vertex      (IN [50] / the OR chain)
```

Item 230 measured that same pair as **17.2 ns against 29.0** and attributed it: a predicate passed
with the node's OWN variable lets `directEqProps` read the element DIRECTLY, where anything it does
not recognize goes through the binding. So `directEqProps` recognizes `=` and not the membership
form, and the gap is one matcher wide.

Recorded as the next target rather than attempted here. Predicted outcome if admitted: `IN`/`OR`
at ~17 ns a vertex, i.e. ~5.9 ms -> ~3.4, for every arity (the k-sweep above is flat, so the win
does not shrink with k) — and it closes a spelling gap rather than only a cost, which is the
stronger reason.

Gates: measurement only, no code change — `bun run check` 0.

### Item 1269 — `IN` and the `=`-OR-chain lift into `memberProps`: 1.53-1.61x, and the spelling spread closes from 1.84x to 1.24x (DONE)

Item 1268 found and located this: three spellings of one question, 1.84x apart in the TS engine, all
reaching `buildNodeCount` but not all reaching the element-direct lift. `directEqProps` admits a
bare `prop`, a `NOT prop`, a dotted compare and a plain compare, and declines its WHOLE chain on
anything else — so an `in` conjunct took the entire predicate to the generic evaluator, which reads
its element back out of the binding `Map`.

```text
  shape                      before     after    ns/vertex before -> after
  age IN [50]                 5.884 ms   3.839     29.4 -> 19.2     1.53x
  age = 50 OR age = 50        5.885      3.815     29.4 -> 19.1     1.54x
  age IN [50,51,52,53]        5.872      3.713     29.4 -> 18.6
  age IN $p (param haystack)  ~5.88      5.032               25.2
  [CTL] age = 50              3.358      3.340     16.8 -> 16.7     already lifted
  [CTL] {age: 50} inline      3.195      3.108     16.0 -> 15.5     already lifted
  [CTL] age > 50              4.006      4.289                      cmpProps, untouched
  [CTL] bare count(*)         0.001      0.001
```

200,000 vertices, one process (item 762), and the TS estimator rule throughout: 14 reps, first three
dropped as warm-up, MEDIAN of the rest, min over three order-alternated rounds. Item 1268 is the
reason that rule is not optional here — a `min`-of-9 summary mis-signed one of its rows as a bug.

Item 230 had already measured and attributed this exact pair (17.2 ns against 29.0): a predicate
passed with the node's OWN variable lets the lift read the element directly. The gap was one matcher
wide.

### ⚠️ ITEM 1268'S READING WAS WRONG IN ONE DETAIL, and the first cut inherited it

That item recorded "IN and OR are already one shape", because they measured 5.884 against 5.885.
They are not: `membershipFromEqChain` is applied inside `compileExpr`'s `case 'or'` — deliberately,
so every ANALYSIS pass still sees the original `or` and `collectHints`' seeding keeps firing — which
is a stage AFTER `directEqProps`. Two shapes costing the same is not one shape. Lifting `in` alone
took it to 3.699 and left the OR spelling at **6.042**, which is how the mistake surfaced. The fold
is now done inside `directEqProps` as well, reading the same function and still not touching the AST.

### `membershipTest`, extracted so the two paths cannot drift

`case 'in'`'s three arms — a compile-time hash for an all-literal haystack, a per-execution hash for
a closed one, a linear scan for a per-row one — are now one function, used by the generic evaluator
and by the lift. Two copies of a three-valued membership rule is the drift this file keeps paying
for, and the call sites differ only in where the needle comes from. A per-row haystack declines the
lift, exactly as it declines hoisting there.

### The consumer audit, which `dotted-predicate-routes.test.ts` demands in writing

A successful lift EMPTIES `where`, so the lifted list becomes the ONLY carrier of that conjunct —
and that file names five consumers, "none discoverable from the list's own definition", where a miss
returns a silent SUPERSET. All five, plus two more:

- **`satisfies`** — patched. The applier.
- **`shortcuts.ts`' `InlinePred`** — covered: `inlineHolds` calls `satisfies`.
- **`mergeFarPreds`** — patched, and this is the one that would be a WRONG ANSWER rather than a slow
  one. Pinned by a test that answers 1 where a dropped list answers 2.
- **`rejectedByElementDirect`** — deliberately NOT extended. Its own comment records why (item 644
  was reverted here): this pre-filter runs BEFORE the binding is built, so rejecting a candidate
  skips a binding that would otherwise RAISE. It is an optimization that may only ever say
  "not decided", so omitting a family costs speed and cannot cost correctness.
- **the two `preFilter` gates in `matching.ts`** — not extended, same reasoning: they gate that
  pre-filter alone.
- **`hasPredicate`** — patched. Its doc is explicit that a new carrier forgotten there reintroduces
  the bug the function exists to prevent.
- **`hop-projection`'s "did anything lift" check** — patched, which is what lets the hop shapes win.

### Raise order: the lift runs LAST among the lifted families, and that is deliberate

A membership test cannot raise — `hashedIn`/`inList` only compare — while `truthProps`/`notTruthProps`
raise on a non-boolean and `cmpProps`/`pathProps` can too. Running the non-raising family FIRST would
let a FALSE membership return before a sibling conjunct the generic path would have raised on,
changing WHICH queries error rather than how fast they run. Running it last cannot.

### Teeth: 6 mutants, 6 caught — and two of them needed tests that did not exist yet

```text
  merge-drops-member                   CAUGHT  the far-hop MERGE test (would answer 2 for 1)
  satisfies-skips-member               CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law + seed-hint fuzz tests
  member-test-keeps-unknown            CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
  member-runs-before-raising-families   CAUGHT  the raise-order test
  has-predicate-omits-member           CAUGHT  the ROUTE test's explicit `hasPredicate` assertion
  or-fold-removed                      CAUGHT  the ROUTE test
```

The last two SURVIVED the first run, both because admitting a spelling to a lifted family is
ANSWER-EQUIVALENT — every answer test passes with the lift reverted and only the cost changes. The
remedy is the one `CLOSED.md` already prescribes for a route choice: assert the PURE decision.
`compilePredicate` is exported, so the route test builds the two `where` trees by hand and checks
`memberProps.length`, that `where` is EMPTIED (a lift that left it would apply the conjunct twice),
and that `hasPredicate` sees it.

⚠️ AND ONE CLAIM IN MY OWN TEST WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED IN PLACE. The product-count case was
written as the thing that catches `has-predicate-omits-member`. It is not — the route test's explicit
assertion is. The case still earns its place, because it pins the product shape's ANSWER where no
assertion on the compiler can, but its comment now says which guard actually lives where.

### Item 1270 — `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` / `NOT (… IS NULL)` lift into `nullProps`: 1.66-1.93x, and all three spellings at once (DONE)

Item 1269 left `directEqProps` admitting a bare prop, a `NOT` prop, a compare, a dotted compare and
a membership. `isNull` is an `Expr` kind of its own and was not among them, so it declined the WHOLE
chain — while the INLINE spelling of the same question, `(n {k: null})`, which this engine reads AS
`IS NULL`, landed in `props` and was already element-direct.

The native engine had the identical omission in its own matcher and paid for it twice: item 1261 for
`IS NOT NULL` and item 1262 for the `NOT (… IS NULL)` spelling that was only noticed after the
first shipped. Both are folded here in one pass for that reason.

200,000 vertices, one process, TS estimator rule (14 reps, first three dropped, median, min over
three order-alternated rounds). The first two rows answer an identical 2000:

```text
  shape                   before    after    ns/vertex          ratio
  nk IS NULL               5.683 ms  2.956    28.4 -> 14.8       1.92x
  nk IS NOT NULL           5.549     3.351    27.7 -> 16.8       1.66x
  NOT (nk IS NULL)         6.438     3.332    32.2 -> 16.7       1.93x
  [CTL] {nk: null} inline  3.317     3.219    16.6 -> 16.1       already lifted
  [CTL] age = 50           3.514     3.453    17.6 -> 17.3       already lifted
  [CTL] age IN [50]        3.876     3.857    19.4 -> 19.3       item 1269's family
  [CTL] bare count(*)      0.001     0.001
```

The spread across the null spellings closes from **1.94x to 1.13x**, and `IS NULL` now reads FASTER
than the inline spelling it was being compared against — the lift is one `isNullish` where the
inline form goes through `structuralEq`.

A by-product worth recording: this fixture tests item 1263's claim directly. `IS NOT NULL` keeps
198,000 rows at 27.7 ns a vertex while `= 50` keeps 2,000 at 17.6 — so a TS filtered COUNT costs per
SCANNED node, not per kept row, which is what makes these rows comparable at all.

### `NOT` is folded by FLIPPING the flag, and the flip is exact

`asNullTest` reads `isNull` as itself and `NOT (… IS NULL)` with `negated` inverted. Exact because a
null test is TWO-VALUED — `null IS NULL` is TRUE, never UNKNOWN — so `NOT` of it is its exact
complement. The NaN hazard that makes `NOT (x >= 2)` unequal to `x < 2` cannot arise: there is no
comparison here to be unordered. (`opt::normalize_pred` canonicalizes the same pair in the Rust
engine for the same reason.)

### Consumers: the same seven as item 1269, same dispositions

`satisfies` and `hasPredicate` patched; `mergeFarPreds` patched and pinned by a test that answers 1
where a dropped list answers 2; `hop-projection`'s lift check patched; `rejectedByElementDirect` and
the two `matching.ts` `preFilter` gates deliberately left alone, because that pre-filter runs before
the binding is built and may only ever say "not decided" (item 644's revert is the precedent).
`shortcuts.ts`' `InlinePred` is covered through `inlineHolds` -> `satisfies`.

The lift runs LAST among the lifted families, beside `memberProps`: a null test cannot raise, so
running it before the families that can would let a FALSE test return early and swallow a sibling's
raise.

### Teeth: 7 mutants, 7 caught — after the ordering mutant exposed a flaw in my own test

```text
  merge-drops-nulls                   CAUGHT  the far-hop MERGE test
  satisfies-skips-nulls               CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
  reject-condition-inverted           CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
  negated-not-flipped                 CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
  has-predicate-omits-nulls           CAUGHT  the ROUTE test's `hasPredicate` assertion
  not-arm-removed                     CAUGHT  the ROUTE test (answer-equivalent otherwise)
  nulls-run-before-raising-families   CAUGHT  the raise-order test — after it was FIXED
```

⚠️ THE ORDERING MUTANT SURVIVED THE FIRST RUN, and the reason is worth keeping. The raise-order test
used `WHERE n.s AND n.k IS NOT NULL`, where ONE vertex passes the null test and then reaches the
raising conjunct — so the query raises whatever the order is, and the test could not see the move.
The discriminating shape needs the null test to reject EVERY vertex: `WHERE n.s AND n.s IS NULL`
matches nothing, so under the wrong order every row is rejected before the raise and the query
answers 0 instead of erroring. Same lesson as item 1267's product case — a guard needs the fixture
that makes it load-bearing, and only mutation says whether it has one.

### Item 1271 — parenthesising a conjunction cost 2.14x, and the note explaining why it was left alone had the right facts and the wrong conclusion (DONE)

`directEqProps` declines its WHOLE chain on the first conjunct it cannot read, and a NESTED `and`
was one of those. The note it carried:

> A nested `and` under an `and` is not flattened here — it declines below as a non-`compare`
> conjunct. The parser produces one flat `items` list for `a AND b AND c`, so the nested shape
> arrives only from parenthesisation, and declining it is a missed optimisation, not a wrong answer.

Both halves are true. The conclusion is wrong twice over: a cost that PARENTHESES alone turn on is
this engine's named bug class, and it was the most expensive decline left in the function. 200,000
vertices, one process, TS estimator rule, all three answering an identical 2000:

```text
  shape                      before    after    ns/vertex        ratio
  a=50 AND b=0 AND c=0        3.558 ms  3.641    17.8 -> 18.2     control, flat already
  (a=50 AND b=0) AND c=0      7.615     3.471    38.1 -> 17.4     2.19x
  a=50 AND (b=0 AND c=0)      6.732     3.740    33.7 -> 18.7     1.80x
  [CTL] a <> 50               3.859     3.839    19.3 -> 19.2
  [CTL] a = 50                3.468     3.655    17.3 -> 18.3
  [CTL] bare count(*)         0.001     0.001
```

The spread across the bracketings closes from **2.14x to 1.08x**.

The flatten is depth-first and left to right, so the conjuncts arrive in WRITTEN order — the same
order the flat spelling produces. That is load-bearing rather than tidy: this loop groups what it
lifts into families, so arrival order is the order a RAISE is reached in, and a flatten that
reordered could change which query errors. A test asserts the order directly (`[a, b, c]` for both
nestings) because no answer can see it, and the mutation run confirms that is the only thing that
can: `flatten-reverses-order` is caught by that assertion alone.

```text
  flatten-keeps-first-only   CAUGHT  existing AND short-circuit tests — a SUPERSET
  flatten-reverses-order     CAUGHT  the ROUTE test's written-order assertion
  flatten-descends-or        CAUGHT  existing seed-hint + Kleene-law tests — a disjunction
```

The "different families" case expected 2 and the answer is 3 — `a = 1 AND c > 2 AND b IS NOT NULL`
keeps three vertices, not two, because only `nulled` and `absent` fail the null test. And the
hand-built unliftable conjunct used `arith` with `left`/`right` where the node is `head`/`tail`,
which crashed `compileExpr` rather than declining. Both were my fixtures being wrong about the
engine, not the engine being wrong.

### Still open from the same pricing run

`NOT (a = 50)` costs 6.467 ms against `a <> 50`'s 3.859 — **1.68x**, same answer (198000). `NOT` of
a compare is neither a bare prop nor a compare, so it declines the chain, while `<>` lifts. The fix
is to invert the operator, and it must be EQUALITY-ONLY: `NOT (x >= 2)` is not `x < 2` when `x` is
NaN (this repo keeps NaN JS-unordered, so the negation is TRUE where the flip is FALSE) — the same
restriction `opt::normalize_pred` carries in the Rust engine, and the reason item 1262's rewrite is
equality-only there. `=`/`<>` are exact under negation for NULL (UNKNOWN both ways) and for NaN
(TRUE both ways). Recorded as the next target rather than folded in here, because it needs that
argument tested rather than asserted.

### Item 1272 — `NOT (k = v)` lifts by flipping the operator, 1.65x, and the NaN hole that keeps it equality-only is now DEMONSTRATED rather than argued (DONE)

Item 1271's pricing run left this open. `NOT` of a compare is neither a bare `prop` nor a `compare`,
so `directEqProps` declined the whole chain on it, while the `<>` spelling of the same question
lifted into `cmpProps`. 200,000 vertices, one process, TS estimator rule:

```text
  shape                      before    after    ns/vertex        answer
  NOT (a = 50)                6.467 ms  3.916    32.3 -> 19.6     198000     1.65x
  NOT (a <> 50)                  —      3.206            16.0     2000
  [CTL] a <> 50               3.859     3.631    19.3 -> 18.2     198000
  [CTL] a = 50                3.468     3.193    17.3 -> 16.0     2000
  [CTL] NOT (a >= 50)         6.467     6.172            30.9     100000     EXCLUDED
  [CTL] a < 50                   —      4.334            21.7     100000
  [CTL] bare count(*)         0.001     0.001
```

Both negated equalities now land on their positive twins (3.916 against 3.631; 3.206 against
3.193), and the EXCLUDED ordering shape did not move — which is the control that proves the
restriction is still in force.

This change adds no new carrier: it reuses `eqProps` and `cmpProps`, so unlike items 1269 and 1270
there is no `hasPredicate`, no `mergeFarPreds` and no consumer audit to get wrong.

### ⚠️ THE EQUALITY-ONLY RESTRICTION IS A WRONG ANSWER, NOT A MISSED OPTIMISATION — and it is reachable

The argument is the one `opt::normalize_pred` carries natively (item 1262): `NOT (x >= 2)` is not
`x < 2`, because every ordering comparison against NaN is FALSE here, so the negation is TRUE where
the flip is FALSE. What was not obvious is whether that is REACHABLE in the TS engine at all — a
stored NaN becomes null on ingest (the numeric model), so there is no NaN cell to trip over.

A NaN **param** is not coerced, and that makes it reachable. Measured, then pinned as a test:

```text
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE NOT (n.k >= $x) RETURN count(*)   with $x = NaN    ->  2
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k < $x        RETURN count(*)   with $x = NaN    ->  0
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE NOT (n.k = $x)  RETURN count(*)   with $x = NaN    ->  2
  MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k <> $x       RETURN count(*)   with $x = NaN    ->  2
```

So widening the flip table to `>=` would make the first query answer 0 instead of 2, silently, on a
shape a user can write today. Equality has no such hole: `= NaN` is FALSE, its negation TRUE, and
`<>` answers TRUE too.

(2 and not 4 on a four-vertex fixture, because `nulled` and `absent` are UNKNOWN under both
spellings and a filter keeps only TRUE — they drop either way and cannot be what distinguishes them.
That arithmetic was wrong in the first draft of the test and is now written down beside it.)

### Teeth: 4 mutants, 4 caught, and the important one is caught TWICE independently

```text
  flip-table-widened          CAUGHT  the NaN answer test (Expected 2, Received 0) AND the
                                      ROUTE test — verified separately, since a route assertion
                                      alone would not show what the widening COSTS
  flip-is-identity            CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
  negated-arm-removed         CAUGHT  the ROUTE test (answer-equivalent otherwise)
  negated-eq-family-swapped   CAUGHT  existing Kleene-law fuzz tests
```

### The enum, after five items

`directEqProps` now admits: a bare `prop`, `NOT prop`, a `compare` (equality and ordering), a dotted
compare, a membership (`IN` / `=`-OR-chain, item 1269), a null test (`IS [NOT] NULL` and
`NOT (… IS NULL)`, item 1270), a nested `and` (item 1271), and `NOT` of an equality (this item).
What it still declines, in rough order of how likely a user is to write it: `xor`, `isTruth`
(`x IS TRUE`), `isLabeled`, a function call (`startsWith(n.s, 'x')`), an arithmetic operand
(`n.a + 1 = 2`), a dotted NEGATED compare, and `NOT IN`. None of these has been priced.
